en: The Tripurāsārasamuccaya [a Tantra Scripture] composed by Śrī Nāgabhaṭṭa.
Adorned with the commentary composed by Śrī Govindācārya; [edited] by Paṇḍita Kulapati, holder of the degree of Vidyāvāridhi (V. E.).
Edited and published by Śrī Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara Bhaṭṭācārya. Second edition.
Printed at the Kalikata Press in the city of Kālikātā.
Iṃ 1897. *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*. First Chapter.

May the auspicious pair of lotus-feet of Bhavānī grant you welfare—feet that are served by a swarm of bees consisting of the clearly visible sapphire-blue gems in the crowns of millions of excellent gods led by the bowing Prācīnabarhis; whose mass of filaments is the radiance shining from the tips of her toenails; and which are made resonant by the humming of the swans that are her tinkling anklets. || 1 ||
Having bowed at the feet of Śaṅkara, this commentary on the *Tripurāsāra* is composed by the illustrious Gīrvāṇaśarman, who perceives the essence.
To that quarter, this handful of flowers is perpetually offered with palms joined in reverence, while sweet-sounding bees hum melodiously;
for there the Blessed One, the venerable Universal Emperor, the director of the drama of the universe’s creation and destruction, remains ever awake.

The *Sampradāyadīpikā* commentary on the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*, composed by the teacher Nāgabhaṭṭa—who has bowed his head with a weight of devotion fixed upon the lotus feet of the venerable and supreme Guru Parameśvara; who has attained wisdom through the mutual grace of the supreme teachers; who has reached the further shore of the ocean of all the Āgamas; and who is a master of spiritual knowledge—is now commenced.

Therein, for the purpose of instructing his disciples, he composes an invocation characterized by a benediction, preceded by the remembrance of the Supreme Deity, which makes known the sacred revelation inferred from the conduct of the virtuous, beginning with the words "Prahvaprācīnavarhiḥ" and so forth.

May the pair of glorious lotus feet of Bhavānī bestow auspiciousness upon you. Of what nature are they? They are served by rows of bees that are the manifest sapphire-blue, spotless jewels belonging to the crowns of the multitude of the foremost of the excellent gods, led by Prācīnabarhis. Prācīnabarhis is the lord of the East; those led by him are his chief [deities]. The host of those excellent gods who have become bowed down—that is, humble—is the group of them. The manifest sapphire-blue, spotless jewel belonging to their crowns is itself the bee; they are joined by a row, a line, of such bees.
He speaks of the illumination of the lotus with the words beginning "nakhāmukha" and so forth.
It is such that its filaments are the mass of rays shining from the tips of her nails;
furthermore, it is made resonant by the *haṃsī*—the tinkling anklets—which are making a sound. || 1 ||

Having bowed with devotion to the atoms of dust from the pair of the venerable Guru’s lotus feet—the cause of the bridge across the ocean of worldly existence—I shall describe the sequence of worship for the Kulanāyikā as instructed by my Guru, O Lambodara. (2)

Having bathed according to the rules, with hands, face, and feet thoroughly washed, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), properly wearing clean garments and the sacred thread (yajñasūtra);
facing either the east or the north, and having assumed a firm posture, he should bow down to Gaṇapati and his Guru.

Then, having joined the individual soul (jīva) with the mantra along the path of the central channel (madhyamā-nāḍī) that is difficult to traverse, one should cause it to reach Śiva, who resides in the lotus and is exceedingly subtle;
together with the Haṃsa preceded by the city of Indra and accompanied by the moon, the mantra should effect the destruction of the ashes of the body.
With the wind [of the letter *sa*] and the letter *ā*, one should remove that entire heap of ashes; with the thunderbolt [of the letter *la*], one should inundate the whole world.
One should contemplate oneself as being in the water by means of the jar [of the letter *va*] together with the drop [of the letter *u*]. (5)

Then, having meditated upon that [space] as possessing a circle of radiant light situated within a vast bubble, one should contemplate all the worlds within it, and finally, this very earth within them. (6)
One should intensely visualize here on all sides a Kadamba forest, beautified by blossoming smiles and overflowing with fresh, irreproachable fragrance;
within that, moreover, one should contemplate a great pavilion adorned with clusters of jewels, fashioned of gold and possessing a radiance like the orb of the sun.
It is provided with four gates and four archways made of gems, and above it is marked by a canopy white with the brilliance of the clear lord of stars.

Having paid homage to his chosen deity, he speaks of the salutation to the Guru with the words "with devotion. Having prostrated before the atoms of dust from the lotus-feet of the Guru and having prostrated before Lambodara, I shall describe the method for the propitiation of the Kulanāyikā. Of what nature are those [atoms]? They are the causes of a bridge for crossing the ocean of worldly existence—which is difficult to cross—and the means for crossing it as easily as play. As for the sequence of propitiation, how is it? It is that which has been taught by the Guru, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of the futility of knowing the Āgamas.
Therefore, one must effect the identity of the Guru and the Deity.
As it has been said: "For that high-souled one who possesses supreme devotion for the Deity as well as for the Guru, these very meanings that have been declared become manifest. (2)

Having prostrated before the Guru, the deities, and others, he describes the method of worship, beginning with the words "having bathed. Having bathed according to the rules in a river or similar body of water, having performed the Sandhyā-vandana and other rites, and having sipped water (ācamana) according to the rules while wearing a pre-eminently pure sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta), one should sit facing east on a suitable seat, either a soft cushion or in the Svastika posture. Having bowed to the Guru on the left, Gaṇeśa on the right, and one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) in the center, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) as will be described hereafter.

Having united the individual soul (*jīva*) with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—who resides upon the peak of the thousand-petalled lotus (*puṣkara*) via the path of the *citrā* channel within the *suṣumnā*, which is difficult to traverse—one should, by the power of one's own voice, lead the twenty-four principles (*tattvas*) as well into that state beyond the knots of the *chatra*.

With the mantra *haṃsa* preceded by *amarendra*, and with the mantra *ram*—where *amarendra* is the letter *la*, preceded by which is the letter *ra*, and joined with the moon (*indu*), that is, the bindu—one should reduce one's own body to ashes; the meaning is that one should contemplate one's own body as having become ashes. || 3 || 4 ||

"Sāsyādinātha maruta" means: "Sā" refers to the *visarjanīya*; its "beginning" (*ādi*) is the *bindu*. "Marut" is the letter *ya*. Thus, with the seed-syllable of Vāyu, *yam*, one disperses the heap of ashes; with the letter *la* accompanied by the *anusvāra*, which is the seed-syllable of Indra (*balabhit*), one causes the entire world to be flooded. One should contemplate oneself as being in water consisting of nectar, using a "pot" (*ghaṭa*) accompanied by the *anusvāra*. By the word "pot," water is indicated through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of denoting its substratum.
And by means of that seed-syllable, the letter *va* with an anusvāra, one should meditate upon oneself in water consisting of nectar; such is the meaning. || 5 ||
Regarding the word "tat" (that):
immediately thereafter, one should meditate upon the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), which stands amidst the force of those waters and consists of a mass of shimmering radiance.
Within that, one should contemplate the fourteen worlds, and within them, the surface of the earth; in the center of that, one should visualize a forest of *kadamba* trees.

One should contemplate a great Kadamba forest, new and fresh, adorned with blossoming flowers, possessing an intense and irreproachable fragrance, and endowed with a desirable scent on all sides; within that forest, one should meditate upon a great golden pavilion adorned with jewels, radiant like the orb of the sun. (6–7)
Of what kind is it? It is endowed with four gates and possessed of four jeweled railings.
At each gate stands a shimmering moon, and Gaṇeśa and Kṣetreśa, together with their retinues, are honored there, wearing beautiful jeweled garlands and garments. (Page 4) 8.

One should meditate with a perfectly composed mind upon Hari-haya (Indra) with his vehicle at the eastern gate, Yama at its southern gate, Varuṇa at the western gate, and likewise Kuvera stationed at the northern gate; the space between them crowded with hosts of celestial women devoted to music and other arts, as well as by the chief Gandharvas. 9.
In its center, upon a lion-throne, one should meditate on a lotus adorned with eight petals, radiant as the orb of the rising sun, with beautiful filaments of a rosy hue. 10.
Having fashioned upon its pericarp a lotus joined with the four vowels and endowed with the human vowel (the *anusvāra*) at its end,
one should meditate with the mind upon the deceased thereon, and above that, the Mother of the Three Worlds, the beloved of the Enemy of Tripura, who is worshipped by the Lord of the Gods.

(Verse 12) With a most beautiful nose, lovely eyes, and a charming surface of the cheeks; with a pure crescent moon set within a mass of reddish-brown matted locks; with a forehead as enchanting as the shimmering eighth-day moon; and with a lotus-face as radiant as the full autumn moon.

She whose teeth possess the lovely hue of the Bandhūka flower, who is clothed in garments [red as] Bandhūka, and who has high, rounded breasts; she who is endowed with four beautiful arms, graceful like the stalks of young lotus fibers;
she who is illuminated by three eyes shining like lotus petals with smiles appropriate to that moment; she who wears earrings of the Moon and the Sun, and whose playful side-glances are radiant.
Her slender waist was made radiant by three folds, and her deep navel turned clockwise;
she shone even with a line of body hair, as if with a streak of musk-paste.
Her fine garments are as red as a fresh bandhujīva flower in bloom; her lovely hips are adorned with a girdle of jewels;
her pair of thighs are as thick as the trunk of an elephant; her gait is like that of a noble swan; and the radiance from the soles of her feet surpasses the petals of the heart of a lotus. || 15 ||
One should contemplate that pavilion which has a white canopy shining above it like that [light], and at each door, Gaṇeśa and Kṣetrapāla standing together with their retinues. || 8 ||
Regarding the phrase "in the east": one should meditate upon Indra accompanied by Airāvata at the eastern gate of that pavilion;
and upon Yama accompanied by Mahiṣa at the southern gate.

One should meditate on Varuṇa at the western gate together with his makara vehicle, and on Kuvera at the northern gate with his human vehicle. One should contemplate the interior as being filled with hosts of celestial women engaged in dancing and other arts, who draw along their respective mounts and follow him in every respect.
One should contemplate it as being crowded even with hosts of gandharvas. || 9 ||
Regarding the word "tasya" (of that):
one should contemplate an eight-petaled lotus upon the lion-throne situated in the center of that pavilion.
Of what kind is the lotus? It means it is as red as the solar orb at dawn; likewise, its filaments are red, crimson, and captivating to the mind. || 10 ||

Regarding the word "tat" (that): having placed the seed-syllable *he sauṃ* upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of that eight-petalled lotus, he explains the method for its extraction: *kaṃ* is water, whose seed-syllable is the letter *va*; its fifth is the letter *ha*; *ambu* is the letter *ra*; its fourth is the letter *sa*. Joined with these, there are fourteen *manavas*; the vowel indicated by that number is the letter *au*; at the end of that is the letter *ṅ*. Joined with these two, it becomes *he sauṃ*.
Having meditated upon this very seed-syllable of the seat as the form of Śiva above it, one should then contemplate the Mother of the Three Worlds, the beloved of Hara, seated upon that. || 11 ||
The Lord to be meditated upon describes His own form, beginning with "surucira" and so forth:

[He is] joined with a mass of reddish-brown matted locks in which the moon is bound as its sixteenth part; likewise, He possesses a navel with clockwise whorls—that is, a navel whose surface has clockwise spirals—endowed with a line of body hair resembling a streak of musk-paste; He wears excellent garments as red as a fresh Bandhūka flower, that is, garments as crimson as a blooming Bandhūka blossom; and His slopes of hips are adorned with a girdle of jewels and a cluster of tiny jeweled bells.

Her pair of thighs are as stout as the trunks of elephants; her hips are as massive as the trunks of elephants; the soles of her feet possess a luster that outshines the splendor of the rising sun; the interior of her womb is reddened by the mass of light from the glittering jeweled crowns of the hosts of gods led by Indra, who bow down within her; her two feet are white and red due to the mass of radiance from the glittering jeweled crowns of the multitude of gods approaching the Lord in their state of prostration—their feet being reddened because of the various kinds of gems whose brilliance shines forth.
Thus it is called "muru-cira" (extremely beautiful).

She who possesses a garland of pearls— beautiful and captivating, fashioned from the drops of divine water falling from the interior of a mass of celestial clouds— which, when worn, pervades the circle of the quarters with the brilliance of her own body, a luster produced by the multitude of rays of the sun moving through the sky;
she who wears that garland upon her head, or rather, upon her lovely neck.
She holds a noose and a goad in her upper left and right hands, while her lower two hands display the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness.
She is beautiful, adorned with ornaments fashioned from the finest jewels— *ratnaprakāṇḍa* meaning the most excellent of gems—
and her pair of feet is reddened by the mass of light radiating from the jeweled crowns of the hosts of gods, headed by Indra, who bow down before her.
The beautiful twilight, having swallowed the circle of the sky and the quarters with its own bodily radiance, was possessed of a portion of the splendor of a rain-cloud. || 16 ||

O beloved, she bears a beautiful single-string necklace of pearls—round and released from the bellies of clouds carrying divine waters—which possesses a spotless and tender luster, while her limbs are anointed with yellow sandalwood paste. 17.
Her lotus-hands are raised, holding a noose, a goad, and displaying the gesture of fearlessness; she is beautiful with ornaments fashioned from the finest jewels;
her face is radiant, and the petals of her lower lip are washed by the waves of light from her lovely teeth; she is worthy of worship by the hosts of gods. 18.
Having thus meditated upon Mṛḍānī, the Mother of the Three Worlds, who is one with oneself and is this very wish-fulfilling cow of one’s own lineage,
one should again bring one’s own life-force (jīva) from the swan seated within the cottage of the sky-lotus back into the heart-lotus.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya* composed by the venerable Nāgabhaṭṭa.

She was made beautiful and captivating by the ornaments she wore; her lovely and enchanting lower lip was cleansed by the waves of the rays of light from her radiant teeth—she whose sprout-like reddish lower lip was purified by the wave-like ripples of those brilliant dental rays. She was worthy of being worshipped and served by hosts of gods.

Having meditated upon this Bhavānī, the mother of the three worlds, as one with oneself—that is, as identical with one's own self—one should again lead the individual soul (jīvātman) from the presence of the Supreme Self, who is seated within the lotus-dwelling of the ether, back to one’s own heart-lotus.
According to the natural sense of other texts, one should also lead the twenty-four principles to their respective places by means of the mantra "Haṃsa.
Thus ends the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). 12–19.
The Second Chapter.
One should place the five arrows upon the pairs of fingers beginning with the thumbs and ending with the little fingers, according to the method taught by the Guru; we shall describe them here.

The first seed-syllable consists of the Lord of Mountains (A), joined with the circle of the mouth (U) and Fire (R), followed by the staff (M); that same syllable, with its face [the letter M] pervaded by the Three Forms (O), shall indeed be the second seed-syllable. || 1 ||
The syllable situated within the mouth [A], joined with the Lord of the Gods [U] and the left eye [Ī], followed by the first of the vowels [A];

then the first of the stars [Bha], joined with the enemy of Vṛtra [Śa] and the sixth vowel [Ū], followed by the half-vowel [R] and the Lord of the Night [M], and the fourth consonant [Ta] joined with the letter preceding Ka [Ph]. (2)

Having also assigned the limbs upon the fingers, the preeminent practitioner should perform the ritual placement of the Kalās (kalānyāsa) by means of their abiding in the two hands; he should assign the syllables from *bhaga* to *para*, from *māyā* to the end of *kula* in sequence.
Having placed the triad of seeds together with the half-moon on his own head, he should assign *sānanta*, *mukhavṛttaka*, *kagataka*, and *saṃvartaka* upon the face. || 3 ||

Having thus performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and realized oneself as the nature of the Supreme Deity, one should perform the network of ritual placements (*nyāsajāla*) to be described hereafter; this is stated beginning with the words "the thumb" (*aṅguṣṭha*), etc.
One should place the five arrows upon the fingers of both hands, starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger.

These are the five arrows: *drāvaṇa* (melting), *kṣībhaṇa* (intoxication), *vaśīkaraṇa* (subjugation), *māraṇa* (slaying), and *mohana* (delusion). He states their seed-syllables (*bīja*) in sequence.

Regarding the term *adrīśa*: the letter *da* (the lord of mountains), followed by *u*, then the letter *kha* (the stalk of the mouth), then the letter *ya* (placed there), and then the letter *ra* (fire); joined with these two, *adrīśa* becomes the first seed-syllable (*bīja*) provided it is accompanied by the *daṇḍa* (visarga) and the *anusvāra*. Thus, the seed-syllable becomes *ṭrām*. That same seed-syllable is "overcome" (*ākrānta*) by the letter *ī* (of the three forms); that which has this as its locus becomes the second seed-syllable. By this much, it becomes *drīm*. || 1 ||

He extracts the third seed-syllable as "mukha. "Placed in the mouth" means that the mouth is the *visarga*; within that is the letter *ka*. Of what kind? The King of Gods is Indra; his seed-syllable is the letter *la*, situated above which is placed the left eye, the letter *i*. Together with that, the *visarga* is placed in the mouth; preceded by that [the *visarga*] is the *bindu*. Joined with that—by this much, the seed-syllable becomes *kīm*. He extracts the fourth: the letter *va* preceded by *bha* (the letter *la*), together with the sixth vowel *ū* and the enemy of Vṛtra (Indra), the letter *la*. By this much, the seed-syllable becomes *lvūm*.

He extracts the fifth seed-syllable: *kaṃ* is water; its seed is the letter *va*. Its fourth is the letter *sa*. Preceded by *ka*, it is the *visarga*; together with that, it becomes *sa*. The phrase "the seed-syllable shall be [extracted] everywhere" is to be supplied as an ellipsis. || 2 ||
"Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*)," means: by means of placing [the mantras] upon the fingers and palms of both hands according to the procedure taught for the *sthitinyāsa*.

Then, one should place the four [mantras], beginning with *sūkṣma*, upon the two eyes; then the crescent moon (*sārddhendu*) upon the two ears; and the pair of *bhṛgu* [mantras] together with the two nostrils upon the two cheeks. (Page 8)
The wise one should then place two white [dots] on the chin, with the head marked by the half-moon, followed by the pair of cheeks and the head endowed with the lunar lineage.
One should then place two faces upon the two rows of teeth, with two lips having a crescent-moon-shaped tooth as their covering;
thereafter, one should assign a pair of jars to the two lips, joined with the face and the preceding pair of teeth.

Having placed this [letter] *ra*, joined with the moon (*u*) in the navel, the practitioner, being attentive, should place the letter *ya* (the wind), ending in a vowel (*s*), upon the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
By performing this placement of the *kalās* here according to the prescribed method, one lives for a long time, free from disease and death, and enjoys happiness in this world. (Page 9) 6.
Afterwards, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of either the *mātṛkā* alone upon the body, or accompanied by the power of Rudra.
Then, O lord of practitioners, one should perform the placement of the *vidyā* and the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), preceded by these [previous] placements.
The practitioner of mantra should perform the placement of the knowledge (vidyānyāsa) with the syllables of the root mantra according to the sequence to be described:
he should place the first seed-syllable on the head, the second in the secret place, and the third in the region of the heart.
One should place the three seed-syllables on the right and left eyes, the forehead, the pair of ears, and the mouth;
likewise, the three seed-syllables on the two shoulders, the spinal column, the two elbows, and the navel.

Indeed, Nyāsa is threefold, consisting of creation (sṛṣṭi), maintenance (sthiti), and withdrawal (saṃhāra), according to the distinction of the qualified practitioners—namely the celibate student (brahmacārī), the householder (gṛhī), and the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu).
They say that placing [the fingers] starting from the middle finger and ending with the little finger is called "maintenance" (sthiti).
Placing them starting from the little finger and ending with the thumb is designated as "creation" (sṛṣṭi)-nyāsa.

The placement from the thumb to the little finger is called the placement of withdrawal (saṃhāra-nyāsa). The wise man should perform the placement for maintenance (sthiti) on the body starting from the navel up to the hair.
The placement beginning from the hair down to the feet is designated as the placement of creation (sṛṣṭi-nyāsa).
The placement from the feet up to the hair is called the *saṃhāranyāsa*.
Having thus performed the placement according to one's qualification, one should perform the placement of the *kalās* (energies) as will be described.
He states that very [placement]: *bhaga* is the syllable *e*, beyond that is the syllable *ai*, *māyā* is the seed-syllable *hīṃ* [which is] *bhuvaneśī*.
The end of the *kula-vidyā* is *sauḥ*.
However, the traditionalists (*sāmpradāyikāḥ*) say that the end of *akula*—where *akula* is the letter *a*—is the letter *kṣa*.
One should place these three seed-syllables upon one's own head.

The letter *kṣa* with a nasalization (*sāmantam*) is the *saṃvartaka*; the letter *kṣa* joined with the vowel *ā* (*sānantam*) is situated at the head (*ke*), meaning it is the *bindu*. Therefore, one should place "kṣāṃ" upon the face-circle (*mukhavṛttake*). 3.

Regarding the phrase "sūkṣmādīn" (the subtle and so forth): *sūkṣma* is the vowel *ī*; those for which it is the first are the "subtle and so forth. This means they are accompanied by the moon (*indu*), that is, with the bindu.
Thus, one should place the six [vowels]—*iṃ*, *īṃ*, *uṃ*, *ūṃ*, *ṛṃ*, and *ṝṃ*—in the two eyes and the two ears.
One should place on one's two cheeks the pair of Bhṛgus (the letter *s*) joined with the pair of Sakaras (*sa*), followed by the two nasals (*ṛ* and *ṝ*), and joined with the half-moon (*ṃ*, *ṃ*).

On the chin, one should place the two white ones—the white letter *ṣa*—and the pair of Gaṇḍas (*ḷ* and *ḹ*), which is the lunar family (*śaśikula*) topped with a bindu; thus, one should place the two seed-syllables *ghṛṃ* and *ghṛṃ* on the sides of the chin. 4.

In the two rows of teeth are the two *vakas* (the syllable *va*) and the two *śakas* (the syllable *śa*). The dot (*bindu*) is the crescent moon; the two lips are the *bindu*-endowed *e* and *ai*. These are the letters of Mīrtyu accompanied by the *bindu*.
With that [seed-syllable], one should place *śeṃ* and *śaiṃ* on the two rows of teeth.

On the two lips, one should place the pair of *ghaṭas*; *ghaṭa* means the letter *va*, and likewise the pair of *ya*s is the teeth. *O* and *au* are the mouth; the *visarjanīya* preceded by that is with the *bindu*—the meaning is "with the *bindu*. With that, one should place the two seed-syllables *roṃ* and *rauṃ* on the two lips. (5)
"Rasaṃ nābhau" means:
*ras* consists of the letter *ra*, the vowel *i*, and the half-measure (*ardhendu*) which is the bindu; with that, one should place "ram" at the navel.
*Pavana* consists of the letter *ya*, the final vowel, and the visarga.
With that [mantra], he should place *yam* on the head.
Being free from distraction and attentive, he should thus place the sixteen digits (*kalās*).

He states the fruit of this placement: performing this placement according to the prescribed method, this practitioner, free from disease and death, lives happily through the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*). || 6 ||
After the placement of the sixteen digits (kalās), one should place the Mātṛkā either alone or conjoined with the Rudras and their Śaktis in their respective locations.
The Rudras are Śrīkaṇṭha and the others; the Śaktis are Pūrṇodarī and the others.
The locations for this placement are described in the Śāradā-tantra.
On the forehead, the face, the circular eyes, the ears, the nostrils,
the two cheeks, the lips, the teeth, the head, the mouth, the arms, the palms, the joints, and the fingertips;
on the two sides, the back, the navel, the belly, the heart, and the shoulders.
One should place the letters of the Mātṛkā-mantra in sequence upon the shoulders, the heart first, as well as the pair of hands and feet, and the belly and face;
they are known to consist of skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the letters beginning with *ya* and *ha*, preceded by the knowledge of the Self and the Supreme.
The ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows: "Aṃ, salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha and Pūrṇodarī on the forehead," and so forth.
Immediately after that, one should perform the placement of the Vidyā. || 7 ||
He describes the method for the placement of the Vidyā (vidyānyāsa) with the words "the Vidyā":
one should perform the placement of the Vidyā using the syllables of the root mantra according to the method being described.
One should place the first seed-syllable on the head, the second at the anus, and the third at the heart.
Thus ends one method of ritual placement (nyāsa). || 8 ||
Regarding "savya" (left):
the first two [syllables] are placed on the left and right eyes, the third on the forehead,
and the other [syllable] is the placement on the pair of ears and the mouth.

One placement (nyāsa) is performed on the two shoulders and the back; another placement is performed on the pair of knees and the navel. (p. 10) With the three seed-syllables alone, the wise one should fashion the six faces, beginning with the upward-facing one.
One should worship the limbs with the root mantra, and the five arrows in the secret place, the navel, the heart, the mouth, and the head.
One should place those five Kāmas, whose powers are seen to agitate the three worlds, upon the forehead, the face, the heart, the navel, and the secret organ, as will be described hereafter. (11)
In this context, Kāmarāja, Manmatha, Kandarpa, and Makaraketana are also mentioned; these names were bestowed by the Mind-born One (Manobhava) in successive order. 12.
The fifth syllable is "ka," joined with the end of a pure vowel; the hand (ha) is endowed with the quality of wind (sa);

the sun-sound (ra) follows, as is the sixth sound of Viṣṇu (the horse of Indra, i.e., "i"); then the strength (va), followed by the letter "ta" joined with the upper part (u), and finally Bhṛgu (ga). || 13 ||
(Verse 14) A wise man should place these five crescent-moon-shaped marks upon their heads; indeed, these five objects of desire have been described by me.
For a man who daily applies these [mantras] of Smara to his own body, the three worlds become subject to his will.
Now I shall declare the three seed-syllables (bījas) of Ambikā, whose teaching is honored by the three worlds;
this must be guarded by those who know the family dharma for the sake of grasping it and for their own spiritual accomplishment. 15.

One who possesses this *vāgbhava* mantra, which begins with the letter "ka" (the moon) followed by the word "kāntā" (the beloved), and is joined with the letter situated in the ocean (the fourth) preceded by the letter at the end of the teeth (the thirty-second), becomes a supreme lord of speech on earth and attains perfection in the nectar-like flow of eloquent words. 16.

The mantra known as Kāmākhyā is said to be excellent for directly agitating the world; it consists of the word *kānta* (end of *kā*), joined with the fifth letter of the first class (*ka*) preceded by *kula* (*ha*), ending with *netra* (*i*), and joined with *danta* (*da*).

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) thus: one [placement] on the upper, lower, and right faces, and likewise one on the left, rear, and middle faces. In this manner, one should place the sevenfold root-vidyā. || 9 ||
Regarding "with the three seed-syllables":
one should perform the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the three seed-syllables of the root-mantra, each repeated twice.
As it is stated in the *Tripurārṇava*: "One should perform the placement of the Vidyā (*vidyānyāsa*) from the top down to the supreme face."
"In the upward direction, the east, the left, the back, and the right, respectively"—this refers to the "secret navel.
One should place the five previously mentioned arrows upon the secret navel, the heart, the face, and the head. || 10 ||

He describes the ritual placement of the desires (*kāmanya-nyāsa*) with the words "on the forehead" and so forth: one should place the five desires to be described hereafter upon the aforementioned locations, beginning with the forehead. (11)
He says to them, "Here they are! These five objects of desire have been described by their names. 12.
He states their seed-syllables as "kapañcamam" (the fifth after *ka*).

*Ka* is water; its seed-syllable is the letter *va*. The fifth after that is the letter *ha*. It is joined with the pure fire-seed-syllable *ra*, and with the letter *ī* ending in the eye (*naya*). Thus, it becomes *hnīṃ*. This is the first seed-syllable.
The left eye is the syllable *ī*; the wind is the syllable *ya*. That syllable of its quality is the third syllable, *la*. The hand is the syllable *ka*.
With the syllables *ka* and *la*, the second seed-syllable named Kāmā is formed.
The solar vowel is the twelfth vowel, *ai*; this is the third seed-syllable.
The letter *la* is Hari-haya (Indra); the letter *ra* is Viṣṇu; then the sixth vowel is the letter *ū*;
the letter *va* is Bala; and with the letters *va*, *la*, and *ū*, the fourth [syllable] is formed.
Thus, it is *lvū*.

The first part is the form of *itri*; the subsequent *ī* is Bhṛgu; the *sa* is [Bhṛgu] again. By means of the *sa*, *ta*, *ka*, *ra*, *pha*, and *ī*, the fifth [syllable] is formed; thus, by that, it is "strī. || 13 ||
The wise one should place half-moons upon their heads;

the meaning is that he should place these seed-syllables (bījas), each joined with a nasal drop (bindu) and associated with the names Kāmarāja, Manmatha, Kandarpa, Makaraketana, and Manobhava. || 14 || 15 ||

"Kāntādibhūtapadagam": *ka* is the anusvāra; that which has this as its end is the vowel *au*. The beginning of that [vowel] is the syllable *ga*, meaning the fourteenth syllable from the beginning, which is the letter *a*. Where there is a *kānti* (splendor), namely the visarga, the "beginning of that" refers to the syllable situated at the start, which is the letter *a*; one should extract that. *Kagatārddhacandram*: *ka* is situated on the head (*masta-ke*) of that which has an *arddhacandra* [dot]; the meaning is that it is the anusvāra situated on the head.

The letter *da* is the vowel *o*; that which follows it is the vowel *au*. This is joined with the letter situated in the ocean [the fourth consonant] preceding it. The fourth letter in reverse order is *e*; this means it is accompanied by the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) at the end of *ka*, together with the nasal dot (*bindu*). When these are combined through the process of *vṛddhi*, the great mantra known as Vāgbhava, namely *Aiṃ*, is extracted.
By reciting this seed-syllable (*bīja*) named Vāgbhava, one attains the perfection of speech consisting entirely of nectar.
Because auspicious speech arises from this, it is called Vāgbhava; this is the first seed-syllable of the root mantra. || 16 ||

He extracts the second seed-syllable as "the end of *kāntā*. *Kaṃ* means "on the head," which refers to the nasal dot (*bindu*). Its "end" is the *visarjanīya*, which is *aḥ*. That which ends with this is the letter *ka*. *Kula* is the letter *sa*. Its fifth preceding [letter] in reverse order is the fifth, *la*. Its end is the vowel *ī*. The dental is the *bindu*. Thus, by means of the letters *ka*, *la*, and *ī*, it becomes *kīm*.

Joined with the end of the tooth (da), together with the true end (sa), this entire family known as Sammohana is accomplished; its eight qualities, delight in the vowels, and constant perfection are attained by one who recites it perpetually. || 17 ||
The seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra is the great-souled one known as Dakṣiṇāmūrti; its meter (chandas) is Paṅkti;
and Sarasvatī, whose power is inconceivable and whose feet are worshipped by the hosts of gods, is declared by the wise to be the deity. 18.
The seed-syllable (*bīja*) of this mantra consists of the letter *ra* followed by *da*, joined with *ja*, ending with *sa*, and preceded by *nakulīśa* (the letter *ka*).

The power (*śakti*), however, consists of the letter *kha* preceded by *sākhaṇḍalakarna* (the letter *pa*), joined with half [of the vowel], and ending with *jaivātṛka* (the letter *ma*) and *āna*. 19.

The color of this king of mantras, along with the three worlds, is white; its toll is declared by the sages to be the Gandhāra note, for one whose intellect has reached the further shore of the scriptures.

This origin of the root of the Vidyā has been told by me; it must be understood in every way by those who desire success. Because this primordial Vidyā was cursed by the Goddess, she previously became devoid of life. (21)
(Verse 22) Therefore, Śambhu placed the seed-syllable of Śiva-Śakti above those two previous seed-syllables;
Akula is above Kula, and below the middle [syllable] is Dahana. From that point onward, she became powerful (urjitā).

If the Bhairavīya Muditā, preceded by Kula, should be present among teachers, that very Vidyā bestows fruit swiftly on earth; it is said to be extremely secret among the people who are bound (paśus). 23.
The eighth [letter] of Śiva is the sole primordial seed; the eighth letter before Bhaga is another.
The supreme [seed] ending with the head (Ś) is declared to be the three-syllabled Saṅketavidyā, which is accessible through the mouth of the Guru. 24.

The syllable *kānta* (k), followed by *vānta* (h), joined with the left-eye of the lineage (*vāmanetra*, i), and likewise the *dantakula* (t) with sound (*nāda*, r)—this six-peaked (*ṣaṭkūṭa*) Tripurā-syllable is said to be extremely secret; it is Smara himself in person. 25.
The seed-syllable known as Kāmarāja has been declared and spoken;
by the mere recitation of this mantra, it becomes the agitator of the world.
He extracts the third seed-syllable.

"Ending with the teeth" means that which is placed in the final row of the teeth; thus, the letter *au* (the "tooth-ending") joined with *kula*—one should extract the letter *sa*. Of what nature is it? "With the teeth" (*sadanti*) means accompanied by the *anusvāra*; "entire" (*sakala*) means together with the *visarga*. From the recitation of these three seed-syllables, the attainment of *aṇimā* and the other powers occurs, as does the attainment of *khecarī*. These are: *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, *garimā*, *prākāmya*, *vaśitā*, and *īśitā*.
Attainment, the power to bring desires to fruition—these are the eightfold sovereignty of Śambhu.
This Tripurā mantra consists of these three seed-syllables; the verse concerning its seer (ṛṣi) and other details is easy to understand. || 17 || 18 ||
Regarding the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and power (*śakti*) of this mantra, he says "of that" (*amuṣya*).

"Rada" is the letter *o*; its end is the letter *au*. "Nakulīśa" is the letter *ha*; preceding that is the letter *sa*. "Danta" is the nasal dot (*bindu*). By this, one should know the seed-syllable to be *sauṃ*—this is to be supplied by ellipsis.

As for the power (*śakti*), one should know it to be the letter *ka*, which is at the end of the face (*ānanānta*), accompanied by "Ākhaṇḍala," the letter *ī* preceding the ear; and by "half-life," the half-moon (*ardhacandra*).
And thus, for this mantra, "sauṃ" is the seed-syllable (bīja), "lkīṃ" is the power (śakti), the color is white (śukla), and the musical note is Gāndhāra. || 19 || 20 ||
Regarding the word "Vidyā": this fundamental origin of the Vidyā has been declared by me; this origin should be recited by those desiring the attainment of the Vidyā.
Regarding the word "Devī": this Vidyā was cursed by the Goddess, and therefore it became devoid of vital breath (prāṇa). || 21 ||
Regarding the word "Śiva": because this Vidyā was cursed by Bhavānī, for that very reason, the seed-syllable of Śiva and Śakti, namely *hasa*, has been placed above those two initial seed-syllables.
For it is said in the Saṅkīca: "Contraction is the Supreme Śakti; expansion is the Supreme Śiva."
Śaṅkīca, Vikāśa, and Hasam—these are the two syllables.
Above the final seed-syllable, the letter *ha* of Akula is placed. Below the middle seed-syllable, the letter *ha* of Akula is placed.
Below the middle seed-syllable, the letter *ra* is placed.
Thus, his own knowledge became radiant with splendor. || 22 ||

Regarding the term *bhairavīyam*: this young *vidyā*, being preceded by *akula*—that is, preceded by the letter *ha*—is called *Bhairavī*. That same [mantra], if it is preceded by *kula*—that is, preceded by the letter *sa*—is then called *Vidyā*. It is not to be revealed among the ignorant folk (*paśujana*), or rather, among those who are uninitiated (*adīkṣita*).
Thus, there are these three divisions of this mantra: the first is the Vāgbhava; Bālā is that which begins with Akula, while Bhairavī is that which begins with Kula, known as Vidya. || 23 ||
He states that it is independent and characterized by the three seed-syllables (bījas), ending with Śiva as the eighth.

Śiva is the letter *u*; its eighth is the letter *ai*. Bhaga is the letter *e*; its eighth preceding it is the letter *ī*. "The other" refers to the third [seed-syllable]. "Śiras" is the nasal bindu (*m*); that which ends with this is the letter *au*. This [syllable *au*] characterizes the third seed-syllable; thus, this is the three-syllabled [mantra].
The conventional science is taught through the instructions of the guru; it is understood by the supreme one. || 24 ||

He states another seed-syllable (bīja) with the words "ending in Kānta" (kāntānta). "Ka" is the bindu; its end is the visarga. That which ends in that [visarga] is "ka. That which has "va" as its end is the letter "la. "Akula" is the letter "ha. That which has "sa" as its end is the letter "ra. "Vāmanetra" is the vowel "ī. "Dantī" is the bindu. "Kula" is the letter "sa" together with the anusvāra and the nāda. These six components, as taught in the Tripurātantra, constitute the six-fold seed-syllable (ṣaḍ-kuṭa) consisting of six letters. This mantra, which must be guarded with extreme care, is Smara himself along with his consort. 25.

He who recites the mantra after joining the first seed-syllable with the middle one, and the middle with the last, and the last with the end, shall have all the hosts of beings within the three worlds brought under his control and made partakers of his sovereignty. (26)

Having placed the first seed-syllable at the beginning and the final seed-syllable at the end, and the middle syllable in the middle and at the beginning, the lord of practitioners who daily recites this mantra becomes liberated while living and attains divine perfection. || 27 ||

One should recite this king of mantras, which causes the delusion of the entire world, interspersed with the Mātṛkā letters, both in direct and reverse order. Whether joined with the god Haṃsa (the *praṇava*) as a whole, or separately, or even otherwise, one endowed with divine qualities attains unsurpassed and perfect success (*siddhi*). || 28 ||
This mantra, endowed with the syllable *haṃsa* and delighting the hearts of all the world—any man who recites it with a steady and pure mind quickly attains perfection. (29)

This lotus, whose middle and final vowels are elided, joined with Īśa (H) and the rest, together with the bindu and nāda, shining with "nigama" at the beginning and "namaḥ" at the end—this is the deity that has entered the heart. 30.
This Vidyā, which grants all desires, is honored by the three worlds and bestows both heaven and liberation; it is more secret than the secret, O Mahodara, and is the leader of the Yoginīs.
It is declared to be the birthplace of Sarasvatī, the bestower of the perfection of good fortune, and it produces immediate conviction even when recited but once upon this earth. (31)

Since this [Vidyā], though constantly recited, does not bestow accomplishment at all while she has entered the state of sleep—yet if awakened, the Vidyā suddenly bears fruit as an illuminator—therefore, I shall here declare the Vidyā that is exceedingly secret. (32)

Now, he states the different mantras to be recited according to the distinction of desires, beginning with the word "ādyaṃ" (the first). Having joined the first seed-syllable (*bīja*) in the place of the middle seed-syllable, the middle seed-syllable in the place of the initial seed-syllable, and the final [seed-syllable] in its own place—one who recites this mantra in this manner brings under his control all living beings existing in the three worlds and attains sovereign power (*aiśvarya*). This is one method. || 26 ||

Another says: "The first. Having placed the first seed-syllable at the end, the last at the middle, and the middle at the beginning, he who recites this mantra every day becomes liberated even while living and attains that which is the perfection of the divine ones. || 27 ||
Regarding the phrase "the king of mantras":
he who recites this supreme mantra both in regular order and in reverse order, having placed it within the *mātṛkā*, partakes of divine qualities and attains incomparable accomplishment (*siddhi*).

In that regard, the sequence is as follows: having uttered the mantra, one should utter the letter *a* at the end; then, having again uttered the mantra, one should utter the letter *ā*. In this manner, one proceeds through the letters up to the letter *la*.

Having performed the recitation with the mantra interspersed, one should again utter the letter *kṣa* alone, devoid of the mantra, as the representative [of the final letter]. Then, in reverse order from the letter *la* down to the letter *a*, one should recite each [letter] with the mantra interspersed. The meaning is that for those performing the recitation with the garland of the letters of the Mātṛkā in this manner, the recitation becomes limited to a count of one hundred in a single round.
This has been explained by Rāghava Bhaṭṭa in the *Śāradātilaka*:
"Having recited the Mātṛkā from the letter *a* to the letter *ha*, one should recite the mantra in the middle."
Oṃ, salutation! Then one should recite the *mātṛkā* beginning with the letter *ca* and ending with the letter *kṣa*.
Thereafter, one obtains incomparable success (*siddhi*). This, however, is another method.
One should recite the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the root mantra, beginning with "haṃsa deva," by joining them with the letters *ya* and *sa*.

"Only the other [seed]" means that one should recite only the first and middle seed-syllables of the Śrīmūla-vidyā, and then join the final seed-syllable with the syllables *haṃ* and *sa*, and thus chant it—this is the meaning. || 28 ||

Regarding "the haṃsa of consonants": having elided the *a*, the *anusvāra*, and the final *visarga* situated between the letters *ha* and *sa*, one should join the pure consonant alone with the *vidyā* and recite it; he too attains the unsurpassed *siddhi*. As it has been said: "The wise one should recite it, having strung together each individual syllable with the *haṃsa*. (29)

"Kamala" (the lotus): one should extract the very form of the lotus. Of what nature? That in which the middle and final vowels are elided—that is, devoid of the final vowel of the letter *ma*, it is simply *lka*.

"Īśa" is Śiva, which is the vowel *u*; its beginning is the vowel *ī*. Together with the *bindu* and *nāda*, that [is joined]. Thus, by means of the letters *ka*, *la*, *ī*, the *bindu*, and the *nāda*, one obtains *lkīṃ*, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) named Kāmākhya.

The syllable *praṇava* (Om) is at the beginning, followed by the word "namaḥ" as the essential form; with the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*) placed in the middle between the *praṇava* and "namaḥ," there arises the four-syllabled Vidyā known as Hṛdayā.
Having spoken incidentally, he now praises Bhairavī. || 30 ||

Regarding "knowledge" (vidyā): that knowledge which exists here on this earth belongs to the Yoginīs; it brings about great prosperity, generates the knowledge of reality (tattva), is a cow of plenty (kāmadughā) bestowing desired objects, and is exceedingly difficult to attain.
Even by reciting it just once, it becomes true and grants direct realization. || 31 ||

Regarding the word *yataḥ*: because this Vidyā has reached seven stages (*saptāvasthā*), therefore, even by reciting it repeatedly, one attains accomplishment (*siddhi*). [The syllables are as follows: the first is the flower-giver (*puṣpamuc*) [the letter *da*]; then the other two syllables are *va* and *ra*; then the long vowel at the end of *vārisakha* [the letter *ai*]; likewise, the two ending in *dhā* [the letters *sa* and *lo*] with the vowel *a*. [Note: The reconstructed sequence based on the provided fragments is: *da-vā-ra-ai-sa-lo-a*.]
This Vidyā, which illuminates the seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbhava), is the very Pārijāta creeper longed for by Sarasvatī herself; it has been uttered by me in its original syllables. 33.
Brahmā is accompanied by Śakra’s eye; Bhagā is joined with Meṣa; Nādinī is with Kāntānta; Sabhaga is with Sapūṣaṇa; Atodhānta is with Tvim; Eṣa is with Sadṛk;
Kāla is joined with Ananta; Viyat is with Sadaśana; Saṃvartaka is with Bhīṣaṇā; Kamalāsana is with Sākrūra; and Vaiśvānara is likewise with Śiva. (34)
This six-syllable mantra is the awakener of the seed-syllable of Manmatha;
it suddenly agitates those dwelling in the heavens, on the earth, and in the intermediate spaces. (35)

This Vidyā, which illuminates the supreme seed-syllable, consists of Sāvitrī with ten thousand faces, Mahādikālī reaching to the end of space, whose extremity is adorned by a crescent moon; it is joined with Mohinī, Sarasijabhū (Brahmā), Yuta (Viṣṇu), and Agni (Rudra). 36.
Whichever mantra is declared here to be the illuminator of a particular seed-syllable, the best of practitioners should utter that very mantra before it;
he should likewise correctly perform the sixfold ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa) upon the faces [of the deity]. 37.
For the man who thus performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the limbs of the Vidyā upon his own body, the three worlds come under his control;
his sins are instantly pacified, and the Rākṣasas along with the Pannagas tremble in fear. 38.
This form of the mantra has been described by me; it is obtained in every way from the mouth of the Guru.
Without the grace of the Guru, this mantra on the surface of the earth does not bestow accomplishment. || 39 ||
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya* composed by the illustrious Nāgabhaṭṭa.

If she does not grant [the fruit] when she is awakened, then she grants the fruit by force; for this reason, I shall declare her secret and hidden *dīpanī-vidyā*. It is remembered that "secret" (*rahas*) refers to that which is to be concealed. 32.
Regarding this, he states "the flower" (*puṣpa*) to explain the illumination of the first seed-syllable.

Water is the "flower" of the clouds; its seed-syllable is the letter *va*, which one should utter. The "other" is the letter *ra*; the "beginning of *dava*" refers to the letter *da*, which is the initial of the word *dava*. Then those two letters, *ra* and *da*, followed by the "long" [vowel] together with *ā*—that is, the water-seed-syllable *vā*—is "with the end of *kha*" (*khānta*); since it exists with the letter *ga* at its end, it is the letter *śa*, which one should extract.

The letter *va* is long in the word *apsu*; therefore, it does not become *vāg-vā*. When joined with the sounds of the world (*loka*), there are two letters ending in *dh*, and that which has *dh* at its end is the letter *da*. The end of *dh* is the letter *la*; thus, *da* and *la* are indicated by the word *loka*, which signifies the number three. Joined with that [third] vowel *i*, this results in: *vada vada vāgvādini*. This eight-syllabled mantra is the science that kindles the seed-syllable characterized by *Vāgbhava* (Aiṃ); for the arising of the qualities of Sarasvatī, it is like a wish-fulfilling creeper for the desired object. || 33 ||

He states the second seed-mantra for illumination as "Brahmā," etc. Brahmā is the letter *ka*; joined with Śakra (Indra), which is the letter *la*, and with *dṛś* (the eye), which is the letter *i*—the short vowel being taken here because it is the first [of the vowels]—one should extract [the syllable *kli*]. Nādinī is the letter *la*; it is to be extracted as conjoined with Bhaga, which is the letter *e*, and Meṣa, which is the letter *la*. Then, one should extract the letter *sa*, which has *kha* at its end (*sakha*), followed by that which has *sa* at its end (*saka*)—meaning the letter *bha* together with Bhaga (*e*) and Pūṣan (*la*)—and immediately after that, the letter *da*, which has *dh* at its end (*dhānta*). Thus, the mantra is *klīṃ bleṃ dhaṃ*.
The letter *la* is the form of Īśvara, resembling [the letter *i*] when joined with *i*;
one should extract the letter *ma*, which is Kālī.
One should extract the letter *ha*, which is Viyat (space), conjoined with Ananta (the letter *ā*).
The letter *kṣa*, which is "possessing teeth" (*sadaśanaḥ*) and accompanied by the vowel *o* (*okāra*), namely *kṣo*, is to be extracted.

The letter *bha* is "terrifying" (*bhīṣaṇaḥ*). The letter *ka*, which is "the lotus-seated one" (*kamalāsanaḥ*), accompanied by the vowel *u* (*ukāra*) and followed by *sākrūra* (the letter *sa* with the *anusvāra*), namely *kṣaṃ*, is to be extracted together with that same *u*. By this much, it becomes: *lkinne lkedini mahākṣobhaṃ kuru* ("O you who moisten, O you who cause trembling, create great agitation!"). || 34 ||
This eleven-syllable vidyā, ending with the letter *va*, serves as the illuminator for my own seed-syllable, which is the middle seed-syllable. || 35 ||
He states the illumination of the third seed-syllable with the words "Sāvitrī" and so forth. By the word "Sāvitrī," the syllable *Oṃ* is indicated; "Mahādikālī" means Mahākālī.

The first letter of that [name], the letter *ma*, is indicated. It is joined with the "mouth," which is the syllable *śrī*. With that, "Vyoma" is the letter *ha*; one should extract that ending in the *anusvāra*. By the "enchanting one," the letter *u*, the "lotus-born earth," the letter *ka*, should be extracted.

Then follows *mohinī*, then *ataḥ*, then *agniḥ*, and then *rephaḥ*; by this much, the seven-syllable mantra "Oṃ mahāmokṣaṃ kuru" is declared as the illuminator (*dīpanī*) of the final seed-syllable. || 36 ||
He explains in what manner the application of illumination (*dīpanayoga*) occurs by saying "yā yasya" (which [vidyā] belongs to which [bīja]):
whichever *vidyā* is said to be the illuminator of whichever *bīja*, one should first utter that *vidyā* before that *bīja*. || 37 ||

Regarding the application of illumination (*dīpanīyoga*) among the various *nyāsas*, he says "vidyā" and so forth. This means that in the *nyāsas* of the *vidyā*, the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) *nyāsa* should be joined during the recitation of the *nyāsas*.

When this is done, the *vidyā* becomes awakened. For a person who thus performs the *nyāsa* of the limbs of the root-vidyā mantra upon his own body, the three worlds come under his control and all sins are immediately pacified. (38)
Chapter Three (pṛ0 18).
Now, this body is stated by the wise to be ninety-six finger-breadths (aṅgula) in length when measured by one's own fingers.
However, according to those who know yoga, the wind known as *prāṇa* is considered to be greater than the body by twelve finger-breadths. || 1 ||

In this world, that man who, through constant practice, brings the vital breath (prāṇavāyu) under his control from every limb and attains equilibrium with his body upon this earth—he is the most excellent knower of yoga, honored by the wise. (2)
In this body, fourteen principal channels (nāḍīs) are traditionally taught; even among those, there are only three:
Iḍā, Suṣumnā, and the one called Piṅgalā. Among these channels, the Suṣumnā alone is the most important. (3)
The channel named *iḍā* is situated on the left side of the body, and on the right is the channel named *piṅgalā*.
Between these two, resting against the spinal column, stands the *suṣumnā*, which reaches as far as the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). (Verse 4)
Situated within the interior of the Suṣumnā is the Citra-nāḍī, radiant with five colors and joined by the five deities;
within that is the extremely subtle Brahmarandhra, resembling a thread shimmering in the midst of a lotus fiber. || 5 ||

This nature of the Māyā-mantra has been described; if it is obtained from the Guru, then the supreme accomplishment is attained. Otherwise, without the grace of the Guru, this mantra will not be accomplished. || 39 ||
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya-ṭīkā*.

Having thus explained the nature of the mantra, which is the essence of all human goals (*puruṣārtha*) for practitioners, [the author] now begins to describe the methods and specific details of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), which is a limb of Yoga, in order to remove obstacles to other human goals, starting with the words "Now, this body... and so forth.
This body is said by the learned to be ninety-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length; that is, the measurement of this very body is according to its own finger-breadths.
The wind known as *prāṇa* is considered to extend twelve finger-breadths beyond the exit points of the body; it moves as far as the limit of twelve finger-breadths. || 1 ||

"Here" means: here on this earth, through constant practice—that is, by perpetual cultivation—a person leads this vital breath (prāṇavāyu) from its state of being inferior to the body toward pervasiveness across all limbs;
or he brings about equality with the body, or pervasiveness throughout the limbs of the posture. He is thus honored among the practitioners of yoga upon this earth. ||2||
He shows that there are fourteen channels (nāḍīs) which serve as the support for the vital breaths (prāṇas).
As it has been said: "The body is the support of the channels; the channels are the support of the vital breath.
In this body, there are fourteen channels that are primary, yet among those fourteen, four are traditionally held to be the most important. (3)
He states the names of those three:
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā; and among these three as well, Suṣumnā alone is the principal one.
The names of the fourteen channels (nāḍīs) are as follows: Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumnā, Sarasvatī,
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Supūṣā, and Yaśasvinī.
Alambuṣā, Kuhū, Śaṅkhinī, Citriṇī,
Viśvī, Darī, and Viśvamukhī— these fourteen indeed pervade [the body].

Among these three as well, there are three principal ones in which yoga is established; even among those, Suṣumṇā alone is the most principal. And she, resting upon the spinal column at the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta), stands straight, facing downward, as the support of all.

The so-called *ādhāra* is a lotus situated two finger-breadths above the perineum (*neḍhrā*) and two finger-breadths below the root of the penis; it is four finger-breadths in length and breadth, one finger-breadth in height, enveloped by the elements such as skin, consisting of four petals, and white in appearance. In the center of its pericarp is a triangular womb (*yoni*). In the middle of that is the power (*śakti*) consisting of consciousness (*cinmayī*), known as Kuṇḍalī, who is the material cause and the source of all phenomenal manifestation; she, who is the root of the sun, moon, and fire, revolves in the form of the three coils and so forth.

The channel named Suṣumnā, which is triangular and upright, hangs from the spinal column—known as the "vīṇā-daṇḍa" (the backbone)—at its upper portion and remains standing vertically until it reaches the *brahmarandhra*.
Thus, the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi* states:
"On the outer side of the spinal column, above the heads of the Moon and the Sun..."
Or rather, in the middle—the Suṣumnā is situated there in the center of the three, having a variegated form.
Right there, the five lotuses beginning with the root-lotus are strung together; they have the form of buds and are supported by the Ḍākinīs and the others.
Having completely covered the root-gate, she stands in the form of Māga;
released by the wind, the firm Citrā leads [the breath] from there.
She is exceedingly radiant with the crest of the intensely blazing Kāma.
Awakened in each successive wheel, she unites the individual soul (jīvātman) with the Supreme Family (pare kule);
through that union, it partakes of immortality for a long time.
Having pierced the void, the Moon and the Sun proceed to the tip of the nose.
Having embraced the great lotus below with the *suṣumṇā*,
having turned back toward the middle of the nose, the *citrā* [nāḍī] reaches that [point];
then, having pierced upward through the *liṅga*.
(Verse 6, p. 20) This very Brahmasūtra is the immortal, singular cause that has become the life-force for embodied beings;
those of noble mind, the ancient sages, call it the "Divine Path."
(Verse 7, p. 21) Since this moon-crested one moves within the iḍā, nectar is declared to be on the left side;
since this sun moves within the piṅgalā, poison is said by the lords of sages to be on the right side.

One should know that the rising of the bodiless [breath] of men occurs in the bulb (kanda) within one's own belly; its dissolution indeed takes place through the nose at the tip of the sun’s rays (the tip of the index finger), as well as at the junctions of the eastern and western [halves of the day].

One should know its constant downward movement as birth and its upward movement as dissolution, as well as night and day, and likewise the moon in the downward movement and the movement of the sun in the upward movement.
When the deity has entered the lunar channel (nāḍī), one should then perform rites such as those for pacification (śāntika);
when the wise one has entered the solar channel during fierce rites (raudra), and during auspicious or mixed rites, one should enter both channels. 9.
Then, [she saw] the other lotuses;
she who desires the longing for the upward movement of the vital currents, who bestows liberation,
who is bound by the unseen destiny of life, and who is steadfast in the supreme proximity.
"He knows this Veda and, having pierced through, goes to the supreme state," and so forth in many places; also in the *Yogārṇava*:
By that very side of the peak of Mount Suraśṛṅga, proceeding gradually to the left, the two channels, Sūryā and Candramas, have gone to the two nostrils.
Having pierced through the second [channel] between them at the center of the lotus in the Suṣumnā,
she has reached the Brahma-randhra, having pierced through the sky and the abode of Bhūḥ.
Having covered that door with ease, the radiant power of the earring [remains];
the Goddess, fallen under the sway of sleep, resembles a slumbering serpent.
On the left and right corners of the triangle, on the left and right sides of the Suṣumnā, the Iḍā and Piṅgalā are firmly established.

Between those two, the channel named *iḍā*, having assumed the form of a female serpent, embraces the *suṣumnā* at the base of the *liṅga* and proceeds to the right side; taking that same shape, it again proceeds to the left side at the region of the navel.
Then, embracing the region of the heart once more, it proceeds to the right side. Thereafter, embracing the root of the left knee, it goes to the left nostril.

Thus, Piṅgalā, arising from the right side, embraces the Suṣumṇā and proceeds to the right nostril. A channel named Sarasvatī is situated rising from the front part of the base of the Suṣumṇā as far as the tip of the tongue; some, however, maintain that there are three.
These are the three Suṣumṇās in which Yoga is established.
And those [channels] emerge from the two nostrils and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra);
Sarasvatī and the other three emerge from the opening of the mouth.
Among them, one is the progenitor of sound, and another is the carrier of the musical notes.
One is the support of the tongue (rasanā), another is the auspicious one that flows through the animals (tiryagvahā);
others six have emerged from the openings of the eyes, the organs of action, and the marrow. Śaṅginī is connected to the navel, while that which flows through the heart is restrained.
By means of this [channel], the embryo situated within the womb is nourished with the essence of food and other nutrients.

From these very channels, three hundred thousand channels arise in the manner of branches and sub-branches. To address the disciple’s inquiry as to which channel remains where, he says: the channel named *Iḍā* rests upon the left side of the body; the channel *Piṅgalā* occupies the right part; and between those two channels, resting upon the spinal column of the body and extending to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), the *Suṣumnā* is situated.
Within the *suṣumnā* resides the *citrā* channel, radiant with five colors—white, red, and so forth—and joined with the five deities: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
As it has been said:
"Brahmā, Janārdana, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva."
And the presiding deities of the five elements are situated within the beginningless and endless expanse known as Citrā.

"Brahman. This very Brahma-sūtra is the life-breath of embodied beings; having become the living soul (*jīva*), it is the sole cause of immortality. In this very [sūtra] death is known not to exist—this is the meaning.
That Brahma-sūtra which the ancient sages call the "divine path" (*divyamārga*)—the meaning is that it is precisely that path which leads to *nirvāṇa*. || 6 ||

Regarding the phrase "in the iḍā": this moon (the cool-rayed one) moves in the channel named iḍā on the left; if it moves from the left side, it releases nectar. Piṅgalā moves from the left and so forth, and she rests upon the right side; that side is designated as "poison" because the sun moves through the sky there. Through the regulation of the vital air (vāyu), [the practice] succeeds. || 7 ||

He states the knowledge of its arising and destruction with the words "one should know. A wise person should know the rising—that is, the emergence—of the wind within the body at the *kanda*, the root-source, the foundational wheel (*cakra*).
Likewise, in the foundational wheel situated above the anus and below the generative organ, the wind remains; it perishes twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) outside the nose.
This refers to those two locations during the morning and evening twilights: from the *kanda*, the aforementioned number [of breaths] goes out twelve finger-breadths beyond the nose.
"Subsequently it comes"—these two states, arising and dissolution (laya), as well as destruction, are to be known by those very [states].
Regarding the "support":
one should know the downward movement of the breath as night, and the upward movement as day.
For it has been said: "Day indeed is prāṇa, and night is apāna. Thus, one should know the moon as having a downward movement and the sun as having an upward movement.
Therefore, in the Yogārṇava it is stated: "The moon rains while facing downwards; the remaining [sun] remains with its face upwards. (8)

He explains which actions should be performed during which wind: "In the moon-channel" (*tuṣārāṃśunāḍī*) means that when the *iḍā* wind is flowing, one should perform actions that produce peace. When the sun-channel, *piṅgalā*, flows by day or night, one should perform fierce and terrible actions.
[This refers to] the cool rays of the moon.
(Verse 10) A wise person should observe the arising of the elements in both nostrils: when the sharp-witted one touches the base of the nose, there is the arising of earth;
when the deity [the breath] touches below, it is water; when it moves upward, fire; when it touches transversely, wind; and when it is touched all around, it is the path of the air.

The rising of the earth is praised for subjugation and immobilization; the rising of water is auspicious for rites of pacification, prosperity, and the like; furthermore, the rising of fire is excellent for the day’s activities.

For the performance of killing, rending, and so forth against an enemy, as well as for expulsion and causing flight, the rising of wind is beneficial; for pacification and neutralizing poison, the rising of space is favorable. (11)

If, at the onset of *dharaṇī*, a messenger approaches those afflicted by disease and suddenly asks, "Is there no affliction born of illness here? then even though properly treated, the suffering does not reach pacification. || 12 ||
When water arises, disease attains pacification; when wealth arises, death indeed occurs. Likewise, upon the rising of wind or space, there is the destruction of ailments in no time at all. (13)

If the deity is in the southern part and a sick man stands on the right and asks as an inquirer, that man will live long and free from disease. But if the Lord is situated on the left and a woman, her body afflicted by pain, stands on the left and asks, she will be freed from her ailment and live for a long time.
When the deity has departed, if a man stands on the right side and asks about the left side,
the wise declare that even from such a reversal, the resulting class of diseases is indeed difficult to cure.
If the querent asks while the deity is "entered," the man lives free from disease;
but if the deity has "gone out," he departs for the city of the King of the Dead due to that very same illness.

If this Lord is present within during all undertakings, there shall be the attainment of one's desires; however, if the Lord is outside, even though He is the master of inauspiciousness, one should know that the fruit of action—whether auspicious or inauspicious—is still realized. 17.
The meaning is that it is because the wind is harsh and piercing.
In both cases—whether the wind is situated in the northeast (Īśāna) or elsewhere—one should perform rites of pacification (śāntika) and fierce rites (raudra) respectively. 9.

Regarding the phrase "of the elements" (*bhūtānām*): in both cases—whether white or black—one should observe and ascertain the emergence (*udaya*) of the elements, namely earth, water, fire, air, and ether.
Among those elements, when the emergence of earth is praised in the air—that is, when the movement takes the form of a staff (*daṇḍākāra*)—then one should know the emergence of earth.
When the divine air touches below, one should know the emergence of water. When the air moves upward, one should know the emergence of fire, which carries heat.

One should know that when the breath touches both sides [of the nose] transversely, there is the arising of air (vāyu). When the pervasive air flows through both nostrils together, one should know that there is the arising of space (ākāśa), the path of the wind. || 10 ||
He states the fruit of this knowledge as follows: "By the word 'vaśya' (subjugation), one should perform rites that produce subjugation and rites that produce paralysis when Mars (Bhūmi) rises;
and when Jupiter (Jalabhṛt) rises, one should perform rites that produce pacification and rites that produce nourishment."
The rising of the fire element is auspicious for actions that involve killing and the like;
the rising of the wind element is auspicious for uprooting a fortress and destroying a city;
and the rising of the space element is auspicious for neutralizing poison and for conciliation. || 11 ||
He states the question regarding the earth:

"When the earth rises, a messenger arrives and asks, 'Will such-and-such a person be free from disease?'—then it should be said that the affliction born of illness, even if its remedy has been applied immediately, will forcibly bring about peace.
When water rises, if he asks, then the disease goes to peace.
If one asks when the Vasu-daya of Agni arises, then death occurs for the one afflicted by disease;
"Vasuhutāśana" is [defined] in the Viśvaprakāśa.
If one asks when the [Vasu-daya] of Vāyu arises, then the meaning is that there is death.
If one asks after the rising of Ākāśa, then the destruction of diseases occurs with great speed. 12, 13, 14.
He states another variety:

when the wind has joined with the south wind, if the messenger stands there constantly and asks [the question], then the person afflicted by disease lives for many three-hundred years free from illness.
When a woman is afflicted by disease, the wind is situated on the left side; if the messenger asks while facing that direction, then she lives for a long time after the disease. || 15 ||
Regarding the term "deva":

if the messenger asks when the wind has moved from the left region to the right side, then one should declare that recovery from illness will be achieved with difficulty. If the messenger asks while the wind is moving toward the right, but he is situated on the left side, then one should say that recovery from illness will be achieved with difficulty. Regarding the term "antargata" (entered within): [the same applies].
If the questioner asks when the breath has entered within, then he lives free from disease.

If he asks when the breath has gone outside twelve finger-breadths from the nose, then by that very [sign] he goes to the abode of Yama due to that same illness. (Page 24) At the beginning of the Darśa, the deity arises in the left nostril for three days.
Then, for three days on the other side, the lunar day (tithi) remains full in this very same manner. || 18 ||
Then, beginning from the lunar days that constitute the junctions of the fortnights, the Lord rises for three days;
in the right hemisphere for three [days], and in the left until the new moon (kuhu)—thus one should observe it in this manner. 19.
In this world, for men, there occurs an affliction by disease through the reversal of one side [of the body];
in the case of both [sides], there is the loss of kinsmen and friends; and in the third period, death shall occur from exhaustion.
(Verse 21) When, due to the power of time, the vital breath (samīraṇa) arises in the self having abandoned its natural state,
then one should restrain the breath and compress it so that it reaches the side of the self in which it was situated.
Only two sustain the entirety of time: the sun and the friend of the night-lotus (the moon). Suṣumnā, however, is the enjoyer of this entire time, consisting of both night and day.

Then, the wise practitioner should gradually apply effort according to the prescribed rule for the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa), by means of the internal pathways of the purified channels. 23.

With diligence, free from drowsiness, and with his mental faculties fixed on the root of the Kālāgni fire, he should slowly fill his abdomen with air through the path of the moon (the left nostril). || 24 ||
Then, with a pure mind, one should retain the wind for sixty-four mātrās once it has filled [the body];
one should exhale it slowly through the radiant [aperture] outside, and hold it inside for half of those [mātrās]. || 25 ||
"The patient departs.
He explains the purpose of that in another context:

if the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has entered within the Lord (*Īśvara*), there is the attainment of the desired success in this undertaking; however, if it has gone outside, having moved more than twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), all undertakings perish.
He says: "For how many days and where does he stay? (16-17)

It should be undertaken as follows: the new moon (*darśa*) itself is the first lunar day (*tithi*). That *pratipad* which has the new moon as its first [day] is the "new-moon-first *pratipad*. By means of that, in the case of the three lunar days beginning with the bright fortnight’s *pratipad*: in the left [channel], the fourth and so forth; in the right, the seventh and so forth; in the left, the tenth and so forth; in the right, the thirteenth and so forth. In the case of the dark fortnight: in the left, beginning with the *pratipad*; in the right, the fourth and so forth; in the left, the seventh and so forth; in the right, the tenth and so forth; in the left, the thirteenth and so forth; and in the right, [the sequence continues].

Now, immediately following this, having begun from the first day of the dark fortnight (the *śulka*) which serves as the starting point, the number of days has already been stated—namely, that for three days the wind blows from the southern side—and in this manner, one should observe the belly of the person. 18–19.
Regarding the phrase "of one":

if there is a reversal of the wind in one side [of the nostril], then that person suffers the onset of disease. If the wind flows through the left nostril for three days starting from the first day of the bright fortnight (śukla-pratipad), and if during that time it occurs in the right nostril—likewise, if such a reversal persists up to fifteen days—then there is an affliction by disease. If the reversal lasts for exactly one month, there is calamity for friends; if the reversal lasts for forty-five days, that person meets with death.
It is a natural principle that when there is a deviation from the normal state of the vital air (vāyu), disease and other ailments arise. || 20 ||
He explains how an auspicious rising can occur when there is a contrary rising with the words "yadā" (when).

When, by the power of one's own past impressions (*adṛṣṭa*), the wind rises in a contrary manner, then, having first understood this, one should press the breath so that it goes into the other nostril. || 21 ||

"Only two"—the friend of the night-lotus (kumudabandhu), namely the moon, and the sun; these two sustain [all] time throughout its entirety. Time consists of day and night, characterized by the division of day and night. Suṣumnā alone, and no other channel (nāḍī), is the "sustainer" (bhoktrī)—that is, the devourer (bhakṣikā). The meaning is that, having attained the state of being a form through the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of reality inherent in the power of consciousness (citkalā), it becomes the devourer of everything. || 22 ||

"Then," [it is said]: at that time, the practitioner, having gradually cleared the internal pathways of the channels (*nāḍī*), should apply effort toward the restraint and regulation of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) very slowly, according to the method already described. || 23 ||
He describes that very method in the verse beginning with "the path of the cool-rayed one" (śītāṃśumārga).
By means of the path of the cool-rayed moon—that is, through the left channel (vāmanāḍī)—one should fill one's own abdomen with the vital airs in a measure of sixteen mātrās.
One whose drowsiness and sleep have departed is thus one whose mental fluctuations are fixed upon the root of the Kālāgni.
He by whom the mental fluctuations—the very activity [of the mind]—are fixed at the root of Kālāgni, which is the Mūlādhāra. || 24 ||
Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then):

one should retain the filled air for up to sixty-four mātrās; one should obstruct its coming and going through the solar path (bhāsvat) by means of the right [nostril]. Then, with half of that—thirty-two mātrās—one should emit (retayet) that air restrained within. || 25 ||
Therefore, the wise man should perform the opposite, and then again the opposite of that;
by this method, O Maruts, one who is well-disposed should constantly practice perfect self-restraint. (26)
That which produces perspiration during the breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) is declared the lowest;
that which causes the body to shake is the middling; and the highest is that which effects the abandonment of the earth by the body for men.
The wise person, composed in mind, should perform breath control according to the rules for as long as the quality of the supreme breath control manifests upon this earth. (28)
This breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is said to be "without the womb" (vigarbha), which destroys all evils; when joined with the "womb" (garbha), it yields a hundredfold fruit.

That which is devoid of recitation (japa) and meditation (dhyāna) is declared to be "without the womb," whereas that which is released [from those] is called "with the womb" by the sages devoted to yoga who surround it. 29.

The self-controlled twice-born man who, being pure, performs sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) accompanied by the syllable Om (praṇava) every day at dawn and at dusk—he purifies himself; for these [prāṇāyāmas] burn away the mass of cotton-like sins accumulated here from the striking of weapons and other such acts. 30.
These six protect one here from the mass of sins accumulated in other births within six months;
and after a year, they indeed reveal that singular state of Brahman known as Acyuta.
