In this world, that mortal who, possessing a steady mind, abandons both exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka) and constantly practices only the solitary retention of breath (kumbhaka), attains swiftness like the mind and is freed from old age and disease.
Indeed, nothing in these three worlds is difficult for him to obtain who sits here solely absorbed in *kumbhaka*;
for him, the eightfold group of powers beginning with *aṇiman* is as if held in the palm of his hand, and truly, the fear of death is cast away from him alone. (33)

Bringing the tongue near the pair of "royal teeth" (the two front upper molars) and other points without touching them, one should drink the air through the hollow of the crow's beak; this is the supreme restraint of the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma). 34.
For one who slowly inhales the breath through both nostrils and mouth simultaneously at the two junctions of day and night,
exhaustion, burning sensations, abdominal diseases, fever, and abdominal tumors are brought to subsidence.

During the muhūrta of the cuckoo’s note at both twilights for a period of three months, one who smells the fragrance from the two beaks of a living peacock shall attain the supreme accomplishment of Sarasvatī upon the earth. || 36 ||
The destruction of snakes who possess fierce poison and intense virulence is brought about;
how much more so, then, here, the destruction of scorpions, insects, and spiders through the drinking of the wind from the mouth of a raven? 37.

The man who, at the two junctions of the day, draws in the flavorful breath through both nostrils and directs it into the mouth of his own Kuṇḍalinī, lives having abandoned the disease of consumption.
The man who, free from all other concerns, drinks here day and night the wind from the two beaks—
this is "the reverse.
Now, "the reverse" means one should perform that which is contrary to what was previously described.

Furthermore, one should practice in this manner: the reverse of that, again according to the sequence of the original order, and again the reverse of that; one should not perform the restraint of the vital air (maruta) otherwise than in this way. || 26 ||
"Perspiration," etc.
This is easy to understand. || 27 || 28 ||

"This" refers to the following: Prāṇāyāma is said to be "with the embryo" (sagarbha) when it is empty of the embryo; such [prāṇāyāma] destroys all misfortunes. When accompanied by the embryo, this is declared to possess a hundredfold fruit. In response to the inquiry, "What is without the embryo? What is with the embryo?", he says: "By recitations and meditations. That which is devoid of these two—recitations and meditations—is "without the embryo"; that which is joined with those two is declared to be "with the embryo. || 29 ||
"Pure," and so forth. The group of four is easy to understand. (30–33)
Regarding "rājajantu":
touching the tips of the two pairs of royal teeth (the upper and lower incisors) and placing the tongue near them, one should drink air with the hollow of a crow's beak;
that is to say, one should drink by making the mouth like the hollow of a crow's beak.
The four central teeth are the "king-teeth" (rājadanta); this is the superior method for the restraint of the vital air (vāyu). || 34 ||
Regarding the term *dvika*:

the crow (*dvika*), characterized by two *ka* sounds, which drinks (*dhayaḥ*) the wind (*samīraṇaṃ*)—the root *dheṭ* meaning "to drink"—destroys exhaustion, burning fever, artificial poison (*garaviṣa*), abdominal diseases (*udarāmaya*), abdominal ailments (*udararoga*), fever (*jvara*), and so forth. || 35 ||
Regarding the phrase "of both":

for a man who, during the two twilights—both morning and evening—for a period of two *muhūrtas* (equivalent to two *daṇḍas*) or for just three *praharas*, drinks the wind from the cleft of a crow’s beak while holding his beard (*kaṃ śmaśru*), the perfection of Sarasvatī arises. The option between "just the *muhūrta* of twilight" or "three *praharas*" is intended as a fixed alternative (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*). || 36 ||
(Verse 29) It is certain that for him there will be hearing within a year, and even seeing from a very great distance.
What is the use of these words spoken repeatedly in many ways? For by drinking the wind with their double beaks, the powerful fear of death that afflicts men quickly perishes along with old age. (40)

Having placed the tongue motionless at the root of the palate and firmly pressing the teeth against the teeth, he who should drink the breath very slowly, together with the nectars that touch the interior of the mouth; || 41 ||
By practicing for six months, that lord of practitioners is liberated from all diseases and from sins;
after one year, having conquered the messenger of death through natural ease, he shall live for a long time upon this earth. 42.
By virtue of three years of practice, he whose hair is as dark as a swarm of bees knows the past and the future;
even when bitten by the most terrible lords of serpents, poison does not spread through his body. 43.

Neither artificial poison nor that found in moving or stationary beings, nor even other *kālakūṭas*, can do so; rather, it is as if Bhairava himself, having assumed the eight qualities under the power of Time, sports upon the surface of the earth.

She who is white with the inhalation and exhalation of breath passing through the cavity between the head and the staff [of the spine], carrying a celestial stream flowing from the moon within the hollow of the sky-lotus—that one who would cause the dissolution of the vessel of the universe within the belly-cave of that channel called Vajra, for him there would be a windless, cloudless state beyond death itself. 45.

When it has entered a state of fainting, it removes the multitude of diseases; when it is obstructed, it causes men to travel through the sky. When the breath (vāta) is mastered, it extends immortality in its entirety; indeed, all this is easily obtained through practice of the vital air. 46.
Then, with his armor fastened and the heel of his left foot placed at the base of the flagpole,
he held his body and neck straight, self-controlled, having turned back the horses of his senses from their objects.

Having repeatedly filled the cavity of the belly with winds drawn in by the tips of the crow-like beaks, and having blocked both nostrils with the two index fingers while the eyes are directed toward the openings of the ears,

one whose intellect is steady and pure should close the nasal passages with the two middle fingers and the mouth with the remaining fingers— not too tightly— and thus fix the mind upon the void (kha) that is the abode of the Lotus-born One.
"Poison," etc.
Kākīlaḥ: the triad is easy to understand. (37–40)
Regarding the phrase "the tongue":

having placed the tongue against the region of the palate and pressed the row of lower teeth against the row of upper teeth, one should inhale the fragrant wind (gandhavāha) together with the drops situated in the front of the mouth; the rest is easy to understand.
He states another method with the words "the tongue."

With his palaces containing the essence within their mouths, he [overcame] natural old age; there was no artificial poison, nor camphor mixed with coconut; there was no stationary [poison] such as that from the snowy mountains, nor mobile [poison] from the mountains, nor that produced from the musk-deer (*vyāghranābhi*); there were the eight qualities and the eight supernatural powers (*aṣṭasiddhi*), for the purpose of the descent of Bhairava—the word "vā" (or) being used [to include these]. 41–44.

Regarding the word *muṇḍeti*: the "cave" (*darī*) is the interior of the channel called *vajrā* which is situated within the *suṣumnā*. For one who performs the regulation (*vidhāna*) of the "void" (*kha*)—that is, the wind (*vāyu*)—residing therein, his "wind" (the body) becomes the "mallet" (*mudgara*), which is the wealth of Death (*mṛtyu*). Death is Yama; that which is the death (destroyer) of him [Yama] becomes an iron mallet. According to Amara, *ghana* means an iron mallet.

What is that [place]? It is the cavity within the hollow of the staff-like skull; the "staff" (daṇḍa) is the spinal column which serves as the support for the skull, and the "interior" refers to the Suṣumṇā situated in its midst. Of what nature is it? It carries—that is, maintains—a stream of nectar as white as the Himalayas, flowing from the moon located within the lotus situated in the region of space. Thus, the meaning is that there is no death for one who drinks the wind residing within the Suṣumṇā. || 45 ||
Regarding "fainting" (*mūrcchā*):
fainting means, that is to say, being motionless.
Truly (*addhā*), by way of reality, it wards off the certainty of disease.

When bound, being restrained within the channels and dependent [on them], it causes humans to travel through the sky by means of movement without support; when dead, it goes with the mind to its desired destination; and likewise, when dissolved, it leads one to immortality. Furthermore: "O Bhairavī! When swooned, it removes disease; when dead, it destroys death; when bound, it grants the power of moving through the sky; and when controlled, the vital air [is mastered]. (46)

He states another method with the word "tathā" (likewise): A man should place his own mind within the lotus-born Brahmā, that is, in the *nilaya*, the supporting lotus. How so? He by whom the anus is closed by the heel—that is, by the ankle of one foot—and he by whom the other heel is placed at the base of the *dhvaja* (the root of the penis). With an upright body, meaning a non-crooked frame, and with a restrained self (*yatātmā*), where the self is like a horse because the senses are as difficult to control as horses. || 47 ||
*Kākī*:

Having filled the cavity of the belly with winds drawn in through the mouth of the female crow (*kākabadhū*), one should block the "hole of the enemy of Nara"—meaning Karna (the enemy of Arjuna), which refers to the ear-hole—with the two thumbs of both hands;
having blocked the two eyes with the two index fingers, the nostrils with the two middle fingers, and the mouth with the remaining fingers. 48.
(Verse 49) For one who practices thus every day according to their capacity, this vital breath (pavana) of the body gradually moves within the Suṣumnā.
Then, the innate sound (nāda) suddenly arises, generating bliss; in due course, it becomes like the soft sound of a lute being played by a skilled musician.
At first, this sound—which steals away the clear tinkling of a row of intoxicated bees from the path of the neck—is like the resonance of a bamboo flute or a bronze vessel filled with water;
thereafter, it resembles the ringing of a bell, deep and steady like the roar of the ocean, as it thunders within the hollow of the supreme Brahma-nāḍī. 50.
By that means, the wind arises within him as an innate clarity;
for him who possesses immeasurable merit and is the abode of great bliss, the qualities such as *aṇimā* come into being.

A mortal suddenly hears [the sound] emerging from within the cavity of the enemy of the son of the King of the Gods, which he restrains with two fingers of his own hand, emitting a deep resonance like that of the ocean. 52.

Even for that person who constantly meditates upon this sound—the enemy of the offspring of the Lord of the Thirty-three—that being, freed from all impurity, attains here an abundance of virtues. (53)

Having properly blocked the tips [of the two bows] with his fingers, the wise man, having restrained the wind bound between the two bows, and likewise the best of bulls—the sixth sense—at that very moment directly beholds the supreme light sung by the Upanishads, the Traipura, which possesses the splendor of ten million moons freed from their dark spots. (p. 31) 54.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya* composed by the illustrious Nāgabhaṭṭa.
The fourth chapter begins.

Then, having applied himself to the yoga of inhalation (*pūraka*), the wise and concentrated practitioner should exert effort at the region of his own root-cakra to pierce the knot associated with the goat (*aja*). || 1 ||
Just as one who has mounted a camel slowly contracts its neck and the path behind it, so the wise man, having fixed his self upon the path, should contract the path within the throat. || 2 ||

Regarding the word *yathā*: in this manner, by practicing daily according to the method described, if this wind moves within the *suṣumnā*, then the *nāda*—the lamp of Brahman that generates perpetual bliss—is produced. Furthermore, it gradually becomes like the sound of a lute (*vīṇā-samarava*), meaning its resonance becomes exceedingly sweet due to its being produced by one who plays the lute. These two [verses] are easy to understand. || 49–51 ||

The king of heroes is Indra; his son is Arjuna; his enemy is Karṇa. If one restrains him there with both hands and two fingers, like the deep sound spreading within the ocean, that mortal hears it; for such a person whose sins have been removed, there is the attainment of virtues—the meaning is that there is the attainment of liberation. || 52 || 53 ||

"Śṛṅgāṇi" (the horns): the "horns" are the sense organs (*indriya*). Having restrained them with the fingers, one who has suppressed the vital breath (*pavana*) in the middle of the "kīḍaṇḍayīrbhuvaḥ" is the best of bulls (*vṛṣabha-śreṣṭhaḥ*).

A "bull" (*vṛṣabha*) is so called because it partakes of the "bull" (*vṛṣī*), which is the object (*viṣaya*); thus, the meaning is that having restrained the mind—the sixth sense organ, which is the most excellent among the "bulls" that are the senses—one attains the goal. He is praised within the three Vedas (*trayyantargītam*), known through the Vedānta, possessing a luster like that of the moon's orb when freed from its spots, and shining with the radiance of many spotless moons risen at once.
This is the meaning:

having restrained the senses with the fingers of one's own hands, he who regulates the internal breath—merged within his own heart—by means of the sequence of his own power, experiences the Self, which is the supreme form of light, knowable through the Vedānta, and possessing the luster of the moon. This is the meaning. || 54 ||
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Tripurāsāra*.

Having thus described the specific methods of yoga for conquering the vital breath (*pavana*) through breath control (*prāṇāyāma)—which leads to immortality and freedom from afflictions—the author now begins to explain the method of binding the *yonimudrā*, which serves as the means for attaining worldly prosperity and the supreme good (*abhyudaya-niḥśreyasa*), and for removing defects such as the "severed" (*chinna*) in mantras, starting with the words "Now, the yoga of filling" (*atha pūrakayoga*).

First, by practicing the yoga of inhalation (*pūraka*) and so forth, one should fix the mind upon the region of one's own *mūlādhāra-cakra* and apply effort toward piercing the knot that has "Aja" as its prefix. Here, "Aja" refers to Brahmā; since he is the origin (*upapatti*) of the word "knot" (*granthi*), the meaning is the "Brahma-knot.
One should thus remain absorbed in meditation through steady practice. || 1 ||

He describes the method for breaking the knot (granthibheda) with the word "śakṛt" (excrement): Just as a horse (arvan), having discharged its excrement (viṣṭhā), contracts its anus (kambuni mārgam) by a certain manner, in that same manner, the person who has joined [the breath] at the foundational wheel (ādhāracakra) should lead his own path [of the breath] into contraction. || 2 ||
(Verse 3, p. 32) With his hands placed upon his private parts, he should repeatedly utter the sound "huṃ" according to the sequence taught by the Guru;
[his organ] being firmly held within the space between the anus and the penis, its tip is like a lotus bud consisting of radiant light.

Then, having conquered the *kambunī* wind, the self-subdued practitioner should slowly draw it back in the reverse direction to the base of the lotus-seated [deity], which is difficult to attain except through the method taught by one's own guru.
By practicing this method repeatedly and gradually, that wind within the *kambu* (trachea) becomes inclined toward the path at the base of the *ajapa*-lotus and effects the breaking of the knots.
Then, having avoided the path of the moon, the jewel of the sky,
that lord of birds entered properly and from above caused the lotus of the one seated upon a lotus to turn its face upward.
Then, when the Lord of Birds had entered the interior of the abode of the Supreme Being, a marvelous eloquence arose,
and there was a great lightness of his body as well as an increased radiance of the fire within his belly.

One should meditate upon Kāma, who resembles ten million flashes of lightning, whose brilliant luster surpasses the glow of the black fire at the end of time, who possesses a radiance like a thousand suns, who is endowed with a splendor similar to a mass of flames, who wanders within the womb, and who has the steady, deep-red hue of the bandhūka flower and the peak of ten million moons. (Page 33) 8.

Above that, the wise one should meditate with an unwavering intellect upon the Self in the form of the *haṃsa*, which is a subtle digit (*kalā*) consisting of pure consciousness, radiant with the luster of a mass of long, flickering flames of fire, situated within the sky of the path to Brahman; and having become one with that [Self], he should contemplate it as motionless, like a lamp in a windless place. 9.

That which is called Śakti is known as Kuṇḍalinī; she is ever-exerted in the creation of the universe, resembling a shimmering flash of lightning, coiled like a conch-shell and shaped like a sleeping serpent, enchanting the world. One should contemplate her in the midst of that [cavity], her form comparable to a thread of a poisonous creeper. 10.

Having awakened her who was asleep by means of the syllable *hūṃ* according to the procedure taught by the Guru, and having then united her with that supreme energy consisting of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), one whose mind is concentrated should, through one's own self, raise up from the foundation that Māyā-Kuṇḍalinī along with the Kauśikī power by way of the Great Path of Brahman. 11.

Regarding the phrase *vidadhauteti*: "Repeatedly," that is, again and again, according to the method instructed by the Guru, one should diligently restrain both lotus-like hands at the base of the navel—the source (*yoni*) of the tip of the fiery lotus situated below the navel—meaning the source at the tip of the fiery *puṣkara* located between the anus and the genitals, which is the *mūlādhāra*.
This is the meaning: the four-petaled lotus situated between the anus and the penis has a source (*yoni*) in its center shaped like a triangle. || 3 ||

Now, regarding the word "atha": having slowly drawn up the wind called *kambu*—the vital air (*māruta*)—from the *mānava* [channel] according to the sequence taught by the teacher, one should cause it to enter the root of the *suṣumnā*, known as the lotus-seat (*kamalāsana*). || 4 ||

"By this method" means that by practicing in this way again and again, having restrained the upward-turning [breath], one effects the breaking of the knots situated within that internal path of Brahman; such is the meaning. || 5 ||
Regarding the phrase "having avoided": because the *apāna* breath, by virtue of its upward movement, possesses the nature of the *prāṇa*, it obtains the name "Lord of Birds" (*khagādhipati*).

Thus, the *apāna* wind, having set out for the upward journey, avoids the paths of *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, which consist of the moon and the sun respectively; then, having settled at the base of the lotus—the base of the *suṣumnā*—it turns its face upward. || 6 ||

Regarding "pratibhānam": when the Lord of Birds, the apāna-vāyu, has entered within the belly of Brahmā, there arises an extraordinary and wondrous intuition (pratibhāna); the body attains a state of intense lightness. || 7 ||
"Resembling ten million flashes of lightning": one should meditate upon the fire of the body of Kāma.

Of what nature? Equal to the brilliance of a flash of lightning. That by which the splendor of the fire of universal destruction (Kālānala) has been surpassed by its own radiance; endowed with a luster equal to the mass of the brilliance of a thousand suns; resting within the womb (the source); shining in the interior of the wheel; having the color of a ruby (bandhūka) as indicated by the word "bandhūka"; and cool like the moon. By this, it is understood that it generates bliss for practitioners.
Granted that the word *kāma* is conventionally established in the secret scriptures (*rahasyāgama*) as referring to the Vaiśvānara within the body;
one should thus meditate upon *kāma*, consisting of light, as returning to its own support.
And so it is said in the Rudrayāmala: "One should meditate on Kāma, who resides in the womb, as being like the Bandhūka flower."
Resembling the blazing fire of time (Kālānala), with a radiance equal to ten million lightning bolts. || 8 ||

Regarding that: above that fire known as Kāmarāja, there is a digit (kalā) in the form of a crest, extremely subtle, resembling a thousand flashes of lightning, consisting of consciousness (cidrūpa), or [simply] that digit is Brahman.
Some, however, maintain that the phrase "the digit consisting of consciousness, resembling a thousand flashes of lightning, should be meditated upon as partless (niṣkalā)" is to be supplied;
one should contemplate the Self, whose nature is the supreme haṃsa, having unified it with that digit. || 9 ||

Regarding the word "śakti": that digit (kalā) of yours which is of the nature of consciousness, the digit called Kuṇḍalinī-śakti—this one should be contemplated as being within the previously mentioned middle of the crest-lock (śikhā).
The meaning is that one should meditate upon her as abiding, having pervaded the interior. || 10 ||

He shows the summarized meaning by saying "with the syllable *hūṃ*": "Then, having pierced the three marks (*liṅga*) with the *hūṃ*-syllable empowered by the mantra, the wise one should lead his own power (*ātmaśakti*) upward through the Brahma-nāḍī from the seat of the lotus-born [Brahmā] to the place of emission (*visargasthāna*).
This is the root of supreme bliss, beloved of the sky-lotus, situated above the moon, and possessing a stream of red nectar flowing down. (12)
Having drunk again the divine nectar-essence of the Kula, the one whose self is concentrated should enter the middle of the Apadhana;
then, O best of teachers, he should proceed from the Kula to the Akula by means of the measure (mātrā) imparted through yoga.

That power, which has become the life-force of the entire body, is called "Prāṇa" here by the foremost of the Tantrikas. But that is recited as "Uddhāta" (the upward stroke) by the lords of sages when the Prāṇa, having been led [upward], touches the interior in succession. 14.
The faithful person, constantly devoted to practice, who day after day focuses on this [seed-syllable] situated in its own support, is perpetually freed from all impurities.
Having cast off old age and death, endowed with a multitude of virtues, he lives long upon this earth like a god, liberated from the ocean of suffering. 15.
(Verse 16) That in which this fourfold creation described here proceeds entirely, and into which the entire universe—beginning from Kālāgnirudra and ending with Śiva—is likewise dissolved; ||| 16 ||

This very Yonimudrā has indeed been described by me; its binding is difficult even for the gods to attain. By means of this binding, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished for the preeminent among practitioners. 17.

Those who were cut down, obstructed, paralyzed, or pinned; those who were asleep, intoxicated, or unconscious; those whose vigor was diminished; those who were burnt, exhausted, or situated on the side of the enemy; and those who were young, old, or arrogant in their youth—[all these were slain]. 18.

Those mantras which are lifeless, those devoid of essence, those that have become impotent, and those lacking limbs or mantras—all these, as well as any other mantras, become endowed with power even by means of the binding of mudrās. || 19 ||

Having awakened that Kuṇḍalinī sleeping in the Ādhāra-lotus by means of that [breath], and having subsequently united her with that supreme consciousness, one should contemplate Māyā—the Kula, which is the Mūlādhāra—as the deity residing there within the body.
It is said: "Akula is called Śiva, and Kula is proclaimed as Śakti;
their union is the transformative splendor (kaula-tejas); such is the determination of the triad. (11)

"Having pierced"—as stated previously—having split the three channels (liṅgas), one should meditate as if leading that Kuṇḍalinī energy upward from the abode of Brahmā through the Suṣumnā, the central channel of Brahman, to the state of "affection for the sky-lotus," which is the station of the emission (visarga) located within the supreme bliss of the sky-lotus. || 12 ||

"Having drunk the essence of the nectar of Kustā"—thus, having led [the breath] up to the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*) and having drunk the divine nectar residing there, one should cause it to reach the center of the body, known as *kula*, the support of the womb (*yonyādhāra*), by that same path in reverse order (*virīhakrama*). This means reaching the support of the root (*mūlādhāra*) in the middle of the body.
How should one cause it to be grasped? He says: "By means of the application of *mātrā*"; one should perform the going and coming according to the sequence of the *mātrā-yoga* taught by the Guru.
As for *mātrā*: "The *bindu*, the *nāda*, and likewise the *śakti*—this is declared to be the triad of *mātrās*."

For in this way, by the word *mātrā*, the three seats (*pīṭha*) are prescribed: the seat named *Pūrṇa*, which is the nature of the Bindu situated in the station of the *Ājñā* and which illuminates the reality of the *Ājñā*; above that, in the middle of the forehead, the second seat named *Nāda*, which consists of Nāda—the throbbing form of Śiva that is the nature of light and is essentially the Bindu; and above that, the crest (*śikhā*), which is the form of the Power (*Śakti*) whose essence is the universe. Indeed, I have stated with certainty that the binding of this Mudrā is difficult even for the gods to attain.
The meaning is that whatever cannot be accomplished by this method of binding the *yonimudrā*, all of that—including the god of love (*smara*)—is accomplished by this mudrā.

What is this [power] here in the world? It refers to the fourfold creation that has been described, from which [all things] proceed and by which they come into being. [The four types are: those born from sprouts, such as trees and shrubs; those born from sweat, such as worms and gadflies; those born from a womb, such as humans; and those born from eggs, such as birds and snakes.
Some, however, maintain that creation is of four kinds: the creation of sound, the creation of the meaning of sound, and the creation of Prakṛti and Puruṣa.

Alternatively, according to the Naiyāyika view, it is the creation of Puruṣa; according to the Sāṃkhya view, it arises from the union of Prakṛti and Puruṣa; according to the Pātañjala view, it arises from Prakṛti alone; and according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, it arises from the unseen force (adṛṣṭa).

This fourfold creation constitutes the entire universe, which dissolves back into that very state—characterized by forms such as Kālāgnirudra—within the specific meditation previously described, which is indeed Mudrā. (13–17)

"Having severed"—this is a couplet. All these mantras become endowed with potency through a specific meditation on the *yonimudrā*. By these [mantras], the "Lord-seed" (*svāmibīja*) is said to be that which is severed at the beginning, middle, and end of the mantra;
it is joined, conjoined with water, and again overcome by wind, and placed within the treasure-chest (*nidhi*).
A mantra that is divided into four or five parts is designated as "severed" (chinna). If it is marked by the pair of seed-syllables *bhūḥ* and *bhuvaḥ* at the beginning, middle, and end,
it should be known as a "blocked" (ruddha) mantra, which is devoid of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Those who commit violating the teacher’s bed, drinking [intoxicants], killing a twice-born, stealing honey, or stealing gold—
all these go to destruction by this very bond, even if practiced but once and properly performed. (20)
But that very best of ministers is indeed that same yogi who has attained the state of perfected virtue;
he is the one who, remaining constantly established in his own appropriate duties and righteous actions, practices this bond here in this world. (21)
By this bond formed through constant practice in this world by embodied beings, neither old age—the victory banner of the King of the Ancestors—nor the fear brought about by Death exists. (22)

(Verse 23) Indeed, by the constant practice of this very bondage, a person attains incomparable supernatural powers such as *aṇimā*, as well as intense consciousness; he also attains matchless yoga, victory over the vital winds (*marut*), or even the deception of Time (*kāla*). Furthermore, he constantly beholds that supreme abode of Viṣṇu which the wise ever behold.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya* composed by the illustrious Nāgabhaṭṭa.
The Fifth Chapter. Now, I shall briefly describe the lotuses that serve as supports, situated within the Suṣumnā,
as well as the deities residing upon the petals of those lotuses, the colors of those lotuses, and the goddesses of the six supports.
That knotless lotus which was previously described by me, Śambhu declares here to be the primordial support;
it is endowed with four petals of golden hue, accessible to yogis, and a source of great wonder. (2)

The *kīlikās* (stake-syllables) are at the beginning, middle, and end: *haṃsa*, *prāsāda*, and *vāgbhava*; the letter *ha* with the bindu (*haṃ*), the *jīvī* (*ha*), and the four-part *vāgbhava* (*aiṃ*). Then the *māyā* (*hrīṃ*) and the word "I bow" (*namāmi*). That [mantra] in which these do not exist is "staked. Those who have been granted [these]: one is in the middle, and itself at the head; in which [are] Indra and Purandara.

That mantra which is paralyzed does not exist as a means for awakening success; likewise, those that are "asleep"—defined as being devoid of the nasal bindu (*n*) and lacking the *haṃsa*—are said to be asleep. Furthermore, those that are "intoxicated" consist of either a mantra or a *vidyā* containing seventeen syllables.
That which begins with the five [syllables] starting with *phaṭ* and is uttered while intoxicated by passion is called "intoxicated" (*madonmatta*). Those that are "fainted" (*mūrcchita*):

a mantra whose fivefold weapon (*astra*) stands in the middle is said to be fainted. Those that are "of little power" (*hīnavīrya*): a mantra situated at a place of pause (*virāma*) is called one of little power. And those that are "burnt" (*dagdha*).

If the syllable *vahni* (ra), conjoined with *vāyu* (ya), appears seven times at the head of a mantra, the knower of mantras should consider that mantra to be "burnt" (*dagdha*). Those [mantras] which consist of two, three, six, or eight syllables and are designated as *astra* (missile) are called "paralyzed" (*stambha*). Furthermore, those situated on the side of the enemy, those whose vowels and other [phonetic elements] are unfavorable, and those that are "infant" (*bāla*)—where a mantra of seven syllables is termed infant—are also paralyzed. Likewise, those that are "aged" (*vṛddha*) [are paralyzed].
A mantra of thirty syllables, sixty-four syllables, one hundred syllables, or even four hundred syllables is designated as "vṛddha" (the aged).

And those that are "youthful" (*yuvānaḥ*): a mantra of sixteen syllables is said to be youthful. And those that are "devoid of life-force" (*jīvahīnāḥ*): a six-syllabled mantra is devoid of life-force. And those that are "devoid of essence" (*sattvahīnāḥ*): a two-syllabled mantra would be devoid of essence. And those that are "deficient in limbs" (*aṅgahīnāḥ*): a mantra of twenty-six syllables, as well as one of thirty-six syllables, or even one of nineteen syllables, is declared to be deficient in limbs.
The meaning is that even mantras perceived as having such defects as these become purified by means of this meditation. || 18 || 19 ||
"Regarding 'the practice of violating the Guru's bed': the meaning is that even by performing the binding of the *yonimudrā* only once, a person becomes liberated from great sins (*mahāpātaka*).

Regarding 'by this': for embodied beings, by constantly performing this binding of the *yonimudrā*, [liberation] becomes certain. Of what kind? Through constant practice of the binding of Yama, the King of the Ancestors, a human being attains the eightfold qualities beginning with sovereignty; he attains supreme realization and knowledge."

One attains the practice of yoga, achieves mastery over the vital breath (vāyu), or the deception of time, or the impelling of everything; [the word "or" (vā) may signify] an alternative, a comparison, a purpose, or a conjunction. And the wise behold that station, the abode of Viṣṇu. (20–23)

Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Padārthadarśana*, a commentary on the *Tripurāsāra*. Having thus described the *yonimudrā*, which serves as the means for those qualified [practitioners] to attain both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), the author now begins to explain the specific yogic practices within the six supports (*ṣaḍādhāra*), starting with the words "Now, the lotuses of the supports" (*athādhārapaṅkeruhāṇi*). The meaning is as follows: that channel (*nāḍī*) called *citrā*, which was previously mentioned as being situated within the *suṣumnā*—the six sections beginning with the *mūlādhāra* located therein are precisely what constitute the six supports.

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: I shall describe the gods, beginning with Brahmā, who are situated upon the petals of those lotuses; the syllables, such as *śukla* and others, which have the color of the mass of water-lilies; and the six supporting deities. || 1 ||

It says "he conquers the lotuses. Regarding the manner of protecting the *yonimudrā*, that which was described as the four-petaled lotus is indeed the primary support for those yogins. One should place the syllables of the waters and the oceans—*va*, *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*—which are restrained by the Goddess, in the sequence starting from the east.
In the reading "water, Indra, fire, and wind," "water" is the syllable *va*; "Indra-fire" is the second [syllable] after Indra (*śa*).
On the four lotus petals, one should place these syllables of the waters and oceans, either joined with the Goddess or alone.
The goddess Ḍākinī resides here, possessing the splendor of the bindu and the amandaprabhā, amidst the blazing light of the Spharajjyotis. ||3||

Through the constant practice of meditation on the *mūlādhāra*, there arise for men, in due order, these six supernatural powers: paralysis, agitation, leaping like a frog, leaving the earth, and the power of moving through the air. (4)
Excellence of luster in the body, clarity of voice, radiance of the digestive fire, keenness of the sense organs, health, and freedom from dejection; || 5 ||
Having made their minds steady in the center of the root-cakra, men, through mere devotion, speak of the past, the present, and the future, as well as of scriptures never before heard. (6)

Having immediately abandoned the lotus-face of the Lotus-seated One due to the surge of waves of affection, Sarasvatī, assuming a divine form, dances within the interior of the hollow of his own lotus-face. 7.
Having attained the perfection of the mantra of the Lord of Mercury and having conquered even irresistible time,
they reach the state of agelessness and immortality at the end, and rejoice with delight in the station of supreme bliss.

In the beginning, the entire world was submerged in the waters of a single ocean; within that, the primordial form of light appeared, whose majesty is most exalted. That Great Lord (Maheśa), the swan who destroys the darkness of the fear of worldly existence, has his self presided over by the six Siddhas, is praised by all the gods, possesses six faces, and is endowed with six sheaths. || 9 ||
From the Lord who bears the body of the Liṅga, Dviraṇḍa became the first [face]; Bāli was the eastern face of Śiva; Mahākāla was his upper face;
that god Pinākin was the southern face; furthermore, this lord Chagalāṇḍa became his western face. || 10 ||

Śakāra: Thus, the third [letter] after *e* is *ṣakāra*, which is said to be the middle syllable. Likewise, the fourth [letter] after *yakāra*, the wind element, is the dental *sakāra*. Therefore, the meaning is that the four syllables—*vaṃ*, *śaṃ*, *ṣaṃ*, and *saṃ*—should be placed in the four petals in this sequence: first the initial seed-syllable (*bīja*), then *vakāra*, then the initial seed-syllable of *tava* (i.e., *śa*). Alternatively, one may place them either alone or joined with the nasal bindu (*m*). In that four-petaled [lotus], the goddess in the form of Ḍākinī resides; because she is the root of this entire phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*), the Yoginīs call it the "Root Support" (*mūlādhāra*).

From the practice of meditation upon this *mūlādhāra*, two states arise for the person: paralysis (*stambha*) and agitation (*kṣobha*). Immobility (*niṣkriyatva*) occurs. Then there is leaping (*utpluti*), purification (*utpavana*), and the "frog-like state" (*dārdurī*), which refers to the bounding motion characteristic of a frog (*maṇḍūka*). Furthermore, the abandonment of the earth-element (*bhūmi-tyāga*) occurs, followed by the attainment of sky-faring (*khecaratva*). One gains the power to move at will even in the ether; in due course, these six qualities arise. (2–4)

It demonstrates other qualities as well: there is an excellence of the body's luster (*kānti*). There is the manifestation of sound (*nādavyakti*), where *nādī* refers to a specific resonance. There is the kindling of the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*) and the absence of impairment in the sense organs, such as the eyes. For yogis indeed perceive objects even when they are not in contact with the senses.
Furthermore, there is health (*nairujya*), which is the absence of suffering; all of this arises from the retention of the vital air (*vāyu*). || 5 ||

Furthermore, he demonstrates the purpose [of this practice] with the words "having done so. Here, having firmly fixed the mind with care upon the *ādhāra* lotus in the center of the root-cakra, they speak of the past, present, and future;
they speak of the past and the future. They speak of and explain the scriptures even though they have not been heard or studied. 6.

He states another purpose with the words "having abandoned" (vihāya). Due to the connection with the wave that is affection itself for the lotus-seated Brahmā, Sarasvatī—possessing a divine form—dances and delights within the interior of the lotus-mouth of the practitioner, having been released from the interior of the lotus-mouth of Brahmā by means of the retention of breath (vāyudhāraṇa) directed toward it. || 7 ||

He states another purpose with the words "having attained" (adhigamya). Having attained mastery over the mercury-elixir (rasendra) and mantras, having conquered time which is otherwise difficult to ward off, and having reached the state of being ageless and immortal, they delight in the state of supreme bliss—the state of liberation—at the time of their end.
Therefore, through this yoga of abiding, one becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta); the meaning is that at the conclusion, one becomes merged into the Supreme Self. || 8 ||

Regarding the word *ekībhūta*: previously, the entire universe was unified, submerged in the waters of the ocean. Within that, Maheśa and the Goddess existed in the form of a *liṅga*. Of what nature was it? It was of the nature of unprecedented light (*apūrvajyotis*); the meaning is that the unprecedented splendor itself underwent transformation into the form of a *liṅga*. Of what nature was it? Its self was presided over by the six Siddhas, beginning with Dviraṇḍa. Among those who bore the body of that Blessed Lord in the form of a *liṅga*, the Siddha-puruṣa named Dviraṇḍa was the first and upper face.
The eastern face was named Vālī; "upper" (*ūrddha*) means upward-facing, and "lower" (*ava*) means downward-facing.

Vāyu is at the right [cakra], Pinākin at the western face, Yugalagaṇḍa at the northern; likewise, Ādhārātmā is Dviraṇḍa, Svādhiṣṭhānātmā is Vālī, Maṇipūrātmā is Mahākāla, Anāhatātmā is Vahni, Viśuddhātmā is Pinākin, and Ājñātmā is Kagaṇḍa. His liṅga is to be meditated upon in these locations. (9–10)

(Page 40) At the base of the banner is a lotus called Svādhiṣṭhāna, possessing six petals and resembling the rising sun. It is marked at the tips of its petals by the letters from *ṭa* to *tha*, and its head is illuminated by the nasal bindu.
This is the station of the Lord who possesses the trident in the form of the *liṅga*, accessible only to the most excellent of yogis; its presiding goddess is Rākiṇī. (11)

Here, in the Svādhiṣṭhāna, the excellent practitioner—whose heart is stilled by the flood of intense waves through the power of absorption in his own innate consciousness, and whose limbs are withdrawn though he remains in the body—delights the company of fawn-eyed women, who are radiant with beauty and possess glances smiling with passion, whether he stands upon the ground or is free from the body. 12.
In this world, that mortal who, having set aside his own mind and the various extensive collections of unlearned scriptures,
has shaken off old age and disease, lives for a very long time, free from the fear of death.
The constant impurity of the human body brings about the highest purity for men here;
even the cool-rayed moon, firmly obstructed within the body as fragile as an autumnal water-lily, attains solidity. 14.
Those virtuous ones who, with steady minds, can hold back the great lord of fluids that has suddenly surged from the sky-lotus upon the sight of Kamalā—they alone, indeed, are the best of men. 15.

Just as a great lordly elephant, intoxicated and difficult to control, comes under subjection through gradual means, so too this powerful Moon here, when restrained by the sequence [of the lunar days], will certainly come under one's own control. (Verse 16)
In this state, for those devoted to the yoga of the vajra and lotus, first dissolution arises from passion; through the power of that dissolution, consciousness also becomes intense.

Then, for those men who partake of the great jewel-like essence of the inner blue [light], when their mind attains manifestation, there occurs the rising of the moon under the guise of intense innate bliss. || 17 ||

Men who constantly meditate upon the Maṇipūraka at the navel, which possesses ten petals with the luster of blue sapphire, with the ten syllables beginning with *ṭa* and *ḍa* situated on the petals and their tips shining with *bindus*, and which is presided over by Lākīnī—they alone perform subjugation, attraction, neutralization of poison, the shaking of cities, and other such feats. (18)

For the virtuous man who has dedicated himself to this place, there shall be the attainment of supreme power in the netherworld (pātāla), as well as the accomplishment of his desired goal on earth through an incomparable sword;

furthermore, there shall be the acquisition of beauty, the power to leave the ground, the ability to enter the cities of enemies, the removal of old age, and the alleviation of all suffering and disease, or even the deception of Time itself. || 19 ||

Regarding "Svādhiṣṭhāna": above that [cakra] is the syllable formed by the six petals of its own family, beginning with the letter *va* (the "back" or *pṛṣṭha*) and ending with the letter of logic (*tarka*, i.e., *ṣa*). Starting from that back-letter, it is composed of *ma*, *ya*, *va*, and *la*, with these letters having their heads adorned with bindus—thus joined with bindus, it resembles the morning sun, like the sun at dawn. The presiding deity of this cakra is Rākiṇī. 11.

Here, indeed, it is said that [the Lord] displays the supreme power of the Yoginīs to those who have mastered their breath and perceive the subtle signs; here, in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, the bodiless one (*anaṅga*), with his limbs joined through the force of absorption (*laya*) by virtue of being seated within the lotus, delights the assembly of deer-eyed women.

Likewise, he delights that assembly whose outer corners of the eyes (*apāṅga*) are smiling with passion (*smara*)—their gaze radiant with the light of desire—and who are filled with beauty and charm (*kānti*). (12)

He describes the specific fruit [of this practice] with the words "here" (iha): that mortal, free from old age and disease, having placed his own mind within this lotus—that is, having offered it—comes to know the various and manifold collections of scriptures; he knows them, being devoid of the fear of death and having abandoned the dread of Yama.

By the sight of another lotus, he constantly effects the purification of the impurity of the human body. That man, like the cool-rayed moon or like semen (śukra), becomes firmly bound and attains density and solidity; yet, like an autumnal lotus, he remains delicate and beautiful. 13–14.

"Moved": those who, by means of beholding this lotus, retain the lord of essences—the semen—moved from the thousand-petaled lotus, they are the best of men; they are capable in the yoga of meditating upon this lotus. || 15 || 16 ||

In this regard, it is called "the diamond" (*kuliśa*). At that very moment, through union with that [state] and through passion for it, the dissolution of the elephants of the senses occurs; for this reason, it is described as being like a diamond. Consciousness becomes powerful. Regarding the phrase "internally blue":

when the consciousness of men who have partaken of that essence—the semen which is internally blue and of great strength—manifests, then, by way of the great and intense innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), and because of the arising of the destruction of ignorance and so forth, it is described as being like the moon. || 17 ||

He speaks of Maṇipūraka as being situated at the navel. It is endowed with ten petals resembling blue collyrium, joined with the desired [consonants] ḍa, ḍha, ṇa, ta, tha, da, dha, na, pa, and pha located on the petals—each accompanied by a nasal bindu and having their tips shimmering with a drop (bindu). It is presided over by Lākinī. Through meditation upon this, there is subjugation, attraction, neutralization of poison, the overpowering of another's body, entry into another's body, and the power of invisibility known as the *lukī-vidyā*.

If it is asked, "Since there is the statement 'from the *ratna* [jewel] to the *maṇipūraka*,' how can it be a blue gem (*nīlaratna*)?"—there is no fault, because even the blue gem is indeed a *ratna*. The accomplishment of the subterranean realm (*pātāla-siddhi*) consists in opening an aperture below (p.
42). In the heart is the mercury-dye (*rasendragopa*), twilight, vermilion, gold, and a lotus;
that which the wise call the "Unstruck" (*anāhata*) is adorned with petals resembling the sun and the moon. (20)
It is adorned with eleven Bhairavas, beginning with Krodhīśa, who possess fierce valor and are endowed with staves;
it is presided over by Kākinī through her divine power, and eternally by the Goddess, the Haṃsa, and the Lord.
Yogis whose minds are constantly absorbed in this place, residing in celestial chariots and endowed with wondrous forms and splendor, are agitated by divine women;

they possess incomparable knowledge pertaining to the three periods of time, as well as the agitation of the city, hearing from afar, vision, the power of moving through the sky, and union with other yogis. || 22 ||
Next, at the throat is the lotus called Viśuddha, possessing the luster of smoky fire, with sixteen petals encircled by the vowels beginning with Śrīkaṇṭhā.
In this place resides eternally the Goddess Śākinī, whose innate power is incomparable, the divine one who pacifies the suffering of those who seek refuge. 23.

For that bull among men whose mind is constantly established here through the yoga of practice, there will be the capacity to perceive the true nature of things on this earth, even without having studied the scriptures. (24)

A person whose mind is fixed on this place becomes a seer of the three times, free from all diseases, and having conquered old age, with hair as black as collyrium, lives for a long time upon the earth, free from death. (25)
If a yogi, having restrained his breath and constantly fixing his mind on this spot, becomes enraged, he can shake the entire triple world;
neither Brahmā, nor Viṣṇu, nor Hari-Hara, nor even the sun, nor Gaṇeśa is able to quell his power.
In the center of the two eyebrows, I meditate upon a lotus named Ājñā, endowed with two petals and shining like the rays of the autumnal moon;
here too, the goddess Hākinī resides, and on the pair of petals, I remember the two final letters joined with the bindu.
For one devoted to the yoga of meditation, there arises recollection of actions performed in previous births;
and in the abode of the *kṣetrabindu*, there is the capacity for seeing and hearing from afar. (28)
Here, with his own mental activity focused upon it, he engages in a dialogue with the image;
and behold, there is even the movement of others into another city and the resurrection of the dead! (29)
Having performed here in this place the gesture (mudrā) without support, learned solely from the mouth of his own guru, the excellent practitioner, with a steady and sharpened intellect,
perceives through constant practice the entire series of stars in the infinite space beyond the abode of the immortal wind, as well as the station of Viṣṇu and even the Lord of the Stars.

Some say that through the practice of the sword (khaḍga-sādhana) by means of [the powers of] muteness, old age, and so forth, one gains the power to enter another's body—whether it be a desired object of attainment or a physical form—even if that body is dead. 18–19.

And the Unstruck (anāhata) [cakra] is called the Heart. It consists of twelve petals and is situated within the pericarp. It is joined with the twelve-syllable root mantra beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with *ṭha*, starting from Krodhīśa and the other [deities], namely: *ka kha ga gha ṅa ca cha ja jha ña ṭa ṭha*. This mantra is presided over by the power (*śakti*) Kākinī and by the Haṃsa, the Self; it is adorned with these syllables accompanied by the *daṇḍa* and the nasal bindu. || 20 || 21 ||
"In this" means: for those yogis whose minds are fixed upon this place, [there arise] celestial women acting as agents who reside in aerial chariots and are endowed with wonderful forms and splendor;
furthermore, there is knowledge of the objects of the three times, incomparable hearing from afar, seeing from afar, and meeting with other yogis. || 22 ||

He speaks of the Viśuddha-cakra, beginning with the word "Viśuddha. It is endowed with petals encircled by the vowels beginning with *a*, accompanied by the vowels starting with Śrīkaṇṭha; that is to say, it is joined with the sixteen vowels: *aṃ, āṃ, iṃ, īṃ, uṃ, ūṃ, ṛṃ, ṝṃ, ḷṃ, ḹṃ, eṃ, aiṃ, oṃ, auṃ, aṃ, aḥ*. This lotus, known as Viśuddha, has a color like smoke, is presided over by the deity Śākinī, and is the one who pacifies the distress of taking refuge [in the Buddha] and quiets the suffering of birth and death.

When the true nature of the scriptures has not been studied, or even when its true nature is present here in this place, the yogi—having fixed his mind and applied his attention—becomes one who has mastered the vital breath (āttapavana). || 23-26 ||

Regarding the wheel of command (*ājñācakra*), he says "the name of command" (*ājñānāma*). It is "endowed with a pair of petals," meaning it possesses two petals. The "last two letters" are *ha* and *kṣa*. What is meant is this: in the middle of the eyebrows, there is the lotus of command (*ājñākamala*), which consists of two petals, is joined with the letter *ha* and the letter *kṣa* together with the nasal bindu (*bindu*), resembles an autumn lotus, and is presided over by the deity Hākinī. For one who has died [there], there is no returning again, because of the absence of further birth. (27–29)

[Page 44] He [worships] Brahmā, whose pair of feet is saluted by the hosts of gods; likewise Mukunda, the Lord who is the leader of the divine assemblies; also the Lord of the Pretas (Yama), the Lord of the Waters (Varuṇa); the Lord of the Day (the Sun), the Lord of Fire (Agni), the Wind (Vāyu), Tārkṣya (Garuḍa), and the Lord of the Yakṣas (Kubera); as well as the Gandharvas, the Kinnaras, and the Siddhas who are renowned for their virtues. (31)

The yogi constantly beholds yakṣas, even the foremost among rākṣasas, sages, and divine beings of auspicious form who are endowed with a multitude of beautiful splendors; he sees the vidyādharas, the Mātṛkā, and the celestial river whose waters possess lofty waves of protection—Svarloka-kallolinī—as well as that golden mountain which shines with eternal luster.
Likewise, there was a multitude of apsarases, whose lovely bodies were bent by the weight of their high and full breasts, who moved with the slow gait of elephants in rut,
whose pairs of eyes were shimmering, and whose restless glances were like those of startled young does.
[He saw] the best of mountains with their exceedingly lofty peaks that shrouded the expanse of the sky and the quarters of the horizon, their ridges adorned with various jewels;
likewise, the delightful forest lands filled with deer and antelopes, and the vast earth endowed with various honored fields. (34)
With high waves, with multitudes of whales and sea-monsters, with formidable clouds, and even with the best of mountains;
likewise, he [beheld] the oceans filled with the waters of pure rivers, as well as lakes abounding in lotuses and frequented by flocks of cranes and swans.

The mass of new clouds—where playful swans sport, where rows of herons form their beaks, which clings to waters made formidable by lightning within, beautiful with peacock plumage, favorable to wives, and the very season for those away on travel. (36)

In this supreme state, which is the singular root of the most wonderful, immutable, and great bliss, the yogi of steady mind should fix his own mental faculty through the mudrā; he gradually attains identity with that [state], and thereafter, by virtue of dissolution, his own great internal bliss manifests within.
When the mind is absorbed there in the abode of the *bindu*, first the elements beginning with fire are perceived; immediately thereafter, the forms of flickering lamp-flames appear.
Then, like the intense radiance of the young sun, a light shines forth—a great splendor resembling a cluster of lotus petals shimmering within the space between the earth and the sky.

He who is celebrated by yogis as the eternal bliss, the Lord of Śrī, the man Śrī-Vāsudeva, the Self, and the infallible one of inconceivable majesty—[he perceives] here, in this abode of the *bindu* at the station of the *ājñā*, having bound the self-moving *mudrā* which is without support (*nirālambā*), [he sees] the immortal abode, the heaven; above that, the entire series of stars, the host of constellations, and the station of Viṣṇu, the sky.

She beholds the Sun, the lord of days, with his pair of shimmering eyes as her pair of eyebrows; she beholds the throngs of Apsarases and even the mountains—beholding them as those by which the vault of heaven and the quarters of space are covered with massive peaks;
and she beholds the forest lands made lovely by deer and other creatures. Here, Mataṅgī beholds the multitude of lakes and the royal swan.

The *vakakoṭi* (the tip of the crane) is called "crane" because it produces joy during the time dear to peacocks. It is favorable to married women (*sadhavāḥ*) who are accompanied by their husbands, yet it is a time of exile for those away from home; thus, the mass of fresh clouds (*navameghajāla*) has the nature of Yama. Of what sort is it? It is submerged in the water within its interior, which is made terrifying (*karāla*) by lightning (*taḍit*). (30–36)

Regarding the phrase "in this": one should place the mind of the self by means of the supportless *mudrā* in that supreme, most wonderful, and imperishable state—the single root-stem of great bliss (*mahānanda*), which is the ultimate locus. Then the yogi attains identity with that, becoming one with Brahman.

The particle *vā* is used for conjunction. Thus, through the supportless *mudrā*, one's own great bliss—the bliss of the bliss of Brahman—arises and manifests within, having entered into the interior by virtue of dissolution.

When this mind has become absorbed, first the signs of fire situated in its rays are seen; immediately after that, the sprouts of lamps, and then the radiance and light of the rising sun; thereafter, it shines and becomes manifest—that great splendor appears and becomes visible. Of what nature is it? It is shining in the midst of space, equal to the rays of moonlight.
In this place, the Imperishable Supreme Lord becomes directly manifest, appearing in the form of the Witness. 37-38.

He asks, "What is that very [reality]? and replies with the words "eternal bliss," and so forth: "Just as Rāhu, situated within the sky, [eclipses] the moon and the sun, so too in this place does the Supreme Lord, the imperishable Blessed One, become manifest as the Witness, like Rāhu situated within the sky in the orbs of the moon and the sun. (39)

This is the great abode of the Blessed One, the supreme resting place of the universe; having fixed their breath there at the departure of life, virtuous men enter that all-pervading Lord—the ancient Puruṣa, the source of the world, the poet known through the Vedāntas, who shines eternally, and whose sole root is perpetual, supreme bliss.
Below the visarga is a thousand-petaled lotus facing downward, with its mass of filaments reddened;
within it rests the moon, possessing three peaks devoid of the deer, shimmering with a web of rays.
Within that is the extremely subtle Brahma-randhra, which serves as the support for the channel called Suṣumnā;
this is the divine state, exceedingly secret, inaccessible even to the gods, well-guarded, and a place of great refuge. 42.
This is the supreme abode of the Kula known as Kailāsa, where the God of gods, Bhava—the swan-like Maheśa who destroys the darkness of fear—resides in the form of the Bindu, his own essential nature.

He is the primordial deity of all beings, accessible through Yoga to yogins, bestowing their desired fruits; he pours forth within the inner self a continuous, celestial stream of the flowing essence of aesthetic delight (rasa). 43.

By the mere knowledge of this state, there shall be no further rebirth for men in this saṃsāra; and through the yoga of continuous placement, they shall possess the complete power to create and dissolve the entire aggregate of beings. (44)

Having fixed his mind here upon the supreme state named Kailāsa, which is the abode of the swan (the *haṃsa*), the yogi—having cast away the afflictions of worldly existence and transcended death—lives for a long time, liberated from mortality. 45.
In this place dwells that sixteenth digit of the moon, free from the states of waning and waxing, eternally risen, facing downwards, and possessing a luster like the rising sun;
it resembles a hundredth part of a hair-tip split into a hundred pieces, and because of its subtlety, it bears a stream of nectar flowing without interruption. 46.
Beyond this stands the Blessed Lady, the sovereign of the presiding deities of the elements; she is known as Nirvāṇa, curved like a half-moon, and is contained within the sixteenth digit.
She who is the mother of the three worlds is similar in subtlety to a single strand of a hair split a thousandfold; she possesses the radiance of twelve suns. 47.

Regarding the phrase "in the maṇḍala," because Piṅgalā consists of the nature of the moon and the sun, Suṣumnā is established as Rāhu, since it is the devourer (bhoktṛ) situated between Iḍā and Piṅgalā. || 39 ||

"Having dissolved" means: that very abode of the universe, which is the nature of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), is the station of the Blessed One. Having caused the vital breath (*samīraṇa*) to ascend to that place—the place of command—virtuous men enter the Puruṣa who is sporting and playing.

Therefore, they enter the one who is ancient, free from old age and death, devoid of decay and mortality, to be known through Vedānta, and the primordial source of the universe; he whose birth occurred at the beginning of the universe, the all-pervading Lord who is the sole original source of great bliss. 40.

He calls the thousand-petaled lotus the "thousand-spoked lotus" (*sahasrārapadma*); the meaning is that the enclosure-petal is a thousand-petaled lotus. It is the state beyond speech (*avāgbhavyā*) belonging to the station of *Kula* and so forth, which is the form of the Visarga transcending all forms.

Upon its downward-facing [surface], there is a cluster of slightly reddish filaments; thus, the meaning is "having red stamens. Devoid of a deer—that is, with its spot destroyed—it is joined with two horns, being triangular in shape, with a shimmering web of rays—that is, a mass of flashing light—the nectar-rayed moon rests there. (41)

"Contained within that" means: in the midst of that [body] is the *brahmarandhra* (the aperture of Brahmā), which is of subtle form. Within the channel called *suṣumnā*, which serves as the foundation, the *suṣumnā* itself is a digit (*kalā*) that constitutes the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the Supreme Lord, whose nature is partless consciousness (*niṣkala-caitanya*).

Residing in the center of the lunar orb and taking the *brahmarandhra* as its support, it has entered the body; this is the meaning. Thus it is said in the *Yogārṇava*: "That very sphere where the Power (*śakti*) dissolves is the foundational sphere (*ādhāramaṇḍala*)."

That which is this *visarga* (the emission), the auspicious word consisting of three [parts], is indeed that which is called Kailāsa; it is the *bindu* (point) whose nature consists of both *puṃs* (spirit) and *prakṛti* (matter). *Prakṛti* is the *mātrā* (vowel/measure), while the *bindu* and the *sarga* (emission) together constitute the *haṃsa*.

This entire world has that as its essence. Of what nature is he? He is the primordial being, the very form of the beginning. He releases a celestial stream within his inner self, in the interior. What kind of stream? One that flows with the overflow of *rasa* (essence/flavor); *rasa* is a particular substance. Therein, he is white (*sitāṃ*); the Lord is accessible through yoga and bestows the desired fruits upon yogins.
Here, at this site of Kailāsa, [the state of] having restrained pride is [attained]; thus [it is said] further on. 42–43.
He demonstrates the excellence of this place with the words "of this place," and so forth; this is easy to understand. || 44 ||

"In the supreme abode": he whose diseases have departed—that is, he by whom both mental anxieties (*ādhi*) and physical ailments (*vyādhi*) have been cast down. His splendor is equal to the morning sun; it is subtler than the sixteenth digit (*kalā*) of the moon (*śaśabhṛt*). Of what kind is the moon? It is such that it is divided into hundreds of parts from the tip of a hair (*bālāgra*); because of its extreme subtlety, each single part is like this. Of what kind is [his splendor]? It shines like a bearer of a continuous stream of nectar (*pīyūṣa*), resembling a cloud raining down nectar. 45–46.

Regarding the phrase "of this": beyond this sixteenth digit (kalā), in the supreme state, resides the Blessed Lady as the sovereign of Maheśvara, the lord of all beings; she has reached that digit known as Nirvāṇa, the sixteenth digit of Nirvāṇa. Of what nature is she? She is like a single part of a hair-tip divided and split a thousandfold, being subtle; her radiance and splendor are equal to twelve suns. || 47 ||

The supreme power of Nirvāṇa, situated above the collection of parts known as Nirvāṇa, possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns; she is profoundly deep, subtler than the tip of a hair, equal to a ten-millionth part thereof.
She is the mother of all, eternally arisen, stainless, and the ground of the state of eternal bliss; from her vast expanse flows a streaming torrent, and she is without support. (48)
Beyond this, higher than the highest, is the station of Nirvāṇa-śakti—the eternal, incomparable, stainless, ever-arisen, and actionless state of Śiva.
The wise call that the station of Viṣṇu; some call it the station of Brahmā, some the station of Haṃsa, some the station of Nirañjana, and others the station of Nirālambana. 49.

Having repeatedly projected his power from its abode in the Lotus-born (Brahmā) along with himself into these locations ending with the Command (Ājñā), and having meditated upon them in sequence with an attentive heart, he should lead it to the end of Nāda;
then, for the attainment of his desired fruit, he should meditate on the Primordial Power, whose form is consciousness, residing within the great lotus-abode situated in the sky (the void).
Having directly drunk the divine flood of nectar—which resembles lac-dye—from the swan residing in the great lotus-abode situated in the sky, one should enter once more into the center of the Kula.

In each and every wheel (cakra), one should gradually satiate those deities, Hākinī and all the others, with the spreading streams of nectar-essence; then, one should satiate that Kuṇḍalinī who dwells in the state of the lotus-born.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya* composed by the illustrious Nāgabhaṭṭa.
(Page 49) The sixth chapter:
The self-manifested liṅga (*svayambhūliṅga*) is within the opening of one’s own source (*nijayoni*), inside the lotus of the heart (*hṛtsarasīruha*).
The wise call the one born from the water of the sky "Bāla" (the Child), while others say it is the opposite; they speak of the other [the "Old"] as being in between. ||1||

Having meditated upon that seed-syllable known as Vāgbhava—which resembles molten gold—as the self-arisen *talliṅga* in its proper place within the hollow of the heart-lotus, one should then, being tranquil in form, contemplate the second seed-syllable called Kāma, which has the radiance of a spreading *bandhujīva* flower and the splendor of the autumnal moon, situated in the other location. || 2 ||

Having fixed the vital breaths within the source (the *mūlādhāra*), they meditate with their mind upon that Bhāratī, known as the Seed (*bīja*), which has risen from the navel-cavity by resting in the aperture of its own source.

Regarding the word "Nirvāṇa": she is the power of Nirvāṇa situated above the station or place called the digit of Nirvāṇa. Her radiance is like ten million suns; she is exceedingly profound. Of what nature is she? She is equal to the tip of the hair on the head of the moon (the crescent). Her station is the state of eternal bliss, the station of Śiva.
In that context, "urū" means great; "vigaladdhārā" refers to one from which streams are flowing; and "nirālambanā" means devoid of support. || 48 || 49 ||

"Having caused [the Śakti] to ascend": having caused the Śakti to ascend from the *mūlādhāra*, the abode born of the lotus, together with the self, and having meditated upon the Śakti in these locations, one should lead her in sequence to the end of the *nāda* and meditate upon her as the form of consciousness situated within the "abode"—that is, the house which is the great lotus of Brahman located in the ether. || 50 ||

"Directly": having drunk the flood of divine nectar, one should enter the central region of the body of the Kula, the *mūlādhāra*, where the haṃsa resides upon a great lotus situated in the sky. Then, one should satisfy the *ḍākinīs* and others who reside in each of the cakras from all sides with the masses of nectar-fluid; thereafter, one should satisfy Kuṇḍalinī, who dwells at the base of the lotus in the *mūlādhāra*. || 51 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Padārthādarśa, a commentary on the Tripurāsāra.

Thus, having described the specific yogas regarding the supports (*ādhāras*), he begins to state the specific features of the *svayambhū-liṅga*, the *bāṇa*, and so forth, within the supports beginning with the *mūlādhāra*, starting with the words "the *svayambhū-liṅga*. Regarding the phrase "between the *yoni* and the *brahmarandhra*": the *svayambhū-liṅga* goes to dissolution in that place shaped like a horn which was previously mentioned, where one should recite [mantras]; for it is said, "that *liṅga* and the *liṅga* consisting of the moving and the unmoving," and "the *liṅga* residing in the heart-lotus."

The "other" *liṅga* means the supreme *liṅga*. Regarding the phrase "between the eyebrows," others explain the word "other" (*itara*) as follows: that other *liṅga* is situated in the drop (*bindu*) within the space between [the eyebrows]. Still others say it refers to the lotus of the sky (*gaganāmbuja*), meaning the stainless state of the supreme *bindu* known as the *visarga*. || 1 ||

He describes the meditation on the three seed-syllables (bījas) of the Śrīmūla-vidyā as being the Svayambhū-liṅga, the Bāṇa-liṅga, and the Īśvara-liṅga, beginning with the words "yadvījam" (which seed). The meaning is: one should meditate on that first seed-syllable called Vāgbhava, which resembles stainless gold, together with the Svayambhū-liṅga at the Mūlādhāra; on that middle seed-syllable called Kāma, which resembles a flower, together with the Bāṇa-liṅga in the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus; and on the third seed-syllable, which resembles the autumnal moon, together with the Paraliṅga (the Supreme Liṅga) in the station of the Ājñā-cakra. || 2 ||

For those who perceive the Blessed Lady, whose splendor is as red as the rising sun, in the form of the Siddhaliṅga, there alone is the incomparable wealth of poetic genius that distills nectar. (Verse 3)

Those of unswerving mind who constantly meditate upon her—who, beautiful with vermilion-red, illuminates the entire lineage, resides within the lotus of the heart, and takes the form of a Bāṇaliṅga—those divine women, afflicted by desire, lament before their feet on the earth with restless hearts until the rising of the moon. 4.

Those who meditate with their own inner luster upon Gaurī, known by other names, in the form of a *liṅga* situated at the station of the *bindu*, manifesting the beauty of the crescent moon; who bear the likeness of the half-moon and the ear-ornament (*śruti*) of the great lotus located at the *visarga*; and who possess a stream consisting of nectar, pale-red as coral—they are the abode of all prosperity. 5.

The excellent practitioner, having fixed his intellect steadily upon these three locations—the three signs characterized by exceedingly intense splendor and endowed with the sacred scriptures—should mutter the mantra one hundred thousand times. Thereafter, he should perform a fire sacrifice at night with fresh flowers from the *brahmataru* tree smeared with honey, using the *cāra* [the movement of the breath]. || 6 ||

Having fearlessly caused the moon, marked by the hare, to descend from the vault of the sky to the depths of the netherworld (pātāla), and having grasped it while stationed there, the wise one—having encircled it with the sun and brought it into the mouth of Rāhu for the commencement of the skull-bowl ritual (*kapālika-karaṇa*)—should offer it into the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) using the hand-vessel (*hastakaraṇḍaka*). This oblation (*homa*) is most extraordinary. (7) [Page 51]
The mortal who, with his mind fixed on Śiva, performs this very [rite] for one year here, immediately conquers death and attains a pre-eminent nourishment of the body;
like the god of love, he shatters the pride of deer-eyed women, and with a mass of beautiful, curly hair as lovely as a swarm of female bees, he shall live for many years. 8.

He describes the specific fruits of the recitation (*japa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*) upon these three seeds with the words beginning "prāṇān yonigatān" and so forth. "By splendors beautiful and crimson like vermilion" means by the entire *kula*, that is, the wheels (*cakras*) starting from the *mūlādhāra*. "Arising as far as the moon" means up to the station of the *bindu*; she is manifested by Maheśa, who captivates the beauty of the moon of nectar. Those who meditate on her in such a form, having the shape of a *liṅga*, they are the locus, the place of all prosperity. With these three verses, he describes in full the specific meditation for those performing the recitation of the three *liṅgas*.

"One should mutter a hundred thousand [times]" means that for whichever seed-syllable resides in whichever *liṅga*, one should perform a hundred-thousand-fold recitation (*lakṣajapa*) of that. By this, the rule is that with the three seed-syllables, there is a hundred-thousand-fold recitation for each, while the collective recitation of all three is three hundred thousand. "With flowers born from the Brahma-tree" refers to *palāśa* blossoms. "At night by movement" means when the *vāyu* (wind) has entered the *iḍā* channel. (3–6)

He states the specific optional rites [beginning] with the words "without hesitation. *Hariṇāṅga* refers to the wind situated in the *iḍā* channel; this is a metaphorical designation of the effect by the name of its cause. From the "vault of the sky," that is, from the location of the nose, one should offer [the breath] into the "root of the underworld," which is the *mūlādhāra*. Having reached the *brahmarandhra*, one should unite the two winds—[the breath] there with the sun, namely the *piṅgalā* wind—and having taken up that wind, one should offer it as an oblation into the mouth of the *kuṇḍalī* located at the "mouth of Rāhu" by means of the "hand-basket," that is, by means of the mind in the form of a hand.

The term *kapālikaraṇapaṇḍitaḥ* means one who is wise (*prājña*) in the procedure known as *kapālikaraṇa*; here, *paṇḍita* signifies one who knows the upward and downward application (*ūrddhādhaḥkaraṇa*). However, the hidden meaning (*guptārtha*) is revealed somewhat: having offered into the sacrificial pit located at the mouth of Rāhu a specific substance belonging to the body of Hari, which has been placed in a specific location and mixed with a specific substance situated in that particular place by means of the Sun, one should sacrifice (*juhuyāt*) using the "hand-vessel" (*hastakaraṇḍaka*), that is, the ladle in the form of a hand.

The notion of it being a physical substance (*dravya*) is not to be disclosed; for explaining this matter, one incurs the derision of the learned. And the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi* states: "Rāhu, having seized the head or the body [of the Sun], enters with his mouth when he is joined with that lunar day (*tithi*) in order to swallow the solar self.

O Lord of Gods, from the station of the sky, the Sun falls into the netherworld (*pātāla*) and reaches Rāhu’s discus. Then, on that day, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) through the mouth of Rāhu."

In that regard, whatever substance is produced therein is indeed the *kuṇḍagolaka*. The *kuṇḍa* [is obtained] through the assistance of Śiva, and the *golaka* from the swan of Śiva. Among these three, the great *svayambhūkusuma* (spontaneously arisen flower) is found in some places by the King of the Gandharvas, or perhaps not at all. O Goddess, if it is obtained, one should mix it with lac juice, combine it with musk and saffron, form it into a pill (*vaṭī*), and keep it secret.

Having written down the King of Mantras, one should perform the ritual application (*prayoga*) with it. Upon reaching that specific lunar day (*tithi*), the entire family rises up of its own accord. O God! There is no doubt that the Goddess will partake of the nectar of both [the practitioner and the deity].

Those mantras and *vidyās* which were afflicted by defects such as being dormant (*supta*) or bound (*kīlita*), become awakened through this application until she returns again. O Goddess! When the second [lunar day] has passed, she who is visible is Kalāvatī; following the sequence of lunar days, that Goddess bestows the fruit of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*). By revealing this meaning, the curse of the deities arises. How then was that indicated so extensively? || 7 ||

He states the fruit of the completed observance with the word "one": being equal to Kandarpa (the god of love), he who shatters the pride of the deer-eyed women shall live for many years—that is, he shall become long-lived.

Of what sort? He whose mass of hair (*kuntalavayaḥ*, i.e., *keśasamūhaḥ*) is curly (*arālaḥ*) and crooked in form. Then there is the compound *bhṛṅgāṅganā-śreṇi-śrī-mān-arāla-kuntalaḥ*, a *karmadhāraya* meaning: he who possesses the beauty (*śrī*) of rows of female bees (*bhṛṅgāṅganā-śreṇī*), and who is curly-haired (*arāla-kuntala*). || 8 ||

Then one should meditate upon the Goddess, whose face is bright with a gentle smile like the full autumn moon; her tresses are as dark as a swarm of bees; she shines with three eyes resembling blossoming blue lotuses, and the luster of her rows of teeth surpasses the brilliance of a string of pearls. (Verse 9)
She bore a lower lip lovely with a luster as charming as the Bandhūka flower or evening clouds, made radiant by the rays of her gentle smile;
she also bore a pair of beautiful earrings and cheeks as pale as the moon’s fragments. 10.
Bending under the weight of her lofty, closely-set breasts, she was as lovely as a *vanamrā* creeper;

she possessed waves of triple folds (*trivalī*) shimmering like those on a forest vine, a deep cavity of the navel, thighs like the best of plantain trunks, and lotus-feet that were rosy-red. || 11 ||
She bears upon her head the digit of the moon, from which flows a stream of pure nectar; she also wears a crest fashioned from the blossoms of the Santāna tree.
She is clothed in fine garments as white as the slough of the moon, and she is mounted upon a great bull, white as ten million moons rising from within her belly.

Holding in her two right hands a rosary made of crystal beads and the auspicious *jñānamudrā*, with her left hands holding a jewel-encrusted crown, a book, and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*);

her hips encircled by a jeweled girdle, adorned with jeweled armlets and necklaces, endowed with divine ornaments, the mother of the three worlds, anointed with divine perfumes—[thus one should visualize her]. (13)
(Verse 14) Though she incessantly disgorges the entire web of scriptures, she is complete in every digit of beauty;
her lotus feet are adorned by the dust from the garlands on the crowns of the hosts of bowed gods and asuras.
