Having meditated upon that Vāgīśvarī, one should bring her from the seat of the Great Bindu situated in the sky to the state beyond; then, immediately after that, one should lead her back to the place from which she came.

From that state of peace beyond, she of incomparable majesty should be led to the solar disc; from there to the lotus of the sky, and from there, she who is praised by all the worlds, one should lead her to the realm of the departed (Pretabhūmi).
From the abode of the Pretas, one should lead her to the half-moon (ardhacandra), and from there to the beginning of the bridge (setubandha).
From that, she reaches the void (vyoma), and from that, one should contemplate her as having reached the immeasurable station of Īśvara.
Therefore, one should lead the Goddess from the abode of Rudra to the station of Viṣṇu;
from the station of Viṣṇu to the station of Brahmā; and from the station of Brahmā to the center of the abode of Kuṇḍalinī.

Then, one should consecrate the Goddess with an uninterrupted stream of nectar shining from the Bindu—known as the Visarga, Ga, Kha, and Ga—situated within that lotus which has a thousand petals, beautiful pericarp and filaments, and radiant splendor, and which is coiled like a serpent. || 18 ||
Then one should meditate upon the Goddess; this is easy to understand. || 9 ||

What kind of goddess? One who bears lips as lovely as the dense mass of *bandhūka* flowers belonging to the Sun; lovely and desirable with a luster like that of their interior, made radiant by the rays of her gentle smile. Furthermore, what kind? One whose waves of the triple-fold (*trivalī*) shimmer upon an abdomen that is charming, unpropped, and bent low by the weight of her lofty breasts.

Her thighs were like the massive trunks of the plantain trees of Rāma; she possessed reddish lotus-like feet; and she bore upon her head a digit of the moon—what kind of digit? One from which a mass of nectar was trickling. This he imagines to be like a crest-jewel, as if fashioned from the flowery shoots of the *santānaka* tree, or like a crown composed of the blossoms of the *kalpa* tree.

The moon is the maker of frost; "nirmokī" means one who has cast off his slough. Likewise, she is pure and stainless, wearing fine garments, and likewise mounted upon the Great Bindu, having ascended to the station of the Bindu above the sky. Furthermore, her belly is as white as ten million moons, resembling a full, perfect ten-million-fold moon. || 10–14 ||

Having thus meditated upon Vāgīśvarī, one should bring her from the seat of the *bindu* (vindu-pīṭha) to the station that lies beyond half of the *bindu*-seat. From that transcendent station (*atīta-sthāna*), one goes to the station of the sun’s heat (*ātapa-sthāna*); from that station of heat to the station beyond peace (*śāntātīta*); from that station beyond peace to the wheel of the sun (*sūryacakra*); from there to the lotus of space (*vyomāmbhoja*); from there to the station of the *preta*, then the station of Śiva; from the station of the *preta* to the half-moon (*ardhacandra*); from there to the beginning (*ārambha*); from there to the bridge-bond (*setubandha*); from there again to space (*vyoma*); from there to the abode of Īśvara; from the house of Rudra to the station of Śakti. || 15 || 16 ||

Therefore, he asks what the abode of Kuṇḍalinī is, and says: "By the thousand. (p. 54) By this constant meditation on the Goddess, performed while situated in the emission (*visarga*) within the [cavity] adorned with a thousand petals, death goes to its destruction;
and those supernatural powers (*siddhis*) which belong to the Lord of the Divine Hosts, those too come to men before long. (19)

Those of pure intellect who, on this earth, meditate upon Goddess Bhavānī—who shines forth from the *ādhāra* (the foundational center) as far as the great lotus situated in *akula*, whose form is like a radiant and stainless luster vibrating through the *brahmanāḍī*, and who is of the nature of the *liṅga*—become knowers of reality, freed from all sins and endowed with every virtue, being accessible through meditation alone. 20.

Those who sprinkle from all sides the entire body of the Goddess of Speech—with streams of nectar flowing from within white lotuses—thereby moistening the pores of her skin which are illuminated by the expansive mass of splendor as white as cow’s milk, frost, or a pearl necklace; they are the very death of Death herself. 21.

Those who constantly sprinkle upon the earth with an abundant stream of divine nectar the Goddess Kālāgradūtī—who bears the form of the *liṅga*, is joined by gods and asuras, resides within the central *suṣumnā* channel, and possesses a luster dark like a mass of collyrium—and who possess the skill of vision that uproots the very form of men, for them, whence could there be decay? (22)

Those with beautiful, limited vision remember Tripura—whoever within their lineage remembers her as being like a fiber from a broken lotus stalk soaked in lac-dye—as one afflicted by passion; yet those fair-browed women, resembling the Lord of Rati himself, forget him and remember [only her]. 23.

Those who, casting aside all shame, meditate upon the radiance of the beloved of Hara—which makes the sky appear as if suffused with a flood of vermilion and the circle of the earth as if moistened with liquid lac—find their beloveds approaching them on this earth according to their desires. (Page 55) 24.

He who, by means of the *haṃsa*, leads the primordial Śakti—who resides in the lotus-born Brahmā—to the interior space within the heart, where she is like a lotus from which a mass of nectar-drops has fallen from the center of the oozing lunar disc, and who constantly remembers her as being situated in the sky (the void) by means of the Self—he shall bring about the dissolution of the cosmic egg, the destruction of the body, and the death of death itself. 25.

One should meditate upon her, who is accessible through devotion, as yellow-hued for rites of immobilization and the like, white as the moon for rites of pacification and the like, smoke-colored for rites of eradication and the like, and glowing like the hibiscus flower for the attraction of the people of the three worlds and for magical operations (kārmaṇa).

One should constantly meditate on her as resembling a pure crystal gem for the attainment of supernatural powers such as moving through the air (khecaratva), and as resembling the cloudless sky for liberation itself.

On this path, one should practice nine hundred thousand [recitations] for the attainment of the imperishable state; thereafter, by means of a hundred thousand [recitations], one attains here the fivefold incomparable accomplishment (*siddhi*) of mantras.

These are located at the base, the generative organ, the navel region, the heart, the throat, as well as the uvula, the space between the eyebrows, the abode of the Lord of Beings (the forehead), and finally at the end of the nine (the crown of the head). || 27 ||

One should consecrate the Goddess with the stream of nectar that shines forth from the point called *kha-ga* (the bindu) located there—shining like the luster of gold at the *ādhāra*, in the form of a radiant lamp at the place of the six faces (*ṣaṇmukha*), resembling the splendor of the rising sun at the navel, and within the lotus of the heart.

[Objection: But surely the abode of Kuṇḍalinī is the *mūlādhāra*; how then can this be said? [Response: This is true; however, the wise know the abode of Kuṇḍalī to extend from the *mūla* up to the *brahmarandhra*.

Having concealed the first [state] within the abode, she shines as the guardian of knowledge; having reached the station of Viṣṇu through good fortune, she radiates in her own temple. There, that goddess Kuṇḍalinī, the supreme deity, is the giver of knowledge, where ignorance and wisdom are manifested together. Having made the entire world like a prison, she remains there as Power (Śakti)—the power Kuṇḍalinī, joined with the Haṃsa. He who, by means of the soul and the Haṃsa-mantra, leads [her] from the root-center to the thousand-petalled lotus and meditates upon her, for him even a dense calamity becomes a mere garment. (17–25)

He describes meditation regarding the specific types of ritual action with the words "having a yellow luster" (*pītābhām*). He describes the recitation performed for desired results (*kāmyajapa*) with the words "on this path" (*mārge'smin*). On this path, namely the *suṣumṇā* channel, one should observe—that is, meditate—upon the aforementioned locations for the sake of attaining imperishable fruit, which is the attainment of the fruit of liberation (*mokṣa*).

And there are five kinds of incomparable accomplishments (*siddhi*): the [eight] accomplishments beginning with the power over the underworld (*pātāla*), the pill (*guṭikā*), gold, the sword (*khaḍga*), and the seal (*mudrā*), as well as those known as mastery over mantras, mastery over yoga, and self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*). || 26 || 27 ||

To the question of where and in what form one should meditate and recite, he says: "The Support" (ādhāra). One should visualize [the deity] in the form of a lamp at the location of the six faces—that is, at the six supports of the body (pṛṣṭha 56)—and likewise as having the radiance of the light of the sun; at the throat, one should visualize her in the shape of a lamp-flame, shining with the luster of a multitude of jewels; and between the eyebrows, [one should visualize her]. || 28 ||
And at the end of the nine [worlds] is that light, skilled in destroying the darkness of the fear of worldly existence; it is called Viṣṇu, the generator of waves of unsurpassed bliss;
difficult to attain by sinners, it is known as Traipura, the sustainer of the three worlds, which stands above all principles (tattvas) and is supreme. 29.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*.
The seventh chapter begins:
Now, [this] which is held even by the lords of the immortals, by the lords of the Dānavas, and by the renowned hosts of Siddhas...
I shall now describe that mantra which is the sole cause of good fortune, prosperity, and all virtuous qualities. || 1 ||

With his entire body smeared with camphor powder, pure and purified by bathing, wearing linen cloth and bright, variegated patterns clearly fashioned from sandalwood paste, the practitioner— having applied collyrium to both eyes, attaining the height of joy through the acquisition of sweet flavors, and with the cavity of his mouth filled with a mouthful of betel— should draw the King of Mantras.

On a vessel made from a section of the moon-stone (*sudhākara-khaṇḍa*), filled with musk, agallochum (*aguru*), cow-meat, and jaggery, along with sandalwood paste and combined with *svayambhū* flowers, one should write within the opening using a golden needle upon a broad leaf of the *bhuja* tree. (Verse 3)
The wise king should draw the petals; inside that [the circle] he should draw the petals for the month, and outside that region the petals for the fortnights.
Furthermore, O King, the wise one should draw the beautiful petals for the days outside those petals.
Then, within the center of the great yoni in the pericarp (karṇikā), one should write the seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbhava) and the seed-syllable of Desire (Kāma), along with Śakti.
Above those two, one should place the god Haṃsa; and above that, on the sixteen-spoked [lotus], one should place the Mistress of the World (Jagannāyikā). || 5 ||
Then, one should again write the sixteen vowels upon the twelve-spoked [wheel], and there, the seed-syllable of Kāma;
one should write it divided by the vowels of the Lord of Days (the Sun), and having thus prepared the final seed-syllable on the other sixteen-spoked [wheel].

The meaning is: in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*. One should meditate upon that light which is fresh, resembling the color of the morning sun, and whose radiance is like the flash of a donkey’s bray or the glare of a woman in labor. That very light which ascends upwards as far as the end of the *nāda* is called the *bindu*; it generates supreme bliss, is not an object of passion for those of sinful nature, and is the sovereign, supreme glory.
It is well-known, it is to be realized, and it stands above the twenty-four principles (*tattvas*). || 28 || 29 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*.

Having thus described the specific meditations upon the seed-syllables (*vāgbhava* and others) located in the *mūlādhāra* and other sites as being of the nature of self-manifested (*svayambhū*) *bāṇaliṅgas*, [the author] next states the mantra for the Yantra that bestows all sovereignty, beginning with the words "Then by the lords of the immortals" (*athāmarendraiḥ*), etc., [verse 1]. This includes the characteristics of good fortune (*saubhāgya-lakṣaṇa*) and so forth.

"One whose entire body is smeared with camphor powder" means one by whom the whole body is anointed with *karpūrakṣoda*, that is, broken camphor; this refers to the functioning of the senses and the mind. "Wearing silken cloth" (*kṣauma*) means wearing a woven silk garment (*paṭṭavastra*). "With a shining forehead-mark (*tilaka*) clearly fashioned from sandalwood paste" refers to one who possesses such a mark in the shape of a sectarian streak (*puṇḍra*).

Having applied collyrium to his pair of eyes, he experiences a joy arising from obtaining betel leaves dripping with sweet flavor; by that joy he is preeminent and excellent. Thus, with the cavity of his mouth filled with a morsel of betel and his internal state uplifted, his voice and physical appearance being such, his mind acting as a bee toward the lotus-feet of Ambikā, he should draw the yantras preceded by prostrations at the feet of his own guru. This is what he says with the verse beginning "karpūracodadigdhāṅgaḥ" (II.2).

He states the materials for drawing the yantra, beginning with "kastūrikā" and so forth. *Sudhākara-khaṇḍa* is a piece of camphor; *paṭīra* is red sandalwood. Substances such as *kuṇḍa-gola* and others, which are to be learned from the mouth of the Guru, have not been disclosed here because they are difficult to obtain even for deities. [One should draw] on a large *ūrja* leaf that is without holes—that is, without fissures—using a golden needle, which is a gold stylus. || 3 ||

He describes the method of drawing the diagram with the words "one should write the sixteen kings" and so forth. The "sixteen kings" (bhūpāḥ) refers to the sixteen sovereigns. Namely: Māya, Ambarīśa, Śaśabindu, Aṅga, Pṛthu, Amarāvāna, Svarata, Svāhādra—[these] letters beginning with *ka*, shining brilliantly as they touch the region of the head by means of the *kalā*, *bindu*, and *nāda* [ornaments], one should write upon ivory plates. All of this, situated within the interior of the temple of the earth, one should fashion. (7)
Then the mantra-practitioner should wrap this venerable king of mantras all around with a hollow tube;
having bound it with a very pure gold band, he should perform this which has been accomplished through his own practice and so forth.

This protection was worn constantly by the Lord who destroyed Tripura, by the beloved of Śrī, by the preceptor of the thirty gods, by Hari, by Kandarpa, by the one whose rays emit nectar, by the son of Vinatā, and even by the one whose luster is exceedingly hot.
It is held by Gandharvas and Kinnaras, by Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, by Siddhas and the hosts of Sādhyas, by the best of Pannagas, Vidyādharas, and Guhyakas;

it is cherished by those seeking good fortune with pure hearts, by beautiful beings who are auspicious to the world, and even by the best of men, kings who desire self-mastery and are full of longing.

(Verse 11, p. 59) Here, in the tumultuous battle, by the power of the king of machines, the lord of men attains the glory of victory with elephants whose broad temples are smeared with streams of rutting ichor.
By holding this most excellent of instruments, even a common man attains victory over disputants in gambling, legal proceedings, and debate within the palace of a king. 12.
For men wandering through forests filled with herds of buffaloes, tigers, elephants,
and bears, no fear arises for long once they bear the excellent weapon of Tripura.
The best of lords of men become submissive and dependent upon him, as do his ministers and their sons;
likewise, women full of passion, rich in youth, bent by the weight of their breasts, and moving with graceful gait [come under his sway]. 14.
Even this most fierce poison here, resembling the Kālakūṭa and expert in the act of destruction, certainly becomes nectar for one who wears this sovereign Tripura-machine. 15.
This fire, though possessing many flickering flames spread and rising within the forest,
acts as a solid ground for this embodied being who holds the supreme mechanical device, and even for the ocean, the storehouse of waters.
Having meditated upon the Lord of the Yantra within the petal above the pericarp of the heart-lotus, the wise practitioner performs the coming and going of the Śakti within the Suṣumnā.

He who is that eternal abode of unbroken merit is never abandoned on this earth by Speech, the Goddess of Fortune, and Wisdom, who share an incomparable state of grammatical coreferentiality with him. 17.

Vāyu, Dilīpa, Giri, Rantideva, Yayāti, Ātmabhū, Raghu, and Bhagīratha—these sixteen lunar kings represent the sixteen petals (the meaning is that they are the sixteen petals). Outside of that are the lunar petals, twelve petals; outside of that, again, sixteen petals; and further outside, the dental petals, thirty-two petals.

Then, in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), in the center of the Great Yoni (*mahāyoni*), within the six triangles, is the leaf of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) consisting of Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti, along with the Peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) and the syllable of wonder (*āścarya*).
Above these two, *kāma* and *rāja*, one should write the *haṃsa-mantra*, and above that, the root-vidyā (*mūlavidyā*).

On the sixteen petals, one should write the sixteen vowels; the reading "the sixteen *ekāra*-vowels" refers to the writing of the sixteen vowels. Furthermore, on the twelve-spoked [wheel], one should write the *kāma-bīja*, which is the second seed-syllable of Bālā. Then, on the subsequent sixteen-spoked [wheel], one should write the *rajobīja* (the *rā* syllable), which is intermingled with the twelve vowels—the lords of the day (*vāsareśa*)—and the *aikāra*-vowels, having been substituted in place of the *aukāra*. || 4–6 ||

Then, with the *kalās*, *bindus*, and *nādas*—that is, with the *bindus* and *nādas* which are the very nature of the *kalās* and are fixed upon the region of the head—one writes [the letters] upon the thirty-two petals using the thirty-two syllables beginning with *ka*.

Others, however, explain it differently: "The *kalā* is the speech-born *bindu*; the *sanāda* is the letter *ha*; [and the others are] the letters *ka* and so forth, distinct from the *aikāra*, *sa*, and *ha*. Thus, [it refers to the mantra] whose essence consists of *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*.

On the earth, the temple is square; in the reading "on the earth, Mount Mandara," the meaning is that it is shaped like Mount Mandara, situated in the center of that [square]. Thus it is said: "The letter *kṣa* is declared to be Mount Mandara, and the letter *kṣa* is named Meru. One should enclose it with the letter *ha*, which is Śiva. This [temple] accomplishes the attainments such as those performed by the Self (Ātmakṛta) and the consecration of life-force (Prāṇapratiṣṭhā), and is supported by the all-pervading Brahmā, by Viṣṇu who is beloved by women, and by the gracious Guru Bṛhaspati. (7–10)

The elephants—those whose scent is "bandhura" (unpleasant) or "amanoratha" (undesirable)—meaning great elephants; in the tumultuous battle, in the gambling match (*durodare*), and in worldly dealings; the "lulāpa" is a buffalo, the "citrakāya" is a specific kind of tiger, the "dvipa" is an elephant, and the "kī" is a well-known species of creature;
amidst these forces crowded together, their graceful movement, their act of gathering, and their act of slaughter—skillful in such actions—the fire behaves like the frost, that is, it acts like snow.

What kind of fire is it? It is the forest fire of the wilderness of passion (*davāgnih*), with its flames spread wide and rising upward, flickering intensely. First, one should write the King of Passion (*kāmādhirāja*) situated within the square of the Mind-born God (*manmathakoṣṭhaka*). Then, one should enclose that pair with two *kandarpa*s. Next, the wise one should carefully draw the Makara-bannered God (*makaradhvaja*) in the corners; six times [the name] of the Mind-born God (*manobhava*) should be written with devotion in the center, and the name of the Mind-born God together with his lineage (*sakula*) should be placed within the belly of this [diagram]. (Verse 18)
This yantra, which resembles the lord of the yantras mentioned previously, brings the entire three worlds under one's control when worn on the head, the neck, or the arm.
Beautiful women with lovely tresses, full and firm breasts, and lovely, drooping slender bodies—those whose minds are agitated by desire and constantly inflamed by passion—become subject to him. 19.

Having meditated thus upon the King of Yantras within the hollow of the lotus in the root-cakra, together with the person to be acted upon (sādhya), whose limbs are radiant like the light of the most youthful sun;

and [having visualized] within that Yantra the person to be acted upon, established in a state of stainless luster and consisting of pure consciousness alone—the practitioner, being joyful, should then perform churning by means of the arrows of Mantras according to his own power. (20)

By means of churning, he who is to be mastered necessarily becomes submissive at all times to the preeminent practitioner; even a god of great majesty [is subdued] within twenty-one nights, so what need be said of a mortal of feeble power? (21)
Having carefully drawn a lotus provided with petals, the wise one should write two *śṛṅgāṭas* (triangular figures) within it, joined to one another.
In the center, he should write the Heart-mantra of the Goddess; then, in the corners, the *madanās*; and within those, his own name and that of the desired object to be accomplished. (22)
One should draw this diagram, renowned here as the "Nectar of the Yantra" (Yantrāmṛta), within the hollow interior of the leaves of a lotus; it consists of the vowels.
O best of men, when this yantra is fashioned upon lotus-petals and worn, the entire world becomes auspicious and remains under one's control. 23.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Tripurāsārasamuccaya.
The eighth chapter:
Now I shall describe the external worship of Ambikā, whose command is honored by the three worlds.
By performing this on the surface of the earth, a human being attains a state of being worthy of worship by all people. || 1 ||
He by whom there are flickering sparks and flames; for Amara states: "The words *jvālā*, *kīlā*, *varcas*, *arci*, *śikha*, and *śikhā* denote flame, with the exception that *śikhā* is feminine."

Having meditated upon the King of Yantras in the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus, situated above the earth-pericarp within the heart-lotus, and while reciting the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*), one should raise the Kuṇḍalinī—the power consisting of consciousness—from the *mūlādhāra*, lead it through the *brahmanāḍī* to the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*), and then, being consecrated by the thread-like stream [of nectar] contained therein, lead it back to the *mūlādhāra*. Through such repeated practice, Speech (Vāk), the Desirous One (Kāminī), Sarasvatī, Gominī, and Lakṣmī—she whose prosperity resides in a single locus—do not abandon that person. (11–17)

He describes another yantra, beginning with the words "At the outset" (ādau). At the outset, that is, at the beginning of the Kāmabīja, one should write the syllable *droṃ*, which is the Kāmabīja, in the center of a triangle (*trikoṇa*). One should encircle that triangle with a six-cornered figure accompanied by Kandarpa. Within the six corners, one should write the syllable *lvūṃ*, preceded by Makaradhvaja. All of this should be encircled by the syllable *strīṃ*, which is the seed-syllable of Manobhava. Where is the [place] of Manobhava? In the middle of the Manobhava-bīja, one should write the names of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the practitioner (*sādhaka*). || 18 || 19 ||

Having meditated upon this Kāmabīja-yantra in the center of the lotus-calyx at the Mūlādhāra of the practitioner (*sādhya*), and having meditated within that [yantra] upon the blissful, slow-moving [breath] which resembles the rising sun and consists of pure consciousness alone, one should perform the churning according to one's own power through the sequence of the Guru’s instruction; thus he says "having meditated thus," and so forth. By means of one's own power, the Kuṇḍalinī, through the yoga of moving along the path of churning, one should effect the attainment of nectar.
Some say it is by way of the right channel (*dakṣiṇavartmanā*); that is to be considered. 20–21.

He states another mantra: Having drawn a sixteen-petaled lotus consisting of sixteen petals, and having drawn within its pericarp a six-cornered figure known as the second *śṛṅgāṭa*, one should write the Heart-mantra of the Goddess, *oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ*, in its center.

In five of the six corners, one should write the syllables *hvīṃ*, *lkīṃ*, *aiṃ*, *lvūṃ*, and *strīṃ*. In the final corner, one should write the name of the desired object to be accomplished (*abhimatasādhya*).
On the sixteen petals, one should write the sixteen vowels in the form of vowels, accompanied by the nasal bindu (*savinduka*), filling the interior of the hollow space.
One should place [the medicine] inside the hollow belly of a round vessel. This machine, when carried by a person, makes him a master over the world in this saṃsāra. || 22-23 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Tripurāsāra*.
Following the description of the jewel-like yantras, he begins to explain the procedure for external worship with the word "atha" (now). Regarding the phrase "yad" (where):
in a pure, pleasing house or underground chamber, free from the gaze of the uninitiated (*paśu*).
Having performed the purification of oneself by means of the previously mentioned path, one should thereafter effect the purification of the site. || 2 ||
O Bhagavat, may I endure [the offense] which is joined with the supreme and unprecedented, as well as the sky, fire, and the left eye;
by the sprinkling of water from *kuśa* grass, I am purified on all sides by this mantra. || 3 ||
With this mantra— consisting of the seed-syllable of the logic of *akula* and *sakula* and others, joined with that which precedes Śiva (the letter *Ha*) and accompanied by the crescent moon (*I*),
forming *Hrīm*)— one whose self is composed should perform the sprinkling of the ritual substances with water from *kuśa* grass.
This mantra, joined with *puṣkaram*, *śivamukha*, and so forth, is proclaimed as the purification of the vessel;
then, with this very mantra, a person should wash the entire collection of vessels with pure water. || 5 ||

Then, one should smear the pedestal, which has been washed with water, with self-arisen flowers, moon-fragrance (karpūra), musk, saffron, and yellow orpiment; and upon it, one should draw all around the diagram that will be described hereafter.
Having drawn a triangle followed by a circle for the petals, then a circle outside that;
again, a six-petaled lotus and another circle outside, one should draw eight petals in the region beyond that. (Page 63) || 7 ||
On the northern side of the pedestal, one should worship the lineages of gurus according to the prescribed rite,
beginning from the northwestern direction and ending at the northeast.

Having worshipped the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti) at the base of the seat, as well as Ananta and Kūrma, the practitioner of mantra should also worship the Earth above them with scents and other offerings. 9.

One should worship, in sequence, the four [principles] beginning with Dharma—namely Dharma and the others—with perfumes and other offerings in the four corners of the pedestal starting from the southeast; and in the directions adjacent to those, the four beginning with Adharma.
Having worshipped the triad of sattva, rajas, and tamas upon the pedestal (pīṭha),
one should worship the lotus above that, and within the lotus, the mandalas of the Vasu, the Sun, and the Moon.
One should worship the *preta* situated in the center of the triangle within the lunar disc;
thereafter, having invoked the beloved of Śaṅkara from the heart-lotus, the abode of the world, upon that [seat]. 12.
Having established, restrained, brought near, and thoroughly restrained [the deity], one should display the mudrā.

While performing this, a person—having first performed self-purification through bathing and other rites—attains the worship of all people by means of the yantra, whether in an underground chamber, a subterranean dwelling, a cave, or a house, such that he is not noticed by anyone even as he stands with his neck upraised. ||1||
Having prepared the sacrificial mandala in such a house, one should subsequently purify it with water and cow dung; thus he says, beginning with the word "pure" (śuddha). || 2 ||

The syllable *bhaga* is the letter *e*; the one following it is the letter *ai*; its mouth is the *visarjanīya*. That is joined with the preceding [letter] and endowed with the *anusvāra*. *Magana* is the letter *ha*; *anala* is the letter *ra*; *vāmadṛk* is the letter *ū*; likewise, the previously mentioned *bindu* is applied.
Thus, by means of this mantra *aiṃ rhrīṃ*, this pair—the Earth—is purified for the sake of purification by sprinkling with water from *kuśa* grass and so forth, using this mantra. 3.

He describes the purification of substances: *Akula* is the letter *ha*, and *Kula* is the letter *sa*. Its initial *tarka*-letter (the fifth consonant of the fifth class) is *ṣa*; by moving backward from that, the sixth letter is *ra* (Repha). *Śiva* is the letter *u*; the one preceding that is *ī*. The "half-moon" is the *bindu*. Thus, with the mantra *hrīṃ*, one should perform the purification of substances. || 4 ||

He describes the purification of the vessel with the verse beginning "puṣkara" and so forth. *Puṣkara* is the sky; its seed-syllable is the letter *ha*. *Śiva* is the letter *u*. The "mouth" is the visarga. That which precedes it is the bindu. With this mantra *huṃ*, one should perform the purification of the vessel. || 5 ||

One should draw the yantra on a pedestal smeared with substances such as *svayambhūta* (autogenous) and the like. The details regarding *svayambhūta* and so forth are not written here because they are not to be used [by the uninitiated]; they must be learned directly from the mouth of the Guru. Having drawn a triangle, one should draw a circle outside it, then five petals outside that, then a circle outside that, then six petals outside that, then a circle outside that, and finally eight petals outside that, provided with four gates—this is the remainder of the instruction. (Verses 6–7)

Since the procedures for placing the *arghya* and so forth are well known, they have not been written here. On the northern part of the seat (*pīṭha*), one should worship the lineage of gurus by their own names.

From the northwest (Vāyavya) to the northeast (Īśāna), [one should worship] as follows: "I worship the venerable sandals (*śrīpādukā*) of Prahlādānandanātha," "Sakalānandanātha," "Kumārānandanātha," "Vasiṣṭhānandanātha," "Śukānandanātha," "Vimalānandanātha," and "Vyālānandanātha. The phrase "I worship the venerable sandals" is to be applied in every case. || 8 ||

One should worship Ādhāraśakti at the base of the seat. At the four corners of the pedestal—namely Agni, Sāna (Īśāna), Nirṛti, and Vāyu—one should worship Dharma and the others: Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya. In the cardinal directions—East, West, South, and North—one should worship Adharma and the others: Adharma, Ajñāna, Avairāgya, and Anaiśvarya. The meaning is that these should be worshipped along with the triad beginning with Sattva, accompanied by their respective seed-syllables (bījas).

Above that is a lotus; upon the lotus are the sun, moon, and jewel, joined with the three seed-syllables of the *praṇava*—meaning the seed-syllables *a*, *u*, and *m*. Above that is the *preta*, the supreme Sadāśiva. The mantra is: *He Sauḥ Sadāśivamahāpretapadmāsanāya namaḥ*.

Upon that, having established Hṛdayānandaśivā, the beloved of Śaṅkara, within the handful of flowers held in the hands by means of the *saṃsthāpana-mudrā*, and having caused her to be present by means of the *sannidhikāriṇī-mudrā*, one should duly perform the secret worship known as *sannirodhana*, including the *arghya* and other offerings according to the rules. (Page 64) || 13 ||
In the left triangular corner, one should worship Rati— who holds a noose and a goad, who resembles molten gold,
and who is dressed in captivating attire— subsequently with her own seed-syllable.

One should worship Prīti in the southern corner with her own seed-syllable; she resembles a conch shell, holds a goad in her hand, has a beautiful face, and is resplendent in her attire—worship her with perfumes and other offerings. || 15 ||
The practitioner of mantras should worship the God of the Flower-Arrow, seated before the Goddess, possessing the hue of the bandhūka flower, and holding a bow and arrow in his hands. (16)
The seed-syllable of desire (kāma), which is the Vāgbhava, is declared to be the seed of passion (rati);
the last one, known as Sambhoha, is likewise said to be the seed of delight (prīti).
The deities of the five arrows are to be worshipped in due order with their own mantras upon those five petals.

The young women—Drāviṇī and the others—are resplendent with luster resembling the moon, gold, twilight clouds, blue lotuses, and madder; they are adorned with all ornaments, intoxicated with passion, holding arrows in their left hands, and offering salutations with their remaining hands. 18.
Then, one should worship the goddess named Bhagā, as well as Bhagajihvikā, Bhagāsyā, and Bhagamālinī; likewise, one should worship Bhagākṣī and Bhagāhlādinikā in sequence upon the six petals. (19)

Resembling the deep hue of autumn clouds, the smoke-colored twilight clouds, or the ripened phalinī flower, these lovely young women were radiant with beautiful ornaments; their minds were gladdened by wine, and they were enchanting to behold. (20)
She holds in her [left] hands a sword, a trident, a snake, a vetāla, a staff, and birds, as well as a shield;
with others she displays a skull-fragment that causes wonder, a small drum, and the mudrās known as Nāda and Bindu. 21.

I shall now declare here the seed-syllables (bījas) of the primordial goddesses, beginning with Vāgbhava, together with its staff (daṇḍa), in sequence within the sky (the letter *i*), which is preceded by the Kula (the letter *ka*), joined with the eight (the letter *u*), the left eye (the letter *ī*), and the crescent moon (*bindu*). || 22 ||

One should worship Brahmāṇī at the base of the quarter presided over by Indra (the East)—she who rides a swan, resembles molten gold, has four faces, and possesses three eyes; she holds in her lotus-like hands the *brahmakūrca* vessel, a lotus, a radiant water-pot, and a rosary of lotus seeds; she is beautifully attired, possesses graceful limbs, and always bears a heavy mass of matted locks. || 23 ||

Having restrained [the deity] with the *mudrā* and veiled it with the *avaguṇṭhana-mudrā*, one should display the *mudrā* called *śuddhi*. Then follows the placement of the vital breath (*jīvanyāsa*). Then comes the ritual of complete integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*). Having worshipped in sequence with the previously mentioned six-limbed mantras—the Eye in the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest, and the Weapon in front and in the cardinal directions—and having honored [the deity] with the sixteen offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), one should worship the deities of the retinue (*āvaraṇadevatā*). 9–13.

He says that very thing: "Vāma," etc. The meaning is: on the left of the Goddess, that is, in the aforementioned left portion. One should worship Rati with the seed-syllable of Vāgbhava—she who has the luster of molten gold, whose attire is exceedingly beautiful, and who holds a noose and a goad in her hands. || 14 ||

Having worshipped Prīti with the third seed-syllable—she who has tips of hair pointing southward, resembles a conch shell, possesses an exceedingly beautiful form, has a lovely face, and holds a goad in her hand—one should worship [Kāmadeva] before the Goddess at the tip of the front corner, resembling a Bandhūka flower and holding a bow and arrow, using the Kāma-seed syllable. || 15-16 ||

He states the seed-syllables for these: for Kāma, the seed-syllable of desire; for Bhava, the seed-syllable of delusion; and for the last [Īśvara], the letter *sa*, which is the final of the five arrows beginning with the "melting" arrow (*drāvaṇa*).
One should worship the arrows in the five petals in the order starting from the east. || 17 ||

*Drāṃ*, salutation to Drāviṇī; *Hrīṃ*, salutation to Kṣobhiṇī; *Lkīṃ*, salutation to Vaśīkariṇī; *Lbūṃ*, salutation to Prakāśinī. These women, possessing splendors like camphor, gold, twilight clouds, sapphires, and madder, holding arrows in their right hands and performing salutations with their remaining hands, are to be worshipped in sequence. || 18 ||
Then one should worship the deities beginning with Bhagā: "Aiṃ Śrīṃ Hnīṃ, obeisance to Bhagā; Aiṃ Śrīṃ Hnīṃ, obeisance to Bhagajihvikā; Aiṃ Śrīṃ Hnīṃ, obeisance to Bhagāhlādinī.
As instructed, they should be worshipped in sequence in the east, southwest, northwest, southeast, northeast, and west, holding weapons in their hands and supporting the universe. || 19 ||

Phalinī, Priyaṅgu, Rātri, and Haridrā—each pair of these, in successive order, bears two weapons: the first pair holds a trident and a sword; the second pair holds a serpent and a reed-staff; the third pair holds a spear and a shield; and the fourth pair holds a mace, the seal of wonder, a human skull, and the seal of the sound of a small drum. || 20–21 ||

He states their seed-syllables (*bīja*): *vāk* is the letter *ai*; *bhava* is the single vowel *ā*. *Kula* preceded by *pūrva* (fire) means *kula* is the letter *da*; that [letter] followed by *prātilomyena anala* (fire in reverse order) refers to the third syllable, which is *śa*. *Ambara* is the letter *ha*. Thus, *śa* and *ha* are joined with the letter *ra* and the *bindu*. With this mantra consisting of the triad of seeds—*aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ*—one should worship the deities beginning with Bhaga. || 22 ||
Then he says that the eight powers beginning with Brahmāṇī are to be worshipped on the petals starting from the east of the Goddess; [this refers to] "Brahmāṇīm" and so forth.
The *brahmakūrca* is a Brahmin made of *kuśa* grass. At the base of the leaf of Hari-haya (Indra), that is, on the eastern petal... [23]

One should worship with perfumes and other offerings that Goddess Māheśī, who stands at the root of a tree whose branches obscure the directions, who holds in her staff-like arms a skull, a radiant *ḍamaru* drum, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a trident, and a large axe; she who shines with three eyes, whose crescent moon is bound within the tips of her ruddy matted locks, and who travels having mounted a bull resembling a cluster of stars. (24)

One should worship Kaumārī, who is rich in youth, with a most beautiful face, radiant like saffron, and exceedingly lovely; she who bears in her right hands the spear, the noose, and the goad, as well as the gesture of fearlessness; she who is intoxicated by wine, possesses large and pure eyes, is adorned with all ornaments, and is seated upon a peacock at the base of the petal in the direction of Yama (the south). || 25 ||

One should daily worship with perfumes and other offerings that Vaiṣṇavī goddess who dwells at the root of the *rakṣodik* tree; she has limbs dark as a water-bearing cloud, possesses beautiful hair, and holds in her long arms a bell, a conch, a skull, and a discus.
Seated upon Garuḍa, she is resplendent with a jeweled crown, and she is ever intoxicated by the honey [of wine], her eyes constantly flickering.

One should worship with perfumes and other offerings that Vārāhī, who is eternally worshipped by the universe, who has the face of a boar, who holds a shield, a sword, a fierce plow, and a mace, whose cheeks resound with jeweled earrings, who sits upon a formidable boar as hard as a mountain peak, and whose body possesses a luster like smoke. 27.

One should daily worship Indrāṇī, who is intoxicated with joy, seated upon the celestial elephant, praised by the best of gods, whose own face resembles the orb of the moon, whose ears are like sapphire, whose eyes reach to her ears, and who wears a jeweled crown; she holds a bow, a conch, a thunderbolt, and an arrow in her four lotus-like hands at the base of the tree in the direction of Vāyu (the northwest). (p. 67) 28.

One should worship Cāmuṇḍā at the base of the petal in the northern direction—she who has a fierce laugh, formidable and terrifying fangs, and a fearsome face; she who is three-eyed and holds in her lotus-like hands a sword, a trident, a skull-cup, and a shield; she who is fleshless, red-eyed, the bringer of fear to the three worlds, adorned with skeletons, dwelling in the cremation ground, with hair standing on end.

Afterwards, one should worship Lakṣmī—who is of wondrous form, with a most beautiful face, and the luster of pure gold; who holds in her lotus-hands a rosary, the gesture of fearlessness, a lotus, and a shining citron fruit;

who is honored by the people of the three worlds, endowed with auspicious marks, and bowed down by the weight of her high, full breasts—at the base of the leaf situated in the direction of Īśa (the north-east).
Then Indra, the infinite one, cast his seed into those wombs— his seed which reaches the end of the long sky, the end of the eye, the end of the high mountain peaks,
and the end of the lineage, joined thereafter with Rudra who has no end.
Tiyīśa, together with Ananta, then Bhṛgu, and Hara accompanied by Ananta; Vakānta, and thereafter Bhītīśa accompanied by Vaka.

One should worship Māheśī in the fire-petal (the southeast). Of what nature is she? She who bears the *kalālottama*, the excellent *ḍamaru*, the formidable trident (*śūla*), the large chisel (*ṭaṅka*), the skull, the human head, the supreme bowl (*kharpara*), the water-vessel (*udabhaṭa*), and the excellent *ḍamaru*—that is, the best of hand-drums—[and] the formidable, that is, terrifying trident, the large, that is, great chisel which is a stone-cutter. [She is] bearing these, that is, holding them. 24.
In the south, [one should worship] Kaumārī, seated upon a peacock in the southeast.
In the southwest, [he worships] Vaiṣṇavī. || 26 ||

In the west is Vārāhī; what is she like? She is seated upon a *kola*—a boar—which is as fierce (*khara*) and formidable (*prakhara*) as a mountain peak (*giriśikhara*), and which is terrifying (*ābhīma*). She is called *Dhūmneti*, meaning she possesses an exceedingly smoky (*dhūmra*) complexion. || 27 ||
In the wind [quarter] is Indrāṇī, and she is joined with Svarmātaṅga and Airāvata. || 28 ||

Kauvera asked Cāmuṇḍā: "Of what sort is she? [He replied: "She who has fierce laughter and formidable fangs. By her fierce laughter, her teeth—meaning the fangs—are uplifted, formidable, and terrifying. [He further described her as being] in the *pitṛvana*, the cremation ground. || 29 ||
One should worship Lakṣmī in the northeast; "having the luster of Jāmbūnada" means having the appearance of gold. || 30 ||

He states the seed-syllables (*bīja*) for these [deities]: *Ananta* is the letter *ā*; *nabhas* is the letter *ha*; *anta* is the letter *kṣa*. Joined with the long *ā*, it becomes *hāṃ* and *kṣāṃ*; these are the two seed-syllables of Brahmāṇī. *Nayanānta* is the letter *ī*; *indra* is the letter *la*; *prāṃśu* is the letter *ā*. Joined with that, it becomes *ī lāṃ*; this is the mantra of Māheśvarī. *Dṛk* is the letter *u*; after that is the letter *ū*; after that is the letter *ma*. *Kula* is the letter *sa*; its end is the letter *ha*. Combined with *ananta* (the letter *ā*), *rudra* (the letter *ra*), and [the others], it becomes *ūṃ hnāṃ*; this is the opening of the seed-syllable of Kaumārī. || 31 ||

The Lord of the lunar days (tithīśa) is the letter *ṛ*; with Ananta (*ā*) and the letter *sa*, and with Bhrigu (*ka*), it becomes *ṛṃ* and *sāṃ*, which is the Vaiṣṇava mantra. Hari (*ha*) and Vaka (*śa*), followed by that [letter] which ends in *ṣa*, thus *hāṃ*, is the Vārāha mantra. The Lord of the elements (bhautīśa) is the letter *ai*; Vaka (*śa*), Ananta (*ā*), accompanied by that [letter], thus *aiṃ*, is the Indrāṇī mantra. *Kī* is the bindu;

preceded by that [bindu] (*kī*), preceded by *ka*, endowed with the end of Sūkṣmā (*ū*), then the forest (*va*), and after that the face (*na*), joined with the Lord of Śacī (*i*), and also the sky (*ha*) endowed with the beloved (*ī*). || 32 ||
Then one should worship Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodheśa, Unmattakapālin,
Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra in sequence within the Palāśa petals.

They bear staffs of collyrium, clouds, and heaps of filth, as well as tridents and skulls, resembling dark blue-black in color; they possess three eyes and are joined with small drums, their staff-like arms as fierce as the trunks of elephants.
Wearing upper garments made of elephant hides, with foreheads knit in frowns, the tips of their hair resembling swarms of curved bees, they were joyful in heart and rich in the bloom of youth. (35)

The third letter from 'Ha', conjoined with 'Bha' and 'Ga', ending with 'Kula' (the letter 'La'), joined with 'A', 'Pitta' (Ra), and the end of 'Vilocana' (the letter 'I'), with its head marked by the half-moon—this, I declare here, is the seed-syllable of them as well. (36)

He who is Hetuka, he who is named Tripurāntaka, those two who are Vahni and Vetālahutāśajihva, Kāla, Karāla, as well as Ekapāda, and he indeed who is known by the name Bhīma of fearsome form. || 37 ||

Then, upon the tips of the petals, one should [visualize] those [deities] whose complexion resembles a dark blue cloud, who sequentially bear with their staff-like arms a trident, a skull-cup, a shimmering serpent-noose, a slender [bow], and a drum, [adorned] with perfumes and other offerings. (p. 69) 38.

The practitioner should worship those of terrifying form, whose wide mouths are formidable with fangs, whose faces are made fierce by three eyes and knitted brows, who are longing for Kādambarī, whose hair stands erect, and who are endowed with youthful vigor; he should worship them together with Bhūtīśa, who is joined with the half-moon. (39)

Then, one should worship Hari-haya in the eastern direction with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings— he whose body is dark like the priyaṅgu plant, whose hand is grasped by her, who wears a shimmering crest-jewel made of gems, whose form is mounted upon a noble elephant, and who bears a thousand lotus-eyes.

Then one should worship Agni—who has the luster of a blooming *kiṃśuka* flower, who holds a goat-skin and a sharp spear in his hands, who wears a jeweled crown, and who possesses earrings set with gems—using fragrant perfumes and the finest flowers. (41)

Thereafter, one should worship the Lord of the Ancestors (Pitṛnātha) on the southern side; he resembles a dark blue cloud, holds a staff in his hand, has reddish eyes, is mounted upon a buffalo, and is resplendent in his attire.

Thereafter, one should duly worship the Lord of the Rākṣasas according to the prescribed rite— he who is mounted upon a man in the southern direction (the direction of the Rakshasas), who possesses formidable fangs and holds a well-grasped sword, whose body is dark like a water-laden cloud, who is lolling with saliva, who devours flesh, whose eyes are blood-red, and who is adorned with various ornaments.

One should worship Varuṇa in his own direction— he who resembles the autumnal moon, who is seated upon a sea-monster (makara), who wears brilliant attire, whose cheeks are adorned with jeweled earrings, and who holds a boon-granting gesture and a noose in his hands.

The syllable *au* produces the power of hearing the excellent vows; its bodily luster is like the smoke from a pure banner. *Au* is water, *va* is Sūkṣmā, and *i* is its end; by means of that *ā* [which completes it], *oṃ vāṃ* is the seed-syllable of Cāmuṇḍā. *Va* is the face, and *visarjanīya* (the visarga) is the secondary face. *Aḥ* is the secondary face, and *ā* is joined with the Lord of Śacī (Indra); *i* is joined with its beloved (the vowel *u*) and endowed with the *anusvāra*: *aḥ hrīṃ* is the mantra of Mahālakṣmī. || 32 ||

He states "now" (*atha*) that the eight Bhairavas are to be worshipped in the middle of the vessel: Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodheśa, Unmattakapālin, Bhīṣaṇa, Saṃhāra, and Vetāla. They have four arms, holding in their hands a staff (*daṇḍa*), a skull-cup (*kapāla*), a trident (*śūla*), a small drum (*ḍamaru*), and a kettle-drum (*dundubhi*). (33–35)

He states the seed-syllables: the third from Hara (Ha) is Aiṃ; Bhaga is the letter E; that is the elemental syllable (the letter Pa); the five-syllabled one is Anusvāra (ṃ), joined with which [makes] Aiṃ. Kuli is the letter Sa; its end is the letter Ha; Appitta is Oṃ; Agni is the letter Ra. Vilocana is the letter I; its end is the letter Ū; Niśākara-ardha is the Bindu (ṃ); that marks the head [of the syllable]. Thus, [the seed-syllable is] Aiṃ Hnīṃ. With these two seed-syllables, one should worship the Asitāṅga Bhairavas. [The mantra is: "Aiṃ Hnīṃ, obeisance to Asitāṅga Bhairava," and so forth. || 36 ||

Then he says that one should worship Antaka and the others. The formula for this is: *Aiṃ hetukāya namaḥ*, and so forth. These eight—Hetuka, Tripurāntaka, Vahni, Vetāla, Hutāśajihva, Kāla, Ekapāda, and Bhīma—are four-armed, fond of *kādambarī* wine, and fond of liquor. He states their mantra as "by the Lord of the Elements" (*bhautīśena*).
The Lord of the Elements is the vowel *ai* (the letter *ai*), joined with the half-moon (*sārddhacandra*) which is the half of the moon (*niśākara`rddha`); thus, *aiṃ*. (37–39)

He states that Indra and the others are to be worshipped outside of that [mandala] with the words "dark as priyaṅgu": "One should worship Vāyu in his own direction according to the prescribed rite—him whose body is mounted upon a noble elephant, who wears a jeweled necklace, and who is foremost among those adorned with flowers. (p. 70) 45.

Then, on the thread (ūrṇāyu), one should worship with beautiful flowers, perfumes, and incenses that god who has the color of gold, the lord of wealth, seated there surrounded by all the yakṣas and treasures, holding a mace in his hand, with tawny eyes and a pair of lotuses, shining with magnificent ornaments in his own quarter. 46.

In the northeastern direction, the practitioner should worship Hara, whose matted locks are adorned with the crescent moon, who has three eyes, whose body is reddened by vermilion, and who always carries a trident and a skull-cup;
who displays the other [mudrā] called Yoga with his four beautiful arms, whose body is smeared with ashes, who moves upon a bull, and who should be worshipped with perfumes and other offerings. 47.

The syllable *sa* joined with the head [letter *a*] and situated in the water-group (the fourth class) starting from the head; the syllable *ya* joined with the end of fire (*ra*) and situated in fire (the third class) starting from the head;
and joined with the subtle (*u*) and the first of the labials (*pa*)—this is proclaimed as the mantra of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). || 48 ||

Thereafter, the lord of practitioners, endowed with devotion, should worship Vaṭuka, Gaṇa, Durgā, and Kṣetrapāla in their respective directions—Agni, Piśitāśa (Nairṛta), Īśa (Īśāna), Vāyu, and the North—using their own seed-mantras followed by "namaḥ," along with sandalwood paste, flowers, and other offerings. 49.
(Verse 50) One should offer oblations to the Vasus, the Rudras, the lords of the day, and likewise to the Bhūtas; thus has the ritual of sacrifice been described.
The wise man who performs this constantly upon the surface of the earth, having attained all his desires like Śiva himself, rejoices.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Śrītripurāsārasamuccaya*, the most excellent among all tantras.
The ninth chapter begins:
Now I shall describe the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*); one should perform it in the direction of Vāsava (the east) of the worship chamber.
Or else, the pavilion may be located in the direction of Īśa (the northeast), of Vittapa (the northwest), of Vibhāvasu (the southeast), or at the corner of the ocean (the southwest). || 1 ||
It should be nine cubits in measure, or else it is considered appropriate to have the height of the arms of Hṛṣīkeśa;
it is elevated with four beautiful side-arches, adorned with auspicious gateways and graced by a white canopy.

He who has occupied that body which is the preeminent lord of elephants, the best of tuskers; he who is Yama, the lord of the ancestors; he whose pure banner is smoke; he who possesses the splendor of the sun and fire; he who is seated upon a sheep (*ūrṇāyu*); and he whose pair of lotus-eyes is tawny—[I bow to him]. 40–47.

He states the mantra for the world-protectors (lokapālas) as "beginning with the head" (*mastakādi*). The "head" is the nasal bindu; *aṃ* is that [bindu]. In reverse order, the fourth syllable is the vowel *ai*. "With the head" means together with the bindu. From that, the third syllable is the consonant *ka*; "mouth" (*vaka*) is the syllable *śa*, and at its end is the syllable *ṣa*. The *ka* joined with that [ṣa] is [kṣa]. "Subtle" (*sūkṣmā*) is the vowel *i*; before that is the vowel *ā*. "Face" (*mukha*) is the visarga, and before that is the bindu. "Joined with that" means together with the bindu (*savindukam*). Thus, by that entire collection, with the mantra *aiṃ kṣāṃ*, Indra and the other world-protectors are to be worshipped. || 48 ||

Then, one should worship Vaṭuka, Gaṇapati, Durgā, and Kṣetrapāla with their respective seed-syllables in the directions of Agni (southeast), Nairṛta (southwest), Vāyu (northwest), and Īśāna (northeast). One should worship them with: "Vaṃ, obeisance to Vaṭuka and the Gaṇas; Gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati; Duṃ, obeisance to Durgā. Then, in the directions of Indra (east), Varuṇa (west), Yama (south), and Soma (north), one should worship in order with: "Obeisance to the Eight Vasus; obeisance to the Eleven Rudras; obeisance to the Twelve Ādityas. Thereafter, [one should contemplate] that which is of the nature of indivisible consciousness, flowing with a mass of the nectar of supreme bliss.

Having worshipped the Supreme Goddess—who is like a climbing vine clinging to the Pārijāta tree—with the services of perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings; having smelled the flower from the mandala with the *saṃhāramudrā*, which is the root of the power that creates, sustains, and destroys all worlds; and having led her from the lotus of the heart to the lotus of one’s own heart and contemplated oneself as being identical with her; then, favored by her grace, becoming himself composed of the bliss of nectar and liberated from the seed-syllables (*bīja*), he may wander at his pleasure. This is auspicious. (49–50)
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śrītripurāsārasamuccaya*.

Following the description of the supreme deity who is the means for attaining happiness in this world, he begins to explain the procedure for the fire-sacrifice (*homavidhāna*) with the words "Now, the fire-rite" (*athāgnikāryyam*). He states the rule regarding the sacrificial hall (*pūjāgṛha*) and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: one should construct a square mandala in the form of a triangle in the northeast corner (*īśakoṇa*) of the altar situated in the center of the aforementioned initiation pavilion (*dīkṣāmaṇḍapa*), as well as a seat for the fire in that same northeast corner. || 1 ||

Now, he describes the characteristics of the initiation pavilion (*dīkṣā-maṇḍapa*) with the words beginning "nine cubits" (*navahasta*). One should construct a pavilion measuring nine cubits on the sides of Indra (East), Varuṇa (West), Yama (South), and Soma (North), having a firm enclosure and adorned with arches (*toraṇa*) at its four gates. Then, regarding the phrase "measured by the mountains and the arms": the mountains are said to be seven; the arms refer to the hands, and the sense organs (*hṛṣīkāṇi*) are five; thus, the meaning is that it should be measured by five cubits. || 2 ||

Then, in the center of that [mandala] which is provided with four entrances, one should construct a single altar (vedī) divided into three parts according to that division; it should be one cubit (aratni) in height, resembling the interior of a mirror, and truly captivating to the mind. || 3 ||

One should construct for her [the sacrificial pit] shaped like a Veda (four-cornered), a Yoni, resembling half a moon, a triangle, a circle, a hexagon, a lotus-shape, or an elephant-shape, starting from the direction of Indra (East).

Some scholars say there should be a circle in the center, between the directions of Gaurīpati (North-East) and the Suras (South-East); a five-cornered pit in the Vāyavya (North-West) direction, and a seven-cornered pit in the direction of Madanari (North).

First, having laid down the primary thread, the one of pure intellect should mark its center with half of that [thread's length]. Then, between the directions of Yama (South) and Kubera (North), he should mark a pair of fish.

Having stretched a thread from those two fish to form a jewel-like point, he should then mark the four corners; thus the field shall become a square, and within it he may construct other sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).

Having cast [the cord] here on the outside of the field into the portion facing forward, one of sharp intellect, holding it firmly, should rotate it by a quarter of a quarter (one-sixteenth) of the side; (p.
73) and likewise, from the center, one should make the fall of two cords as far as the opposite corner. This becomes the *manmathāvāsa* sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). || 6 ||

Having set aside two parts, the wise man who possesses the knowledge of the lines should rotate [the cord] above and below by that measure; thus this well-formed pit called the "Half-moon" (ardhacandra) is produced. || 7 ||
Having divided the field into three parts and placed two parts on both sides, the wise man should lay down two lines using that measurement;
this shall be the *kuṇḍa* with eleven corners (triangles).
One of sharp intellect should draw a line outside from the field [of the center] toward the direction of the world-elephant (diggaja), starting from a portion exceeding [the previous] row;
by means of this single part, one should rotate it all around, and thus an excellent circle is formed. || 9 ||
Having placed two parts outside on both sides from the middle of the earth-portion in this [diagram], one of pure intellect should, by that measure, construct the width of the field.

He describes the method for constructing the altar (*vedikā*) with the words "Then, in the middle of that," and so forth. One should construct the altar with one part out of three parts of that pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). Just as previously [four lines] were drawn from east to west, one should likewise draw five lines from south to north. When this is done, that pavilion becomes composed of nine squares. In the central square among them, one should make the altar one *aratni* in height, resembling the interior of a mirror, and as stainless as the center of a mirror. 3.

In the remaining petals of the eight directions starting from the east, one should proceed in order with those to be described, beginning with "the four-armed" (vedāsram) and so forth. These are: the divine-armed (devāsram), which is square; the womb-shaped (yonim); the form of an *aśvattha* leaf; the half-moon-shaped (*ardhoḍupanibham*), which is semicircular; the fire-armed (*analāsram*), which is triangular; the circular (*vṛttam*); the six-armed (*ṣaḍasram*), which is lotus-shaped; the elephant-armed (*gajāsram*), which is octagonal; and the eight-armed (*aṣṭāsram*). "Starting from the direction of Hari-haya" means starting from the eastern direction.

In the *Śāradātilaka*, however, it is stated that "the preceptor’s pit (ācāryakuṇḍa) should be in the middle between Gaurīpati [the North-East] and Mahendra [the East]"; thus, the preceptor’s enclosure (*vṛtta*) is circular. Others, however, say: one should make a circular enclosure between Indra [the East] and Īśāna [the North-East], a five-cornered one in the Vāyavya [North-West], and a mandala-corner [nine-cornered] in the Īśa corner [North-East]. || 4 ||

He describes the layout of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the words beginning "the eastern thread" (*prāksūtram*). First, having stretched a thread toward the east (*prāk*) with its tip facing east, and having fixed it at the center, one should stretch four threads in the directions of south and north using that same measurement. When this is done, a square mandala arises, equal on all sides and measuring four cubits and a quarter. This constitutes the pit situated in the eastern direction; this indeed is the square. || 5 ||

Having made it square, they say one should draw out the other *kuṇḍas* by projecting [the measurements] into the field (*kṣetra*). Having drawn two lines from the southeast, northwest, southwest, and northeast within the square already made, and having again made a square, one should project one part outside the five-fold division; then, having worshipped according to the measure of half of half the corner, one should rotate [the cord]. By the word "corner" (*koṇa*), the corner-line is understood.

Half of that [line] is the point where the two diagonal threads intersect; half of that again is the position of the second diagonal thread in the pair of western squares. From that position, one should rotate [the thread] with that same measurement so as to touch the corners; this is the *yoni* altar (*kuṇḍa*) situated in the direction of Agni (southeast). ||6||

Regarding the half-moon-shaped *kuṇḍa*, he says "having abandoned," etc. Having divided the square plot of ground into ten parts, one should abandon two parts at the bottom and top—specifically one at the top and one at the bottom. Then, having laid down the chord-line (*jyāsūtra*) of its own respective measure in front, one should rotate [the compass] from the base with that measurement as the diameter. One should erase the other segments of the cord. This is the *kuṇḍa* called the half-moon, situated in the southern direction. || 7 ||

Regarding the *asrakuṇḍa*, he says "śarvarī" and so forth. Having divided the aforementioned square field into eight parts—each part being half a *bhāga*—one should increase each side by two parts along the horizontal lines on both sides of the east-west axis (*prācīsūtra*). One should then erase all the [original] lines. The *kuṇḍa* in the northeast corner is located in the direction of Nirṛti (the southwest). || 8 ||

Regarding the circular *kuṇḍa*, he says "dig" and so forth. When the area has been divided into eleven parts with eight remaining, one should thus place one part outside on each of the four sides and rotate [the cord] in the form of a circle. One should exclude the other circular segments. This is the circular *kuṇḍa* situated in the western direction. || 9 ||
On both sides, one should draw six lines with a slight offset, forming two pairs of squares; thus this charming pit (kuṇḍa) comes to have six corners. || 10 ||
Having laid out one-tenth of this [area] on the outside and rotated it by that same measure, the wise man should draw the circle for the petals;
he should also form the pericarp between the outer and middle [circles], and thus there shall be an eight-petalled lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (padmakuṇḍa).

Having cast [the cord] here on the ground in each direction at a distance of two parts of the sun (twelve units), and having made one part with this, the wise man should again take half from the corner to form a four-cornered (square) figure. From those two corners, he should indeed mark points all around using that same measurement; thus it shall become an octagon, and he should extend the application of eight threads all around.

Having set aside one part from the horse-portion (seven parts) here and drawn a circle around it, then using three parts out of those divided into four, the length of the cloth-band is established; by the application of five threads according to this reduction, the five-cornered sacrificial pit (pañcāsra-kuṇḍa) is formed.

(Verse 14) On the diameter of the site, having set aside one part out of ten parts toward the exterior, one should fashion a perfect circle according to this measurement. Then, having again divided this [circle] into sixty-four parts, a person of firm intellect should, by means of thirty-three parts including three additional units, determine the length of the cloth [for the cord]; thus, through the application of seven cords, this becomes a seven-cornered (saptāsra) sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Whatever the measurement of the width of the pit is, that same measurement is prescribed for its depth.
A wise man should fashion the girdle so that its shape corresponds exactly to the shape of the pit. || 15 ||
One should make three girdles for the pit, or two girdles, or even just one girdle.
Above the girdle, one should fashion the *yoni* in the shape of an elephant’s trunk, located here in the direction of the Hotṛ priest.
When the girdle is only a fist in width, its height and breadth should be two fingers, one finger, and half a finger respectively;
when it is only a span in width, those same [girdles] should again have heights and breadths of three fingers, two fingers, and one finger. 17.
In this sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit (hasta), these [measures] should have a height and diameter respectively of four, three, two, and one finger-breadths (aṅgula).
Furthermore, in a pit measuring two cubits, they should have a height and diameter of six, four, three, and two finger-breadths.
In this pit measuring four cubits, they should have a height and diameter of four, six, four, and two finger-breadths.
In this [mandala] measuring six cubits, there are ten squares, each possessing a height of one finger-breadth. || 19 ||
In this ground measuring eight cubits, these lines of the sun should be marked at intervals of eight finger-breadths;
one should then fashion a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp in the center, along with water for the navel and for movement.

Regarding the six-cornered (*ṣaḍasra*) sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), he says: "O King, having divided the field of sight into sixteen parts by means of the earth-measure (*bhūpāṃśu*), and having placed one [part] on each side from the central thread, then, upon the pair of sides, there is a set of four fish-marks; from that, one should drop six threads. By that, the pit consisting of six corners shall come into being, situated in the north-western direction. (10)

Regarding the lotus-shaped pit (padmakuṇḍa), he says "ten parts" and so forth: having divided the square field into ten parts and expanded it, one should rotate [the cord] in a circular form; then, rotating again by that same measure, one forms the central circle which constitutes the pit itself, two circles for the pericarp, the filaments on the third, and the eight petals on the fourth—the lotus-pit being situated in the direction of Kubera (the north). || 11 ||

Regarding the eight-sided [altar], he says: "The field" and so forth. Having divided the square field into twenty-four parts—each part being two-twelfths (one-eighth)—and having added one part to each direction, one should form four corners. Then, taking half from the corner and taking half of the half of the inner square's corner, one should mark points in each direction from the two outer corners of the square. By dropping lines to those eight points, an eight-sided sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) facing the northeast is formed. || 12 ||

Regarding the five-cornered (pañcāsra) pit, he states another teacher’s opinion: "In the horse-portion" (hayāṃśe). Having divided the square into seven parts and having increased one part by means of a circle on the outside, and having again divided it into four equal parts (yugāṃśīkṛtya), one should make the length (āyāma-dairghya) with three parts; that application of the cord constitutes the five-cornered pit situated in the northwest corner. || 13 ||

Regarding the seven-sided sacrificial pit (*saptāsra-kuṇḍa*), it says: "The field's width," and so forth. Here, one should divide the square under discussion into ten parts, extend it outward by one part, and then draw a circle all around using that same measurement. Furthermore, having divided the square into sixty-four parts, one should omit thirty-one parts; with the remaining thirty-three parts, one should divide the circular line into seven sections, mark seven points, and strike seven lines.
In this way, one should construct the seven-cornered [pit] with its tips meeting without overlapping. || 14 ||

He states the measurement of the excavation with the words "as far as": four *arpitas* [for the *yuga*], three *aṅgulas* for the *netra*, two *aṅgulas* for the *sindhuvāc*, six *tarkas*, and four *abdhayas*. He describes the extent of the navel with the words "here, the navel": within the pit (*kuṇḍa*), at the distance of a fist (p. 76), the *yoni* is said by the wise to have a length and breadth of six, four, and two *aṅgulas*, and a height of one *aṅgula*;
the navel here also has a height and breadth of two and four *aṅgulas*, and its tip extends one *aṅgula* beyond the edge of the *yoni*. (21)
This which has been declared regarding a pit measuring one *ratni* applies indeed to that which is measured by one *hasta*, as stated by Māyā. 22.

With an intellect sharpened by constant practice, one should gradually increase this [fire] in other sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), whether they are shaped like a womb (yoni) or like a brinjal (vṛntāka), or indeed according to the specific form of the pit;
however, in a pit shaped like a womb, one should not place a lotus-like [altar] nor a navel.
For a pit measuring one cubit, they say the *yoni* should be one *bhūta* (five) finger-breadths in length and breadth;
it should be provided with a height of one part of its width and made in conformity with the petals of the lotus of the awakening ground. 24.
The wise man should fashion from the pit a lotus with a stalk equal in height to two fingers, provided with pupils, and having petals at the two shoulders [of the pit];
he should place its pericarp in the middle portion according to a fraction of the square root of the fire [the number nine].

The circumference of a single *kuṇḍa* should be one beautiful finger-breadth (*aṅgula*). From that, starting from two fingers, the wise man should increase it by half a finger for each subsequent *kuṇḍa*, up to ten fingers. Outside of that, he should indeed construct three girdles (*mekhalā*) according to the prescribed order.
(Verse 27) For a homa of fifty [offerings], the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should indeed be one fist in measure; for a hundred offerings, it should be one aratni;
for a thousand, one cubit (hasta); for ten thousand, two cubits; and for a hundred thousand, this [pit] is prescribed to be four cubits.

Those who know the scriptures declare that for a homa of one million [oblations], the sacrificial ladle (rasahasta) is eight cubits long; for ten million, it is sixteen cubits; and for half a crore, it is eight cubits. || 28 ||
Some say that for a homa of one hundred thousand oblations, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be one cubit; for two hundred thousand, two cubits; for three hundred thousand, three cubits;
for four hundred thousand, four cubits; and for five hundred thousand, five cubits. || 29 ||
At eight hundred thousand [recitations], there shall be eight cubits; at seven hundred thousand, seven cubits.
At eight hundred thousand, there shall be eight cubits; at nine hundred thousand, nine cubits. (30)
For ten lakhs [of oblations], the pit should be ten cubits; likewise for ten million oblations here, it should be ten cubits. Indeed, there is no pit larger than ten cubits on this earth.
The southeast corner (dhikoṇa) bestows all accomplishments and is said to be the abode of the mind-born god (Kāma); it grants sons.
The southeast corner (agnikoṇa), resembling a half-moon, bestows auspiciousness and is the cause for the crushing of enemies.
The *śāntika* jewel should be perfectly round; that which effects *māraṇa* is six-cornered.
Here, a lotus-shaped pit brings about prosperity, while an eight-cornered one effects the pacification of diseases.
In this world, the sacrificial pit for Brahmins is square, for kings it is circular,
for merchants it has the shape of a half-moon, and for Śūdras it is triangular.
Some teachers say that for all [rites], the square shape is recommended;
however, both types of sacrificial pits grant the desired fruit and bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

The sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for producing progeny is hexagonal and also crescent-shaped. Regarding the type of the womb (*yoni*), he says "fist" (*muṣṭi*): its length and width are six and four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) respectively, according to the number. He speaks of the measurement of the navel (*nābhi*) with the word "eye" (*netra*). He speaks of the tip of the womb with the words "tip of the womb" (*yonyagra*); that is, in a *yoni*-shaped pit one should fashion a *yoni*, and in a lotus-shaped pit a navel—this he states with the passage beginning "one finger-breadth" and ending with "and one should fashion the navel."

Regarding the phrase "of the *kuṇḍa*," some experts in the Āgamas describe the measurement of the *yoni* differently for a *kuṇḍa* measuring one cubit (*hasta*) in size: its length and width are five and four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) respectively. "Width" (*vyāsa*) refers to the breadth; within that length, this number six—meaning six finger-breadths—is the measure corresponding to the leaf of the *bodhi* tree (the earth-born tree), shaped like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree. This is what is meant: it is six finger-breadths wide, two finger-breadths high, and shaped like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree for a *kuṇḍa* of exactly one cubit. (15–24)

Regarding "netre" (the eyes): one should make them with a height and width of two or five finger-breadths. On two parts [of the area], one should fashion eight petals; and for the central pit (*madhyakuṇḍa*), one should fashion the pericarp (*karṇikā*) using a third part—that is, a portion consisting of three fire-parts (*vahny-aṃśa*)—of the diameter or the width. For a one-cubit pit, the rim (*nemi*) is everywhere around it by this single part; thus, starting from two cubits, one should increase [the dimensions] by two [parts] at a time.

In this manner, from the *dikkarakuṇḍa* up to the ten-cubit *kuṇḍa*, one should not increase [the measurement] by half an *aṅgula* for each; rather, one should indeed construct three girdles (*mekhalā*) on the outside of that. || 25 || 26 ||

Regarding the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) corresponding to the number of oblations (*homa*), he says "half of a hundred" (*śatārdha*) and so forth. For ten thousand [oblations], the pit is two cubits (*dvihasta*); it is measured by the diagonal cord (*karṇasūtra*) of a one-cubit pit. Thus, one should construct a two-cubit pit according to the measurement of that cord. "By the measurement of the diagonal cord of a one-cubit pit, one should construct a two-cubit pit; thus do those who know the Tantras understand. (27–31)
The five-pointed [triangle] bestows liberation, while the horse-cornered [six-pointed star] and the womb [triangle] grant sovereignty in this world. (36)
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Śrītripurāsārasamuccaya*.
The Tenth Chapter:

Regarding the daily (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, those of perfectly pure intellect have declared that the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be triangular with four corners, measuring one cubit (*hasta*), resembling the abode of Smara (the god of love), or else a circular one is recommended.

Then, a sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila) should be constructed from sand, well-proportioned, measuring one cubit in length, and slightly less than a thumb-breadth in height; it should be hexagonal and resemble the moon in its half-moon shape. || 1 ||
Some wise ones say that it should be four-cornered, four cubits in height, and one cubit in width;
then the learned man should perform the purification, washing, or even the sprinkling of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

There, one should draw three lines with the tips pointing upward using *varhiṣa* grass while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*; likewise, four lines pointing eastward, for which the deities are Brahmā, Yama, Varuṇa, and Śiva.

Among those, the deities situated on the line with the tips pointing northward are Indra, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Kubera; and similarly, those on the lines pointing eastward are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Kubera.

Having sprinkled [the area] with water using the root mantra and having worshipped its center with perfumes and other offerings, one should meditate here upon Vāgīśvarī, who resembles a dark blue cloud and has just bathed after her menses. (4)

Having produced fire from a sun-crystal, from a sacrificial hearth, or from the house of a Vedic scholar, and having placed it in a vessel made of excellent gold or even a copper vessel—or in a skull— the practitioner of mantra, possessing pure and expansive intellect, should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters by means of the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ), and thereafter purify it with the Astra-mantra. || 5 ||
Then, having veiled [the deity] with the armor-mantra (kavaca), and subsequently, with self-restraint, having displayed the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā),
one should then perform the rite of nectarization (amṛtīkaraṇa) by means of the water-seed-syllable (vaṃ) together with the bindu of fire (raṃ).

Having properly circumambulated three times in a clockwise direction, the practitioner of mantra should then place this [fire] facing himself within the womb of the fire-pit of Vāgīśvarī, using the root mantra. || 7 ||

Regarding specific desires, he states the specific type of sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) that brings about all accomplishments with the words "sarvasiddhikaram" (bringing all success). Regarding the specific caste, he states the specific type of sacrificial pit characterized by a number of yoni-shapes that produces the mind-born [son] with the word "caturasram" (quadrangular). || 32–36 ||
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Padārthādarśa, a commentary on the Śrītripurāsāra. 9.
