Thus, immediately after the description of the pavilion and the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), he begins to explain the ritual for the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and the ritual for the fire-oblation (homa) with the verse beginning "nitye" and so forth. Regarding the daily and occasional rites, the teachers have declared that the sacrificial pit should be one cubit in measure. He states the measurement of the sacrificial mound made of sand with the word "sthaṇḍilam". || 1 ||

He describes the method for purifying the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the words "Then" (*tataḥ*): having prepared the pit and the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and having cleared away nails, hair, clods of earth, stones, and so forth; having smeared the pit with cow-dung water and sprinkled the mound; having purified it with the seed-syllable of Vāyu and performed a slight sprinkling with the seed-syllable of Varuṇa; and having drawn three lines with *barhis* grass—that is, with double-folded *kuśa* grass—using the Heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*) or the mantra "Namaḥ," starting from the west and proceeding to the east with the tips pointing southward, [and then] upon those [lines], from south to north, with the tips pointing upward...

One should meditate upon Brahmā, Yama, and Soma as the presiding deities of the middle, western, and eastern sections respectively; furthermore, one should remember that the deities of the middle, southern, and northern directions—located from west to east—are Śrī, Īśa, and Murādhipa. Then, having placed the perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and other materials for the oblation on the right side, and having spread darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward on the left side, one should fill the vessels placed upon them according to the prescribed method with water from a sacred ford (tīrtha) and the aforementioned collection of substances.

Having consecrated the vessels with the previously mentioned mantra, one should worship them with perfumes and other offerings in the center of either the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). || 2 || 3 ||
Having meditated upon Vāgīśvarī, who has bathed after her menses, is united with Vāgīśvara, possesses two arms, and holds a lotus—thus [one should meditate]. || 4 ||

Having brought a single fire—produced from a sun-crystal, from a fire-drill, or from the house of a prosperous Vedic scholar—and having placed it in a vessel with the seed-syllable of fire (vahnivīja), one should discard a small piece of wood intended for the flesh-eaters (kravyāda) and protect [the fire] with the weapon-mantra (astra). || 5 ||

Having veiled [the deity] with the *kavaca* mantra, having rendered it nectarine by means of the *amṛta* seed-syllable and the *dhenumudrā*, having raised [it], and having circumambulated the sacrificial pit (*sthaṇḍila-kuṇḍa*) in a clockwise direction, one should place it facing oneself.
With the awareness of its own seed-syllable, one should offer that [deity] into the womb of the Goddess in the center of the pit. 6–7.

(Verse 8) Then, with a concentrated mind, one should offer seven oblations with *aṃj* using the Heart-mantra; thus, this rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*) for the fire, which has a movement other than white [i.e., red], will be properly performed here.

Likewise, the practitioner of mantras should then perform the rite of the male-organ (*puṃsavana*), and then the parting of the hair (*sīmanta*). By that same method, he should perform here the rite of birth (*jātakarma*) for the fire.

Then [he saw] Agni, seven cubits tall, with three feet, two heads, and four tusks; bound in three places, glowing, joined with tawny eyes numbering six (the count of logic), roaring as he brought about destruction, and possessing four ears.
He has a face like a red lotus, with one foot firmly planted and the other extended behind upon the back of a lordly bull;
he is endowed with four arms extending to his right and three to his left, all facing toward himself.

He holds in his right hands a spear, a hole, and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles; in his left hands, he holds a javelin, a palm-leaf fan, a vessel full of clarified butter, and a vessel with the color of molten gold, as well as his own seven tongues of flame.

That which is golden, yellow, red, and joyful, located on the right side of the face and known as Rasajñā; and that which is called Suprabhā, extremely red, situated on the left side of the face, and possessing many forms—[these are the tongues]. 12.
(Verse 13) Hiraṇyā, possessing the beautiful color of well-refined gold, stands in the direction of the wielder of the trident;
she who is named Kanakā, with the color of lapis lazuli, is seated in the direction of Vāsava.
That which is red, with the hue of the rising sun, is the tongue of Agni, well-situated in the south-east.
That which is black, with the luster of a full-blown blue lotus, belongs to Varuṇa and is fixed in the quarter of the western direction.
Blazing with a luster like that of a ruby, Suprabhā is situated in the direction of Varuṇa;
she who resembles a great silver flower is Atiraktikā in the direction of Gandhavāha.

The tongue known as Yathārthasaṃjñā, which has many forms and is situated to the south of the upper [tongue], is praised when located in the center of the sacrificial pit; this is the Hiraṇyā tongue, used on earth for rites such as Kārmaṇa.

The one named Kanaka is intended for rites of immobilization and the like; the Red one is indeed intended for rites of hatred and the like; the Black one is declared on earth for the rite of killing; and Suprabhā is used here by those skilled in ritual for the rite of pacification.
She who is intensely red in the Uccāṭana [rite] bestows success in the Bahurūpottara;
she extends prosperity from the right side, and always spreads auspicious things in the center. || 18 ||

But other wise men, whose intellects have reached the further shore of the scriptures, declare her to possess a beautiful radiance: as dark as a rain-cloud when situated in the quarter of Indra (the East); as black as the Lord of the Ancestors (Yama) in the South; as golden-yellow in the quarter of Varuṇa (the West); as multiform in the quarter of the Destroyer of Cities (Agni, the Southeast); as red in the North; as deep crimson in the Southeast; and as golden in the center of the circle.

The wise practitioner should likewise visualize the tongue as named Hiraṇyā for rites of pacification (śāntika), as named Kanakā for rites of subjugation (kārmaṇa), as red for rites of influence (kārmaṇa), and as black for minor magical acts (kṣudrakriyā). 20.

There, having first worshipped the Yoga-pīṭha, the preceptor should afterwards offer water for sipping (ācamana) and other services to the God and the Goddess. Then, with this mantra, the preceptor should kindle the fire:

*Oṃ cit piṅgala hana hana daha daha paca paca sarvāṅgāni jñāpaya svāhā*. "I revere the blazing fire, Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations—spotless, golden-hued, well-kindled, and facing in all directions. With this mantra, he should worship the Purifier (Pāvaka) according to the prescribed rite. He should then project the tongues of the fire and the sacrificial offerings upon his own body with the appropriate mantras.

In the penis, anus, head, mouth, nose, and eyes, on all sides, are the syllables *sa*, *da*, and *va*, joined with *arghīśa* (the letter *ha*) and accompanied by *bindu* (the nasal dot). Thus, the mantras for the tongues have been declared by the teachers of the seventeen [tongues] as: *syūṃ*, *dhruṃ*, *śruṃ*, *lvuṃ*, *yyuṃ*.

Having performed seven oblations each for the rites of conception (*garbhādhāna*), the quickening of the male fetus (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), and the birth ceremony (*jātakarman*) using the previously mentioned heart-mantra, one should [offer] the seven-fold [oblation] consisting of the meters Gāyatrī, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī. || 8 ||
Consisting of the Gārhapatya, Āhavanīya, and Dakṣiṇāgni fires, this [sacrifice] is three-footed, with the sacrificer as its individual self; it has two heads and four horns.

It has the four Vedas as its four shoulders, and its body is bound by the three variegated periods—morning, midday, and evening—and for the illumination of the Vedas, it possesses the Pañcarātra, Buddhism, and Jainism as its five eyes.

In the three *puṃsavana* rites, [one should meditate on] the essence of the sacrificial oblation (*havya*), consisting of the four Vedas—Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva—with a mobile, radiant body, mounted upon the back of the lordly bull (*vṛṣendra*). Seated upon the back of the lordly bull, he likewise holds a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) suspended from it. With his four right hands below, he holds a spear (*śakti*), a seed-syllable (*bīja*), a *sruk*, and a *sruva* ladle;
with his three left hands, he holds a triple-headed drum (*tālavṛnta*), a golden vessel filled with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and so forth. (Verses 9–11)

Having meditated upon Jātavedas and worshipped him with the ritual services beginning with water for the hands (*arghya*) and feet (*pādya*), and ending with incense and lamps, one should then spread *darbha* grass with tips pointing eastward and northward around the sacrificial pit—either below the rim in a single-rimmed pit, between the two rims in a double-rimmed pit, or upon the rim in a triple-rimmed pit. If it is on a leveled mound (*sthaṇḍila*), then having placed three enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) in the southern, northern, and western directions and sprinkled [the site], one should perform the following rites: first, the impregnation (*garbhādhāna*), then the male-making rite (*puṃsavana*), and the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*). Immediately after that, the birth-rite (*jātakarma*) and likewise the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*).
That which is called Suprabhā, they say, is the tongue that brings about liberation;
it is exceedingly red, multiformed, and bestows all accomplishments when drawn forth. (21)

The practitioner, having understood [the deity] as endowed with all ornaments and appearing in this form for all rites, should meditate correctly upon Citrabhānu, who is joined with seven tongues of flame, while remaining restrained in speech and with his face turned upward.

At the conclusion of the birth-rites, the mantra-practitioner, having worshipped [the child] duly with water for the feet, the arghya offering, and so forth, should offer seven oblations of clarified butter with the heart-mantra, [reciting]: "Obeisance to the illustrious name of this person, whose fire is smoke-bannered. || 23 ||
Then, one of sharp intellect should properly surround the fire-pit with *kuśa* grass, having its tips pointing eastward and northward;
in a pit with a single girdle, the [grass] should be beneath the girdle.
In the case of two girdles, one should spread [the grass] over the second girdle;
but in the case of three girdles, one should spread it over the middle girdle.

On the surface of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), the wise practitioner should first place sand and then arrange the enclosing sticks (paridhis) on the front, sides, and to the south, north, and west of the pit (kuṇḍa).
The eastern portion is prescribed for the Hotṛ priest; the left side is the southern portion of Agni;
one should know the right side as the northern portion; and the rear portion is declared by the wise to be the front.
Then, having spread darbha grass on the left side with their tips pointing toward the direction of the beloved of Puloman’s daughter (Indra),
the wise man should place all the vessels in pairs above that, with their openings facing downward.
In rites such as those for pacification (śāntika), vessels made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay are highly recommended here.

However, for acts such as inciting enmity (vidveṣaṇa), expulsion (uccāṭana), concealment (ucchādana), and killing (māraṇa), vessels made from the śelu, akṣadruma, and śigru trees are exceedingly praised.
(Verse 30) Then, when these vessels have been turned face upwards, the wise man, having filled one with water and having clearly visualized the sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*) therein,
should sprinkle the collection of materials situated on the left side with those *darbha* grasses used for purification (*kūrca*).
Having performed the purification with ghee and possessing a perfectly clear intellect, one should offer seven oblations here;
one should likewise perform the first feeding of solid food, as well as the tonsure and the initiation ceremony (upanayana), in this same manner.
In all auspicious rites such as the Godāna ceremony, he, being attentive, should offer oblations with that same [mantra]; likewise for the Samāvartana and the marriage. || 32 ||
Then, having prepared that seat previously described according to the ritual in a well-refined fire,
he should duly worship Ambikā there along with her retinue, using the oblation known as *asūn*.
One should offer ten oblations for each member of the retinue and for each goddess;
thus Bhairavī’s fire is generated, and then one should perform the homa.

By offering oblations of *pālāśa* flowers sprinkled with the three sweets (*madhuratra*), a person attains all desires and the splendor of the fire-sacrifice (*homa-śrī*). With *kapāṭala* and *vicikila* flowers, one obtains a kingdom; likewise with *bilva* leaves or fruits, one gains common prosperity. With lotuses, one gains wind; with the shoots of *śāhvala* and jaggery, peace; and with sesame seeds mixed with rice, one gains food.
By worshipping with the Aghora mantra, men obtain wealth; by using white mustard seeds, they attain eloquence; with priyaṅgu leaves, they find joy; and with its fruits, they gain sons and happiness.

Through oblations of parched grain one gains good fortune; through oblations of grain, lordship over the world of the Yakṣas; through *punnāga* flowers, a mortal attains a status surpassing that of the Vidyādharas; and through *mālatī* flowers, the worlds of the Siddhas and Gandharvas.

Next, the departure [of the child] is prescribed, followed by the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), then the tonsure (*caula*) and the initiation (*upanayana*), and further the *mahānagni* and *mahāvrata*, and so forth. At the conclusion of the ritual procedure, one performs the *garbhādhāna* (conception-rite) for the fire named Maṅgala with the mantra: "Obeisance, Svāhā! and so on. Accordingly, there is the installation of the fire named Maṅgala in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Thus, she who stands to the south [of the fire] bestows prosperity (*ṛddhi*) in the north, in the middle, and in the east.
Regarding the name "Śrīmān," Rāghavabhaṭṭa states in the *Śāradātilaka*: "You are the illustrious name of this fire whose banner is Dharma; you are the auspicious name."

The term *paridhi* refers to sacrificial wood measuring two *prādeśas* (the distance between the thumb and the forefinger). *Śelu* is a specific type of tree; *śelu* is the *śleṣmātaka* (see p. 84). Through oblations of *arjuna* flowers and mustard seeds mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhura*), there shall be the summoning of *yakṣiṇīs*. By means of *kiṃśuka* flowers, prostitutes (*veśyās*) will become submissive. Through *karṇikāra* flowers, the gods of the earth (*dharaṇisurāḥ*)—namely the Kṣatriyas—will become submissive. For Vaiśyas, [oblations] of *kāsamarda* are used; for the *gaṇas*, *kiṅkirāta* flowers bring them under control here; and for Śūdras, [oblations] resembling *pāṭala* flowers are used. (38)

By performing a fire-oblation with the flesh of a goat or the meat of a wild animal, an entire enemy kingdom shall come under one's own control; or else, the enemy force shall turn its back in retreat by means of an oblation of large pieces of meat soaked in honey.
By performing oblations at night with the leaves of the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), *nimba*, and hair, mixed with jaggery,
human flesh, and pungent oil, enemies perish within three days of a sage (twenty-seven days).
It is said that a Homa performed with turmeric-grain scrapings from the bones of Nagnajit rendered the powerful army of the kings who marched against him paralyzed for seven days. 41.
Through oblations of black gram (māṣa), one suffers from muteness; through kodrava grain, affliction by disease; through peas (kalāya), there shall be the pain of illness;
through fuel-sticks of the akṣaja tree, one becomes insane; and through those made from the śālmalī tree, death occurs within seven days.

A man who, with a concentrated inner self, offers a million oblations at night into a six-cornered sacrificial pit using barley, wheat, and sesame seeds combined with the ghee of a tawny cow, attains the power of moving through the sky.

Having kindled the sacrificial fire with palāśa wood and offered oblations of bandhujīva flowers sprinkled with sandalwood water, all beings shall become submissive through this homa; the same result is achieved with offerings of priyaṅgu blossoms.
(Verse 45) A person who offers various foods, edibles, grains, and drinks shall attain supreme prosperity in this world.
By offering sprouts of the *vaṭa*, *udumbara*, and other trees, along with sweet varieties and jasmine buds, one shall attain health and renown.
Satisfaction shall come from oblations made with blue lotuses; one will attain one's own power before long.
Here, the best [pitcher] is sixteen finger-breadths high and multiplied by ghee-oblations; the middling one is half of that.
The lowest [grade] is an elevation of one elephant’s finger-breadth; likewise, there is the *tilodbhava* and the *mādhvika*, combined with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
There is also one *bullaka* of milk, and similarly of curd, sugarcane juice, and so forth. 47.
The measure for each individual cake is equal to that [of the previous];
likewise for each plantain fruit, orange, and citron. 48.
The *yanasa* fruit consists of ten segments; the *guṇa* fruit has segments, while the fruit of the *vailva* tree is without segments.
From the *karkaṭikā* fruit, the petals, flowers, and fruits are without segments.

The *vyañjana* (condiment) should be equal to four thumb-breadths; *piṇyāka* (oil-cake), *kṛsarā* (rice and pulse mixture), *culvāka*, and *ardhāhi* (half-portion); sesame seeds should be measured by a handful, and *śaktavaḥ* (flour) should be measured by a *gatī*. || 50 ||
Parched grains (lājāḥ) should be measured by a handful; mustard seeds are said to be half a karṣa;
mung beans, black gram, and rice are each equal to one karṣa and measured by a handful.
Sixteen silver coins (māṣas), wheat, and likewise red rice, or seven, eight, or five barley grains, are prescribed. || 52 ||
Half a pala is the measure for jaggery; half a handful is said to be the measure for rice;
and saffron, musk, sandalwood, and camphor should each be of the size of a chickpea (canaka). || 53 ||
*Uddāla* is *bahuvāraka*, according to Amara; it is commonly known as *kṣudramaṃśātā*. *Dravaśākha*, *śipha*, and *kṣupa* are synonyms, according to Amara.

*Śigru* is known as *śailaja*. *Vicikila* is a specific flower; some say it is *bandhujīva*. *Kāsamarda* refers to the flowers of *kālakāsunda*. *Kiñcirāta* is a specific flower. *Chāgalāṅgaja* is goat meat. *Jaṅgala* is a specific type of substance, as before.

Alternatively, the enemy force (ari-balam) shall turn its back [in retreat]. Just as the word "great" (mahat) is not applied to "great meat" (mahā-palalam)—meaning human flesh—when it is smeared with honey according to the medical treatises, nor to Brahmins, oil, meat, and so forth; likewise, [the enemy is subdued] by the three pungents (kaṭutraya), nimba leaves, and hair, combined with human flesh.

By performing a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with human flesh, birds die within twenty-one days, or at least after three weeks. Likewise, a *homa* performed with the bones of a naked ascetic, cotton seeds, some *rudrākṣa* fruits, goat hair, and pieces of turmeric causes the immobilization (*stambhana*) of rival kings within seven days; this is easily accomplished through the sacrifice of the flesh of a powerful man. When the breath has entered the *iḍā* channel during the night-wanderer [the moon], there is success through fuel-sticks made from the *akṣaja* plant. (12–44)

He states the measurement of the substances: A stream of ghee sixteen finger-breadths high and double that in volume (thirty-two finger-breadths high) is the most excellent (*vara*) oblation; half of that is middling (*madhya*). Likewise, oil produced from *tolā* measures the size of a jujube fruit (*badara*), while honey is the same. A *pura* is two pieces, the size of a wood-apple (*kapittha*) fruit.
One should seek sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) from other trees, having avoided the *śleṣmātaka*, which is the tree of the *piśācas*. 54.

One should avoid cow-tails and blades of grass for the sacrificial strewing, using other types of grass instead; likewise, one should avoid gold for the fuel-wood and use silver for the clarified butter-oblations and the sacrificial porridge.
One should offer white mustard seeds into the Bahurūpā fire, bamboo pieces into the Raktā fire,
parched grain into the Kṛṣṇā fire, and flour into the Vaiśuprabhā fire.
If the flame is excessively red, there is affliction by disease; if it is golden, there is danger from fire;
if it flickers toward the ear during the oblation, there is blindness; and if toward the nose, there is disease. || 57 ||
The loss of wealth would occur at the head; therefore, the wise man should always perform the internal fire-sacrifice within the mouth. 58.

The sound of the fire is auspicious when it resembles the resonance of a kettledrum, an elephant, or a war-drum; it is of beautiful color, resembling gold and bringing about auspicious results. When it is of the color of vermilion, it brings equal prosperity. It may also resemble the rising sun, or be as red as saffron, honey, or the indragopa insect. Furthermore, its fragrance is like that of campaka, pāṭala, and vicikila flowers, or even like clarified butter.
Resembling the fragrance of the *punnāga*, *nāga-kesara*, and *guggulu* trees, it brings about accomplishment.
Furthermore, a crest (*śikhā*) shaped like a parasol for the peacock (*śikhin*) bestows auspiciousness, as does its conceptualization. (60)
Smoke from fire that resembles jasmine is a bringer of auspicious results, as is smoke resembling the color of Kāśa flowers;
however, a sound from fire resembling the noise of a donkey or a jackal portends destruction.
A black horse with the color of fire destroys the sacrificer before long;
a reddish-brown one causes many diseases, while one resembling silver brings about the ruin of the kingdom.
A smell resembling excrement from fire brings about sufferings;
one like urine causes loss of strength, and that born of sweat effects the destruction of auspiciousness. (63)
For one whose sacred fire has been interrupted, a flame shaped like a crest causes death;
smoke resembling the color of a parrot’s plumage quickly brings about the loss of strength and the destruction of the vehicle of the fire.
If the fire resembles a dove, it causes the destruction of cattle;
however, a clockwise whorl of the sacrificial fire bestows auspicious results.
If lightning strikes, or if a frog appears, or if sparks fly from the fire at the time of the oblation, there will be misfortune;
if the flame turns to the left or the fire becomes divided, fear shall arise for the Hotṛ priest from a host of malevolent spirits.
In cases of afflictions where pacification is desired, the lord of practitioners should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the Vasu mantra;
then he should perform the worship of the wheel with the Astra mantra.
By means of a hundred-thousand-fold homa (lakṣahoma), the lord of the earth inevitably comes under one's control;
by half a hundred thousand, a minister; and by a quarter of a hundred thousand, a vassal ruler.
By six thousand [recitations], the wives of kings and their sons shall behold [the deity];
by one thousand oblations, auspicious women and courtesans shall become submissive. (69)
By ten million [of these merits], all the Vasus, the Nākasads, and the foremost among the lords of the gods become [attained];
by three million, the wives of the gods, the sages, and other deities likewise [attain their state]. 70.
By means of the hundred thousand senses, the hosts of Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas are brought under control;
by means of the twenty thousand, all the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) become subject to one's power.

Honey and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) are to be understood as before for the removal of muteness. One should offer oblations of *uḍumbara* twigs—that is, fuel-sticks from the tips of the *uḍumbara* tree—one by one. Seasoning such as soup and the like, oil-cake, boiled rice, *kṛśara* (rice and sesame), and sesame grains—each measuring four finger-breadths and surrounded by four [other ingredients]—[should be offered]. Regarding "half a *karṣa*": according to the scriptures, this is measured at eighty *guñjās*, which is two *tolakas*. A *karṣa* is thus defined; in the description of the sacrificial ladle (*śruva*), it is stated that its head is grasped with two *karṣas*. Two *karṣas* constitute a *śukti*.
Sixteen *māṣakas* constitute a *rājamāṣa*. *Reṇuyava* and *cūrṇayava* are types of barley. *Pura* is *guggulu*. *Śleṣmātaka* is a specific tree mentioned previously. *Piśācetaru* is *vaheḍā*.

Having discarded the *gopuramīṣikā*—the remnants of grass—one should spread other grasses as fuel. On the seven-tongued fire (*saptajihvā*), one should offer oblations with separate substances; he states those very substances: one should offer *caru* on the *hiraṇyā* tongue and clarified butter (*āghāra*) heated with ghee on the *kanakā* tongue.
Regarding the *karṇādi-homa*, he speaks of the ornament for the fire. (Verses 45–56)

He states the result of the sound of fire with the words "bherī" (drum). *Bherī* is a specific type of musical instrument; *vāraṇa* is an elephant. He states the result of the letter with the word "varṇa".
With the *astra-mantra*, one should perform the worship of the discus (*cakrapūjā*) and the binding of the ten directions (*daśadigbandhana*).
Regarding the pacification of defects, he describes the method for the daily recitation (*nityajapa*) after the [special] recitation (*japa*) with the words "janma" (birth).
From the interior of the house that is the foundation of birth—the hollow of the *mūlādhāra*—those born from the lotus-eyes of Sadāśiva become submissive by means of half a million [repetitions];
through a hundred thousand, one attains the eternal abode. (72)
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and having bid farewell to the beloved of the Enemy of Tripura with firm devotion,
the practitioner of mantra, with a concentrated mind, should thereafter dismiss Svāhā’s Lord.
In the daily *anuhoṃma* accompanied by the ritual strewn grass (*paristaraṇa*), the wise practitioner should not burn the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*);
however, in the occasional (*naimittika*) homa, the mantra-master should burn both the enclosing sticks and the strewn grass.

Then, having worshipped the Goddess in the Sudhākara [mandala], and having bowed down with dances, songs, and hymns of praise, the wise practitioner should perform the ritual dismissal (udvāsya) with the root mantra and offer oblations with *kādambarī* [liquor] as instructed by the Guru. 75.

Having emerged from the interior of the house that is the womb, the unborn-faced one speaks with a livelihood exhausted by mere wandering; bound by the *Śakti-tantra* and holding a rosary of beads, he recites the mantra arising from his own power.
With each step, there is the bliss of the inner hope; the immutable *liṅga* stands victorious, eternally before him through constant recitation. 76.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Homa," in the *Tnipurāsārasamuccaya* composed by the venerable Nāgabhaṭṭa.

By means of the *ātman* situated within the triangle located inside the "Goat-Face"—the *brahmarandhra* residing at the *mūlādhāra*—through its repeated encircling with a subtle flame in the form of light, the mantra speaks—that is, brings about the realization of—that particular light which resides above the *liṅga*, facing the western direction yet facing all directions, at every step and for each substance situated upon the *liṅga*. Of what nature is this mantra?

Skilled in the Śaktitantras, likewise equipped with a thread and a rosary—meaning possessed of the garland of letters from *a* to *kṣa* which takes the form of a thread—one thus becomes the eternal reciter of the Cintāmaṇi. (57–76)
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya* composed by the venerable Govindācārya.
